topics.label: 8 hours of sleep
topics.blurb: Eight hours a night, same bedtime and wake time every day, including weekends.

topics.label: Morning sunlight
topics.blurb: 10–20 minutes outside within an hour of waking, no sunglasses (never look at the sun). Longer on cloudy days.

topics.label: Floss & brush
topics.blurb: Brush twice a day for two minutes, floss once.

topics.label: Water, 1 gallon
topics.blurb: About a gallon (3.8 L) through the day. That is above the usual guidance of about 2.7–3.7 L of total water from all food and drink, so spread it out and add electrolytes on sweaty days.

topics.label: 10,000 steps a day
topics.blurb: Walk. Every day. The single cheapest longevity habit with a clear dose-response curve.

topics.label: Sauna
topics.blurb: Regular heat exposure, roughly 20 minutes at 80°C+, ideally 4–7 sessions a week.

topics.label: Wim Hof breathing
topics.blurb: Rounds of deep cyclic breathing followed by breath holds. Sit or lie down, never in water or while driving.

topics.label: Dr. Greger's Daily Dozen foods
topics.blurb: Greger's checklist: beans, berries, other fruit, cruciferous veg, greens, other veg, flaxseed, nuts & seeds, herbs & spices, whole grains, water, exercise. Evidence below is for its main food groups.

topics.label: Apple cider vinegar
topics.blurb: About 1 tablespoon diluted in water with a meal. Rinse after; it is hard on tooth enamel.

topics.label: Complete protein
topics.blurb: Get enough complete protein, meaning all nine essential amino acids: eggs, fish, meat, dairy, soy, quinoa, or plant proteins combined (beans + rice). Around 1.6 g per kg of body weight a day is where muscle gains level off in the research.

topics.label: 20 minutes of stretching
topics.blurb: Twenty minutes a day of static or dynamic stretching, hitting hips, hamstrings, chest and shoulders.

topics.label: Creatine monohydrate
topics.blurb: Blueprint: 2.5 g in the Longevity Mix plus 5 g on its own.

topics.label: Collagen peptides
topics.blurb: Blueprint: collagen peptides at breakfast and mid-morning.

topics.label: Omega-3 (EPA/DHA)
topics.blurb: Blueprint: EPA/DHA softgels.

topics.label: Vitamin D3
topics.blurb: Blueprint: 2,000 IU in the Essential Capsules.

topics.label: Vitamin B12
topics.blurb: Blueprint: 125 mcg methylcobalamin in the Essential Capsules.

topics.label: B vitamins & folate
topics.blurb: Blueprint: B1, B2, B3, B5, B6, biotin and methylfolate in the Essential Capsules.

topics.label: Vitamin C
topics.blurb: Blueprint: in the Longevity Mix.

topics.label: Vitamin E

topics.label: Vitamin K1 + K2
topics.blurb: Blueprint: K1, K2 MK-4 and K2 MK-7 in the Advanced Antioxidants softgel.

topics.label: Magnesium
topics.blurb: Blueprint: in the Longevity Mix.

topics.blurb: Blueprint: 15 mg zinc bisglycinate in the Essential Capsules. Copper is my addition: long-term zinc without copper can cause copper deficiency.

topics.label: Selenium
topics.blurb: Blueprint: 28 mcg selenomethionine in the Essential Capsules.

topics.label: Iodine
topics.blurb: Blueprint: 200 mcg in the Essential Capsules.

topics.label: Calcium & manganese

topics.label: Boron

topics.blurb: Blueprint: in the Longevity Mix.

topics.blurb: Blueprint: in the Essential Capsules.

topics.blurb: Blueprint: 200 mg broccoli seed extract (20 mg glucoraphanin) in the Essential Capsules.

topics.blurb: My addition; not in the Blueprint stack.

topics.label: Fenugreek
topics.blurb: My addition; not in the Blueprint stack.

topics.blurb: My addition; not in the Blueprint stack. Take with black pepper and fat for absorption.

topics.label: Leg day
topics.blurb: Squats, lunges, deadlifts, step-ups. Once a week, hard.

topics.label: Arms & back day
topics.blurb: Rows, pull-ups, curls, presses.

topics.label: Full-body workout
topics.blurb: One session that hits everything.

topics.label: Long run, 5K+
topics.blurb: One easy long run a week of at least 5 km.

topics.label: 7 hours of Zone 2
topics.blurb: Seven hours a week of easy, conversational cardio (about 60–70% of max heart rate): you can talk, but not sing.

topics.label: Zone 5 training (VO2 max)
topics.blurb: One session a week of near-max intervals. The best-studied version is the Norwegian 4×4 method from NTNU: after a warm-up, 4 minutes at 90–95% of max heart rate, then 3 minutes of easy recovery, repeated 4 times (about 40 minutes in all). It is the protocol most consistently shown to raise VO2 max.

topics.label: Sprints
topics.blurb: One sprint session a week: 4–8 all-out efforts of 10–30 seconds with full recovery between.

topics.label: Social time
topics.blurb: Real time with friends or family, in person, every week.

topics.label: Time in nature
topics.blurb: About two hours a week in parks, forests, beaches or trails. It can be split up across the week.

topics.label: Fish
topics.blurb: Fatty fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel) once or twice a week.

topics.label: Red meat
topics.blurb: Unprocessed, once a week. The benefit lives in moderation.

topics.label: Liver & organ meat
topics.blurb: A small serving once a week; more than that risks too much vitamin A.

topics.label: A walk in the woods once a week
topics.blurb: Spend a few unhurried hours in a forest or large park once a week, aiming for 2+ hours of nature time across the week. Recommended by Dr. Greger: Greger: natural killer cell activity stays up about a week after a forest visit, so walking in the woods once a week (or a forest day trip even monthly) may keep anticancer immune activity elevated.

topics.label: Mushrooms at least a few times a week
topics.blurb: Work cooked mushrooms (button, shiitake, oyster) into at least three meals a week; always cook them rather than eating raw. Recommended by Dr. Greger: Greger highlights that eating mushrooms more than twice a week (Singapore) or three or more times a week (Japan) was linked to roughly half the odds of mild cognitive impairment and lower dementia risk; he also suggests a cup of white button mushrooms a day.

topics.label: A handful of whole nuts most days of the week
topics.blurb: Eat a small handful (~28 g) of unsalted whole nuts at least 3-5 days a week; this is already covered if you hit the Daily Dozen nut serving. Recommended by Dr. Greger: Greger (quoting the researchers he covers): whole raw or chopped nuts, not nut butters, at least three times a week; his nuts topic page cites a handful five or more days a week for about two extra years of life.

topics.label: Brown, black or red rice at least once a week
topics.blurb: Swap white rice for brown, black or red rice at least once a week, cooked in plenty of water and drained to cut arsenic, and rotate in other whole grains. Recommended by Dr. Greger: Greger highlights the Adventist finding that brown rice just once a week or more was tied to 40% fewer colorectal polyps, and says he cooks red, black or purple rice with lentils instead of white rice.

topics.label: Algae-based DHA two or three times a week
topics.blurb: If you don't take algae omega-3 daily, a capsule (~250-500 mg DHA/EPA) two or three times a week is a low-effort way to keep levels up. Recommended by Mic the Vegan: Mic the Vegan: get ALA from chia, flax and walnuts, or take an algae-based DHA supplement two or three times a week, as many plant-based doctors suggest.

topics.label: Long run, 10K+
topics.blurb: Once a month, go long: 10 km or more.

topics.label: Threshold session
topics.blurb: Once a month, one session at your limit: 20–30 minutes at lactate threshold (comfortably hard, about 8/10 effort), or a 20-minute time trial to re-test your threshold and track progress.

topics.label: Cold plunge
topics.blurb: Cold-water immersion, around 10–15°C for 2–5 minutes. Not right after strength training: it can blunt muscle growth.

topics.label: 24-hour fast
topics.blurb: Once a month: dinner to dinner, water, tea and black coffee only. Skip it if you are on insulin or glucose-lowering drugs without a doctor's plan.

topics.label: Four Brazil nuts, once a month
topics.blurb: Eat about four Brazil nuts (~20 g) in one sitting once a month; don't make it a daily habit because selenium adds up fast. Recommended by Dr. Greger and Mic the Vegan: Greger: eat four Brazil nuts once a month for a possible month-long LDL drop without nearing the selenium limit. Mic the Vegan: about four nuts every few weeks, which likely also covers selenium.

topics.label: Dentist cleaning
topics.blurb: A professional cleaning and checkup at least once a year (most dentists suggest every six months).

topics.label: Parasite cleanse
topics.blurb: Once a year. The options: ivermectin (prescription), pyrantel pamoate (over the counter in the US), or papaya seeds with pumpkin seeds. The studies below were all done in people with confirmed infections, so a stool test first (ova & parasites) tells you whether there's anything to treat. Ask a doctor before taking ivermectin.

topics.label: Annual blood test
topics.blurb: Once a year at minimum (Bryan Johnson draws blood every 3–6 months). The markers below are the ones in his Blueprint baseline panel.

topics.label: 3–5 day fast
topics.blurb: Once a year, water-only or a fasting-mimicking diet. Do it with medical supervision: electrolytes matter, and breaking it (refeeding) needs care.

studies.title: Sleep duration and all-cause mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of prospective studies
studies.authors: Cappuccio FP, D'Elia L, Strazzullo P, et al.
studies.summary: Pooled 16 prospective studies (27 cohorts, about 1.38 million adults, 112,566 deaths) relating self-reported sleep duration to all-cause mortality. Short sleep (usually under 6-7 hours) carried a 12% higher risk of death (RR 1.12) and long sleep (usually over 8-9 hours) a 30% higher risk (RR 1.30). Sleep was self-reported and long sleep may partly mark existing illness, so the takeaway is a U-shaped curve with the sweet spot around 7-8 hours, not that more is always better.
studies.quote: short duration of sleep was associated with a greater risk of death (RR: 1.12; 95% CI 1.06 to 1.18; P < 0.01)

studies.title: Sleep regularity is a stronger predictor of mortality risk than sleep duration: A prospective cohort study
studies.authors: Windred DP, Burns AC, Lane JM, et al.
studies.summary: Prospective UK Biobank cohort of 60,977 adults whose sleep timing was measured by wrist accelerometer for a week and who were followed for about 6.3 years. People in the more regular sleep-timing quintiles had a 20-48% lower risk of all-cause death than the least regular quintile, and regularity predicted mortality better than duration did. It is observational and based on one week of data in older UK adults, but it suggests keeping consistent bed and wake times matters as much as the hours.
studies.quote: Higher sleep regularity was associated with a 20%-48% lower risk of all-cause mortality

studies.title: Recommended Amount of Sleep for a Healthy Adult: A Joint Consensus Statement of the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and Sleep Research Society
studies.authors: Watson NF, Badr MS, Belenky G, et al.
studies.summary: A 15-member AASM and Sleep Research Society expert panel used a modified RAND Appropriateness Method to review the evidence and vote on how much sleep adults need. The panel concluded that adults should sleep 7 or more hours per night on a regular basis, and that habitually sleeping under 7 hours is linked to weight gain, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, depression, impaired immunity and more errors. It is expert consensus rather than new data, and it notes that more than 9 hours may help young adults or people recovering from sleep debt or illness but is otherwise uncertain.
studies.quote: developed a consensus recommendation for the amount of sleep needed to promote optimal health in adults

studies.title: Time spent in outdoor light is associated with mood, sleep, and circadian rhythm-related outcomes: A cross-sectional and longitudinal study in over 400,000 UK Biobank participants
studies.authors: Burns AC, Saxena R, Vetter C, et al.
studies.summary: Cross-sectional and longitudinal analysis of about 400,000 UK Biobank adults who reported how much daylight time they spent outdoors. Each extra hour outdoors per day was tied to lower odds of depression and antidepressant use, fewer insomnia symptoms, less tiredness, and easier waking (OR about 1.46-1.49 for ease of getting up). Outdoor time was self-reported and light intensity at the eye was not measured, so this shows association, not proof that morning light specifically causes the benefit.
studies.quote: low daytime light exposure is an important environmental risk factor for mood, sleep, and circadian-related outcomes

studies.title: Brighter nights and darker days predict higher mortality risk: A prospective analysis of personal light exposure in >88,000 individuals
studies.authors: Windred DP, Burns AC, Lane JM, et al.
studies.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
studies.summary: Prospective UK Biobank study of 88,905 adults who wore a wrist light sensor for one week, followed for about 8 years (3,750 deaths). Those with the brightest daytime light had up to 17-34% lower all-cause mortality (aHR 0.66-0.83 for the top decile), while bright light at night raised risk by up to 21-34%. It is observational with one week of measurement, but it supports the practical rule: bright days, dark nights.
studies.quote: Minimizing night light, maximizing day light, and keeping regular light-dark patterns that enhance circadian rhythms may promote cardiometabolic health and longevity

studies.title: Effects of light on human circadian rhythms, sleep and mood
studies.authors: Blume C, Garbazza C, Spitschan M
studies.journal: Somnologie : Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin = Somnology : sleep research and sleep medicine
studies.summary: Narrative review of how light reaches the brain's master clock (the suprachiasmatic nucleus) via the retina and how light timing shapes circadian rhythms, sleep and mood. Light is the main signal that sets the body clock; morning light advances it, evening and night light delays it and suppresses melatonin, and bright light therapy is an effective low-risk treatment for some sleep and mood problems. This is a mechanism review rather than an outcome trial, so it explains why morning light should help more than it quantifies how much.
studies.quote: light can also be used as an effective and noninvasive therapeutic option with little to no side effects, to improve sleep,mood and general well-being

studies.title: Home use of interdental cleaning devices, in addition to toothbrushing, for preventing and controlling periodontal diseases and dental caries
studies.authors: Worthington HV, MacDonald L, Poklepovic Pericic T, et al.
studies.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
studies.summary: Cochrane review of 35 randomized trials (3,929 adults) comparing toothbrushing plus floss, interdental brushes, sticks or water irrigators against toothbrushing alone. Flossing on top of brushing modestly reduced gingivitis at 1, 3 and 6 months (SMD -0.58 at one month), and interdental brushes looked somewhat better than floss. The evidence was low to very low certainty and short term, with no trials measuring cavities between teeth, so the benefit is real but smaller and less proven than often claimed.
studies.quote: Using floss or interdental brushes in addition to toothbrushing may reduce gingivitis or plaque, or both, more than toothbrushing alone

studies.title: Improved oral hygiene care attenuates the cardiovascular risk of oral health disease: a population-based study from Korea
studies.authors: Park SY, Kim SH, Kang SH, et al.
studies.summary: Korean national cohort of 247,696 healthy adults aged 40+ who had an oral health screening and were followed for a median 9.5 years (14,893 major cardiovascular events). Each additional daily toothbrushing was associated with a 9% lower risk of cardiovascular events, and yearly professional cleaning with a 14% lower risk. It is observational and brushing habits travel with other healthy behaviors, so it supports but does not prove that oral hygiene protects the heart.
studies.quote: Performing one more tooth brushing a day was associated with a 9% significantly lower risk of cardiovascular events after multivariable adjustment

studies.title: Periodontal health, cognitive decline, and dementia: A systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal studies
studies.authors: Asher S, Stephen R, Mäntylä P, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 47 longitudinal studies on periodontal health (gum disease, tooth loss, bone loss) and later cognitive decline or dementia. Poor periodontal health was linked to 23% higher odds of cognitive decline (OR 1.23) and 21% higher risk of dementia (HR 1.21). The authors rate the evidence as low quality and note reverse causation is likely part of it (declining people stop caring for their teeth), so this is a plausible but unproven link.
studies.quote: Poor periodontal health and tooth loss appear to increase the risk of both cognitive decline and dementia

studies.title: Middle-age high normal serum sodium as a risk factor for accelerated biological aging, chronic diseases, and premature mortality
studies.authors: Dmitrieva NI, Gagarin A, Liu D, et al.
studies.summary: NIH analysis of 15,752 adults from the ARIC cohort enrolled at ages 45-66 and followed for 25 years, using serum sodium as a marker of habitual hydration. Mid-life serum sodium above 142 mmol/L was linked to 39% higher risk of chronic disease (HR 1.39), up to 50% higher odds of being biologically older than chronological age, and above 144 mmol/L to 21% higher premature mortality. Serum sodium is an indirect proxy and no one was told to drink more, so this supports staying well hydrated, not a specific target like a gallon a day.
studies.quote: have increased risk to be biologically older, develop chronic diseases and die at younger age

studies.title: Treatment effect, adherence, and safety of high fluid intake for the prevention of incident and recurrent kidney stones: a systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Cheungpasitporn W, Rossetti S, Friend K, et al.
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of 9 studies (2 RCTs with 269 patients, 7 observational studies with about 274,000 people) comparing high versus low fluid intake for kidney stone prevention. High fluid intake cut the risk of kidney stones by roughly half to 60% (RR 0.40 in RCTs, 0.49 in observational studies), including recurrent stones. This is the best-established hard benefit of drinking more water, and it matters most for people prone to stones; safety data were thin.
studies.quote: This analysis demonstrated a significantly reduced risk of incident kidney stones among individuals with high fluid consumption

studies.title: Water, hydration, and health
studies.authors: Popkin BM, D'Anci KE, Rosenberg IH
studies.summary: Narrative review in Nutrition Reviews of water intake, hydration physiology, and effects on energy intake, weight, kidney function, physical and cognitive performance. It reports that mild dehydration impairs mood and performance and that replacing sugary drinks with water reduces calorie intake, while noting that US guidance (the NASEM Adequate Intake of about 3.7 L/day for men and 2.7 L/day for women) counts total water including roughly 20% from food. There are no long-term randomized trials of higher water intake, and 1 gallon (about 3.8 L) of plain water per day exceeds typical guidance for most people unless they are large, very active or in heat; very high intake can rarely cause hyponatremia.
studies.quote: there are also few longer-term systematic interventions and no published randomized, controlled longer-term trials

studies.title: Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts
studies.authors: Paluch AE, Bajpai S, Bassett DR, et al.
studies.summary: Participant-level meta-analysis of 15 cohorts covering 47,471 adults followed for a median of 7.1 years with device-measured steps. Compared with the lowest quartile (about 3,500 steps/day), the highest quartile (about 10,900 steps/day) had a 53% lower risk of death (HR 0.47). Benefits levelled off around 6,000-8,000 steps/day in adults 60 and older and 8,000-10,000 in younger adults, so 10,000 is not a magic threshold.
studies.quote: Taking more steps per day was associated with a progressively lower risk of all-cause mortality, up to a level that varied by age.

studies.title: The association between daily step count and all-cause and cardiovascular mortality: a meta-analysis
studies.authors: Banach M, Lewek J, Surma S, et al.
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of 17 cohort studies with 226,889 participants followed for a median of 7.1 years. Each extra 1,000 steps/day was associated with a 15% lower risk of all-cause death, and each extra 500 steps/day with a 7% lower risk of cardiovascular death. The data are observational, so sicker people walking less (reverse causation) may inflate the benefit, but no upper limit of benefit was found.
studies.quote: A 1000-step increment was associated with a 15% decreased risk of all-cause mortality

studies.title: Daily steps and health outcomes in adults: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis
studies.authors: Ding D, Nguyen B, Nau T, et al.
studies.summary: Systematic review of 57 prospective studies (31 in meta-analyses) linking device-measured steps to mortality, heart disease, cancer, diabetes, dementia, depression and falls. Compared with 2,000 steps/day, 7,000 steps/day was associated with 47% lower all-cause mortality, 25% lower cardiovascular disease incidence and 38% lower dementia risk. Most gains came by 5,000-7,000 steps/day, and several outcomes rested on only two to four studies.
studies.quote: 7000 steps per day is associated with clinically meaningful improvements in health outcomes and might be a more realistic and achievable target for some

studies.title: Association between sauna bathing and fatal cardiovascular and all-cause mortality events
studies.authors: Laukkanen T, Khan H, Zaccardi F, Laukkanen JA
studies.summary: Prospective cohort of 2,315 middle-aged Finnish men (Kuopio study) followed for a median of 20.7 years. Men using the sauna 4-7 times a week had a 63% lower risk of sudden cardiac death (HR 0.37) than once-a-week users, with similar trends for heart disease and all-cause death. It is one observational cohort of men only, and frequent sauna use may partly mark better health, wealth and leisure time.
studies.quote: Increased frequency of sauna bathing is associated with a reduced risk of SCD, CHD, CVD, and all-cause mortality.

studies.title: Sauna bathing is inversely associated with dementia and Alzheimer's disease in middle-aged Finnish men
studies.authors: Laukkanen T, Kunutsor S, Kauhanen J, Laukkanen JA
studies.summary: Same Kuopio cohort of 2,315 men aged 42-60, followed about 20 years for dementia and Alzheimer's diagnoses. Compared with once a week, sauna use 4-7 times a week was associated with a 66% lower dementia risk (HR 0.34) and 65% lower Alzheimer's risk. Case numbers in the top group were small and the cohort is all male and Finnish, so this is a hypothesis, not proof.
studies.quote: moderate to high frequency of sauna bathing was associated with lowered risks of dementia and Alzheimer's disease

studies.title: Cardiovascular and Other Health Benefits of Sauna Bathing: A Review of the Evidence
studies.authors: Laukkanen JA, Laukkanen T, Kunutsor SK
studies.summary: Narrative review of observational, experimental and interventional studies on Finnish sauna bathing and health. It reports links to lower blood pressure, cardiovascular disease, dementia and mortality, with plausible mechanisms such as better endothelial function and reduced arterial stiffness. It is written largely by the same group that produced the main cohort data, and randomized evidence on hard outcomes is lacking.
studies.quote: regular sauna bathing may improve cardiovascular function via improved endothelium-dependent dilatation, reduced arterial stiffness, modulation of the autonomic nervous system

studies.title: Voluntary activation of the sympathetic nervous system and attenuation of the innate immune response in humans
studies.authors: Kox M, van Eijk LT, Zwaag J, et al.
studies.journal: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A
studies.summary: Small randomized trial in which 12 healthy men trained 10 days in Wim Hof-style breathing, meditation and cold exposure, versus 12 untrained controls, before an injection of bacterial endotoxin. The trained group had sharply higher adrenaline, higher anti-inflammatory IL-10, lower inflammatory cytokines and fewer flu-like symptoms. With 24 young men, a lab endotoxin model and no long-term outcomes, it shows a physiological effect, not a health benefit in daily life.
studies.quote: voluntary activation of the sympathetic nervous system results in epinephrine release and subsequent suppression of the innate immune response in humans in vivo

studies.title: Effect of breathwork on stress and mental health: A meta-analysis of randomised-controlled trials
studies.authors: Fincham GW, Strauss C, Montero-Marin J, Cavanagh K
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (785 adults) on breathwork of many styles versus non-breathwork controls, with secondary analyses on anxiety and depression. Breathwork produced a small-to-medium reduction in self-reported stress (g = -0.35), with similar effects on anxiety and depressive symptoms. Most trials had moderate risk of bias and few tested Wim Hof breathing specifically, and the authors warn against hype outrunning evidence.
studies.quote: we urge caution and advocate for nuanced research approaches with low risk-of-bias study designs to avoid a miscalibration between hype and evidence

studies.title: Does the Wim Hof Method have a beneficial impact on physiological and psychological outcomes in healthy and non-healthy participants? A systematic review
studies.authors: Almahayni O, Hammond L
studies.summary: Systematic review of studies on the Wim Hof Method or its breathing component, finding only nine papers from eight trials. The most consistent signal was an anti-inflammatory effect via raised adrenaline; effects on exercise performance and breathing parameters were mixed. The evidence base is tiny and heterogeneous, so claims beyond short-term inflammation changes are not well supported.
studies.quote: the findings of this review show promising use of WHM in the inflammatory response category

studies.title: Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality-a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
studies.authors: Aune D, Giovannucci E, Boffetta P, et al.
studies.summary: Dose-response meta-analysis of 95 prospective studies on fruit and vegetable intake and heart disease, cancer and death. Each 200 g/day was associated with 10% lower all-cause mortality, with risk falling up to about 800 g/day (roughly 10 servings). The studies are observational and produce eaters tend to have healthier lifestyles, though the dose-response pattern is consistent.
studies.quote: Fruit and vegetable intakes were associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer and all-cause mortality.

studies.title: Whole grain consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all cause and cause specific mortality: systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
studies.authors: Aune D, Keum N, Giovannucci E, et al.
studies.summary: Dose-response meta-analysis of 45 prospective studies on whole grain intake. Each 90 g/day (about three servings) was associated with 19% lower coronary heart disease risk and 17% lower all-cause mortality. Refined grains and white rice showed little association, and residual confounding by overall healthy diet cannot be ruled out.
studies.quote: whole grain intake is associated with a reduced risk of coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease, and total cancer, and mortality from all causes

studies.title: Nut consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer, all-cause and cause-specific mortality: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
studies.authors: Aune D, Keum N, Giovannucci E, et al.
studies.summary: Dose-response meta-analysis of 20 prospective studies on nut intake and disease and death. A daily handful (28 g) was associated with 29% lower coronary heart disease risk and 22% lower all-cause mortality. These are observational associations for one component of the Daily Dozen; no trial has tested Greger's full checklist on hard outcomes.
studies.quote: Higher nut intake is associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality

studies.title: The effect of apple cider vinegar on lipid profiles and glycemic parameters: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials
studies.authors: Hadi A, Pourmasoumi M, Najafgholizadeh A, et al.
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of nine clinical trials (10 arms) testing apple cider vinegar for at least two weeks. It lowered total cholesterol by about 6 mg/dL, fasting glucose by about 8 mg/dL and HbA1c by 0.5 points, with no effect on LDL, HDL, insulin or insulin resistance. Trials were small and highly heterogeneous, and effects mostly appeared in people with type 2 diabetes.
studies.quote: We found a significant favorable effect of ACV consumption on FPG and blood lipid levels.

studies.title: Effects of apple cider vinegar on glycemic control and insulin sensitivity in patients with type 2 diabetes: A GRADE-assessed systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of controlled clinical trials
studies.authors: Arjmandfard D, Behzadi M, Sohrabi Z, et al.
studies.summary: Dose-response meta-analysis of seven controlled trials of apple cider vinegar in people with type 2 diabetes. Vinegar lowered fasting blood sugar by about 22 mg/dL and HbA1c by about 1.5 points, with no change in insulin resistance. Only seven small trials were pooled, and the effects apply to diabetics, not healthy people.
studies.quote: ACV had positive effects on FBS and HbA1c in T2DM patients.

studies.title: Vinegar Consumption and Health: An Umbrella Review of Meta-Analyses of Randomized Controlled Trials
studies.authors: Shahmohammadi F, Khosroshahi RA, Derakhshanian H, et al.
studies.summary: Umbrella review re-analysing 10 meta-analyses covering 38 trials of vinegar on cardiometabolic markers. Vinegar modestly improved fasting glucose (-9.4 mg/dL), HbA1c (-0.7%), body weight (-1.06 kg) and systolic blood pressure (-2.9 mmHg), with no effect on LDL, HDL, triglycerides, BMI or waist size. The effects are small, and a widely publicized 2024 BMJ Nutrition trial of apple cider vinegar for weight loss was retracted in 2025, so big weight-loss claims are unsupported.
studies.quote: Vinegar intake was associated with statistically significant improvements in FBG (moderate certainty), PPG (moderate certainty), HbA1c (moderate certainty)

studies.title: A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults
studies.authors: Morton RW, Murphy KT, McKellar SR, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 49 randomized trials (1,863 participants) of protein supplementation during at least 6 weeks of resistance training. Protein added about 2.49 kg to one-rep-max strength and 0.30 kg of fat-free mass, with no further gains beyond a total intake of about 1.62 g/kg/day. The effects are modest, shrink with age, and depend on actually doing resistance training.
studies.quote: Dietary protein supplementation significantly enhanced changes in muscle strength and size during prolonged RET in healthy adults.

studies.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults
studies.authors: Nunes EA, Colenso-Semple L, McKellar SR, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle
studies.summary: This meta-analysis of 74 randomized trials in healthy non-obese adults tested whether eating more daily protein increases lean mass, strength and physical function. More protein produced small gains in lean mass during resistance training (SMD 0.22), significant in adults 65+ at 1.2-1.59 g/kg/day and in younger adults at 1.6 g/kg/day or more. Effects on strength were slight and on physical function minimal, so protein is a helper to training, not a substitute.
studies.quote: increasing daily protein ingestion results in small additional gains in LBM and lower body muscle strength gains in healthy adults enrolled in resistance exercise training

studies.title: Dose-response relationship between protein intake and muscle mass increase: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
studies.authors: Tagawa R, Watanabe D, Ito K, et al.
studies.summary: This dose-response meta-analysis included 105 articles (5,402 participants) from randomized trials of protein intake and lean body mass. Each extra 0.1 g/kg/day of protein was linked to 0.39 kg more lean mass below a total intake of 1.3 g/kg/day, but only 0.12 kg above it. The practical takeaway is diminishing returns: raising protein matters most for people starting from low intake.
studies.quote: These findings suggest that slightly increasing current protein intake for several months

studies.title: Chronic effects of stretching on range of motion with consideration of potential moderating variables: A systematic review with meta-analysis
studies.authors: Konrad A, Alizadeh S, Daneshjoo A, Anvar SH, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of Sport and Health Science
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 77 studies (186 effect sizes) on regular stretch training in healthy people. Stretching reliably increased range of motion with a moderate effect (effect size about 1.0), with static and PNF stretching beating dynamic stretching. Volume, intensity and frequency did not clearly change the gains, so 20 minutes a day is likely more than needed for flexibility alone.
studies.quote: stretch training can increase ROM with a moderate effect compared to the controls

studies.title: Stretching is Superior to Brisk Walking for Reducing Blood Pressure in People With High-Normal Blood Pressure or Stage I Hypertension
studies.authors: Ko J, Deprez D, Shaw K, Alcorn J, et al.
studies.summary: Forty adults (mean age 62) with high-normal blood pressure or stage 1 hypertension were randomized to 30 minutes of stretching or brisk walking, five days a week for eight weeks. Stretching lowered sitting systolic pressure from 146 to 140 mmHg and reduced other measures more than walking did. It is a single small trial, and walking's lack of effect is unusual, so treat this as promising rather than settled.
studies.quote: An 8-week stretching program was superior to brisk walking for reducing blood pressure in individuals with high-normal blood pressure or stage 1 hypertension.

studies.title: The effectiveness of exercise interventions to prevent sports injuries: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
studies.authors: Lauersen JB, Bertelsen DM, Andersen LB
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 25 randomized trials with 26,610 participants and 3,464 injuries, comparing stretching, strength, balance and combined programs for injury prevention. Stretching showed no protective effect (RR 0.96, confidence interval crossing 1), while strength training cut injuries to under a third (RR 0.32). Stretch for range of motion and how it feels, but do not count on it to prevent injuries; strength work does that better.
studies.quote: consistently favourable estimates were obtained for all injury prevention measures except for stretching

studies.title: Effect of creatine supplementation during resistance training on lean tissue mass and muscular strength in older adults: a meta-analysis
studies.authors: Chilibeck PD, Kaviani M, Candow DG, et al.
studies.journal: Open Access Journal of Sports Medicine
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 22 randomized trials (721 adults, mean age 57-70) comparing creatine with placebo during 7-52 weeks of resistance training. Creatine added about 1.4 kg more lean mass (95% CI 0.97-1.76 kg) and modestly larger gains in chest press and leg press strength. The benefit depends on lifting at the same time, and the strength effects are small to moderate.
studies.quote: creatine supplementation increases lean tissue mass and upper and lower body muscular strength during resistance training of older adults

studies.title: Effects of creatine supplementation on cognitive function of healthy individuals: A systematic review of randomized controlled trials
studies.authors: Avgerinos KI, Spyrou N, Bougioukas KI, et al.
studies.summary: This systematic review looked at 6 randomized trials (281 healthy people) testing oral creatine on cognitive tests. Short-term memory and reasoning may improve, while results for attention, executive function, and reaction time were conflicting and young people showed no change. The evidence base is small, so the cognitive case is promising but unproven, with the best signal in older, stressed, or vegetarian people.
studies.quote: Oral creatine administration may improve short-term memory and intelligence/reasoning of healthy individuals but its effect on other cognitive domains remains unclear

studies.title: International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine
studies.authors: Kreider RB, Kalman DS, Antonio J, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition
studies.summary: This position stand from the International Society of Sports Nutrition reviews the research on creatine for performance, recovery, aging, and clinical uses. It concludes creatine reliably improves high-intensity exercise performance and training adaptations, and that doses up to 30 g/day for 5 years have been safe in healthy people. It is a consensus review by an industry-adjacent society rather than a fresh meta-analysis, but the core guidance of about 3-5 g/day is well supported.
studies.quote: short and long-term supplementation (up to 30 g/day for 5 years) is safe and well-tolerated in healthy individuals

studies.title: Effects of Oral Collagen for Skin Anti-Aging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Pu SY, Huang YL, Pu CM, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 26 randomized trials (1,721 participants) of hydrolyzed collagen versus placebo for skin. Collagen significantly improved skin hydration and elasticity (both p < 0.00001), with hydration effects varying by collagen source and duration. The authors flag bias in many included trials, several of which are industry-funded, so the effect is real-looking but likely overstated.
studies.quote: the findings suggest that HC supplementation can have positive effects on skin health, but further large-scale randomized control trials are necessary

studies.title: The effects of collagen peptide supplementation on body composition, collagen synthesis, and recovery from joint injury and exercise: a systematic review
studies.authors: Khatri M, Naughton RJ, Clifford T, et al.
studies.summary: This systematic review covered 15 randomized trials of collagen peptides combined with exercise, mostly in recreational athletes. The clearest benefit was improved joint function and less joint pain, with 15 g/day raising collagen synthesis but not muscle protein synthesis compared with higher-quality protein. Collagen is not a substitute for regular protein for muscle, and the trials were small.
studies.quote: The results indicated that COL is most beneficial in improving joint functionality and reducing joint pain

studies.title: Effect of collagen supplementation on knee osteoarthritis: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
studies.authors: Simental-Mendía M, Ortega-Mata D, Acosta-Olivo CA, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 11 randomized trials (870 people with knee osteoarthritis) of oral collagen-based supplements versus placebo. Collagen improved pain scores (mean difference -13.6) and function scores (mean difference -6.5). Heterogeneity was very high (I2 75-88%) and the collagen products varied, so the size of the benefit is uncertain.
studies.quote: The results of this meta-analysis suggest that oral collagen administration relieves OA symptoms

studies.title: Marine Omega-3 Supplementation and Cardiovascular Disease: An Updated Meta-Analysis of 13 Randomized Controlled Trials Involving 127 477 Participants
studies.authors: Hu Y, Hu FB, Manson JE
studies.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 13 randomized trials (127,477 participants, mean 5 years) of marine omega-3 supplements. Even excluding REDUCE-IT, omega-3 lowered heart attack risk by about 8% (RR 0.92) and cardiovascular death by about 7% (RR 0.93), with larger doses linked to larger reductions. The relative reductions are small, so the absolute benefit for a healthy person is modest.
studies.quote: Marine omega-3 supplementation lowers risk for myocardial infarction, CHD death, total CHD, CVD death, and total CVD, even after exclusion of REDUCE-IT

studies.title: Omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
studies.authors: Abdelhamid AS, Brown TJ, Brainard JS, et al.
studies.summary: This Cochrane review analyzed 86 randomized trials (162,796 participants) lasting at least a year. Long-chain omega-3 had little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97) or total cardiovascular events (RR 0.96), may slightly reduce coronary events (NNT 167), and cut triglycerides by about 15%. It is the most sober read of the evidence: fish oil is a triglyceride tool, not a broad heart-protection pill.
studies.quote: increasing LCn3 slightly reduces risk of coronary heart disease mortality and events, and reduces serum triglycerides

studies.title: Omega-3 Fatty Acids for the Management of Hypertriglyceridemia: A Science Advisory From the American Heart Association
studies.authors: Skulas-Ray AC, Wilson PWF, Harris WS, et al.
studies.summary: This American Heart Association science advisory reviews trial data on prescription-strength omega-3 (about 4 g/day EPA+DHA or EPA alone) for high triglycerides. At 4 g/day, omega-3 lowers very high triglycerides by 30% or more, and EPA-only cut major cardiovascular events by 25% in REDUCE-IT among statin-treated high-risk patients. These results apply to pharmacological doses in people with high triglycerides, not to a typical 1 g fish oil capsule.
studies.quote: In treatment of very high triglycerides with 4 g/d, EPA+DHA agents reduce triglycerides by ≥30%

studies.title: Vitamin D Supplements and Prevention of Cancer and Cardiovascular Disease
studies.authors: Manson JE, Cook NR, Lee IM, et al.
studies.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
studies.summary: The VITAL trial randomized 25,871 US adults aged 50+ (men) or 55+ (women) to 2,000 IU/day vitamin D3 or placebo, following them for a median of 5.3 years. Vitamin D3 did not lower invasive cancer (HR 0.96) or major cardiovascular events (HR 0.97), and all-cause mortality was unchanged (HR 0.99), though cancer death showed a non-significant trend (HR 0.83). Participants were mostly not vitamin D deficient, so the results argue against routine D3 for disease prevention in replete adults rather than against correcting a deficiency.
studies.quote: Supplementation with vitamin D did not result in a lower incidence of invasive cancer or cardiovascular events than placebo.

studies.title: Vitamin D supplementation to prevent acute respiratory tract infections: systematic review and meta-analysis of individual participant data
studies.authors: Martineau AR, Jolliffe DA, Hooper RL, et al.
studies.summary: This individual-participant-data meta-analysis pooled 25 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials covering 11,321 people aged 0-95. Vitamin D cut the odds of an acute respiratory infection by 12% overall (OR 0.88), and by 70% in people who started out severely deficient (below 25 nmol/L) and took it daily or weekly. Large monthly or yearly bolus doses did not help, so steady daily dosing matters, and the biggest gains go to people who are deficient.
studies.quote: Patients who were very vitamin D deficient and those not receiving bolus doses experienced the most benefit.

studies.title: The D-Health Trial: a randomised controlled trial of the effect of vitamin D on mortality
studies.authors: Neale RE, Baxter C, Romero BD, et al.
studies.summary: D-Health randomized 21,315 Australians aged 60 and older to 60,000 IU of vitamin D3 or placebo once a month for 5 years. Vitamin D did not reduce deaths from any cause (5.3% vs 5.1%; HR 1.04), and exploratory analyses hinted at more cancer deaths. Most participants were not deficient to begin with, so for people with adequate levels, high-dose monthly D3 is not a longevity tool.
studies.quote: Administering vitamin D3 monthly to unscreened older people did not reduce all-cause mortality.

studies.title: Oral vitamin B12 versus intramuscular vitamin B12 for vitamin B12 deficiency
studies.authors: Wang H, Li L, Qin LL, et al.
studies.summary: This Cochrane review found three randomized trials (153 people) comparing oral and intramuscular B12 for deficiency over 3-4 months. High-dose oral B12 (1,000-2,000 mcg/day) raised blood B12 as well as injections did, and cost less. The evidence is low quality because the trials were few and small, and none measured symptoms or quality of life.
studies.quote: Low quality evidence shows oral and IM vitamin B12 having similar effects in terms of normalising serum vitamin B12 levels, but oral treatment costs less.

studies.title: Long-term Metformin Use and Vitamin B12 Deficiency in the Diabetes Prevention Program Outcomes Study
studies.authors: Aroda VR, Edelstein SL, Goldberg RB, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of Clinical Endocrinology and Metabolism
studies.summary: This secondary analysis of the Diabetes Prevention Program followed about 2,000 adults with prediabetes randomized to metformin or placebo, with B12 measured at 5 and 13 years. Each year of metformin use raised the odds of B12 deficiency by 13%, and low or borderline B12 was about twice as common on metformin at 5 years (19.1% vs 9.5%). Anyone on long-term metformin should have B12 checked; the study shows risk, not that routine supplements fix outcomes.
studies.quote: Long-term use of metformin in DPPOS was associated with biochemical B12 deficiency and anemia.

studies.title: How prevalent is vitamin B(12) deficiency among vegetarians?
studies.authors: Pawlak R, Parrott SJ, Raj S, et al.
studies.summary: This literature review pulled 18 studies that measured B12 deficiency in vegetarians and vegans using sensitive markers (methylmalonic acid, holotranscobalamin). Deficiency rates were high across groups, including 11-90% of older adults and 62% of pregnant women, and were higher in vegans than vegetarians. It is a narrative review of varied studies, but the message is consistent: people eating little or no animal food should take B12.
studies.quote: vegetarians develop B12 depletion or deficiency regardless of demographic characteristics, place of residency, age, or type of vegetarian diet

studies.title: Homocysteine-lowering by B vitamins slows the rate of accelerated brain atrophy in mild cognitive impairment: a randomized controlled trial
studies.authors: Smith AD, Smith SM, de Jager CA, et al.
studies.summary: VITACOG was a 2-year randomized, double-blind trial giving 271 adults over 70 with mild cognitive impairment folic acid 0.8 mg, B12 0.5 mg and B6 20 mg daily or placebo, with MRI scans in 168 completers. Brain shrinkage slowed from 1.08% to 0.76% per year, and by 53% in people whose starting homocysteine was above 13 umol/L. The benefit was concentrated in people with high homocysteine, and brain volume is a surrogate; the trial did not show fewer dementia cases.
studies.quote: The accelerated rate of brain atrophy in elderly with mild cognitive impairment can be slowed by treatment with homocysteine-lowering B vitamins.

studies.title: Efficacy of folic acid therapy in primary prevention of stroke among adults with hypertension in China: the CSPPT randomized clinical trial
studies.authors: Huo Y, Li J, Qin X, et al.
studies.summary: The China Stroke Primary Prevention Trial randomized 20,702 adults with high blood pressure to enalapril plus 0.8 mg folic acid or enalapril alone for a median of 4.5 years. Adding folic acid cut first strokes by 21% (2.7% vs 3.4%; HR 0.79). China has no folic acid food fortification, so baseline folate was low; the benefit is unlikely to be as large in countries like the US where flour is fortified.
studies.quote: the combined use of enalapril and folic acid, compared with enalapril alone, significantly reduced the risk of first stroke

studies.title: Homocysteine-lowering interventions for preventing cardiovascular events
studies.authors: Martí-Carvajal AJ, Solà I, Lathyris D, Dayer M
studies.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 15 randomized trials (71,422 people) of B6, folic acid and/or B12 given to lower homocysteine. B vitamins did not reduce heart attacks or deaths, but slightly lowered stroke risk (4.3% vs 5.1%; RR 0.90). Lowering homocysteine with B vitamins is not a heart-attack prevention strategy; the small stroke benefit is the only consistent signal.
studies.quote: there were no differences in effects of homocysteine-lowering interventions in the form of supplements of vitamins B6, B9 or B12

studies.title: Vitamin C for preventing and treating the common cold
studies.authors: Hemilä H, Chalker E
studies.summary: This Cochrane review pooled placebo-controlled trials of at least 0.2 g/day vitamin C, including 29 comparisons with 11,306 people for cold incidence and 31 comparisons for cold duration. Regular use did not prevent colds in the general population (RR 0.97) but shortened colds by 8% in adults and 14% in children, and halved cold risk in people under heavy physical stress such as marathon runners and soldiers. Starting vitamin C only after symptoms begin showed no consistent benefit, so the payoff comes from taking it daily, and it is small.
studies.quote: In adults the duration of colds was reduced by 8% (3% to 12%) and in children by 14% (7% to 21%).

studies.title: Effects of vitamin C supplementation on blood pressure: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
studies.authors: Juraschek SP, Guallar E, Appel LJ, Miller ER
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 29 randomized controlled trials (median 500 mg/day for a median of 8 weeks, 10-120 people each) of oral vitamin C and blood pressure. Vitamin C lowered systolic pressure by 3.84 mm Hg and diastolic by 1.48 mm Hg on average. The trials were small and short, and no long-term trials have shown fewer heart attacks or strokes.
studies.quote: The pooled changes in SBP and DBP were -3.84 mm Hg (95% CI: -5.29, -2.38 mm Hg; P < 0.01) and -1.48 mm Hg

studies.title: Extra Dose of Vitamin C Based on a Daily Supplementation Shortens the Common Cold: A Meta-Analysis of 9 Randomized Controlled Trials
studies.authors: Ran L, Zhao W, Wang J, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis of 9 randomized placebo-controlled trials asked whether an extra dose of vitamin C at the start of a cold helps people who already take it daily. The extra dose shortened colds by about half a day (MD -0.56 days) and reduced time stuck indoors, fever and chills. The effect is small and the pooled trials vary in dose and quality, so it is a modest, low-cost option rather than a cure.
studies.quote: Extra doses of vitamin C could benefit some patients who contract the common cold despite taking daily vitamin C supplements.

studies.title: Vitamin E and the risk of prostate cancer: the Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT)
studies.authors: Klein EA, Thompson IM, Tangen CM, et al.
studies.summary: SELECT randomized 35,533 healthy men (aged 55 or older, or 50 or older for Black men) to 400 IU/day vitamin E, selenium, both, or placebo, with follow-up extended after the supplements were stopped. Men taking vitamin E alone had 17% more prostate cancer than placebo (HR 1.17), about 1.6 extra cases per 1,000 person-years. This is direct trial evidence of harm from a common supplement dose in healthy men.
studies.quote: Dietary supplementation with vitamin E significantly increased the risk of prostate cancer among healthy men.

studies.title: Vitamins E and C in the prevention of cardiovascular disease in men: the Physicians' Health Study II randomized controlled trial
studies.authors: Sesso HD, Buring JE, Christen WG, et al.
studies.summary: The Physicians' Health Study II randomized 14,641 US male physicians aged 50 and older to 400 IU vitamin E every other day and/or 500 mg vitamin C daily, followed for a mean 8 years. Vitamin E had no effect on major cardiovascular events (HR 1.01) or death, and was linked to more hemorrhagic strokes (HR 1.74). The participants were healthy, well-nourished doctors, but the result is a clear null for heart protection.
studies.quote: neither vitamin E nor vitamin C supplementation reduced the risk of major cardiovascular events

studies.title: Meta-analysis: high-dosage vitamin E supplementation may increase all-cause mortality
studies.authors: Miller ER, Pastor-Barriuso R, Dalal D, et al.
studies.summary: This dose-response meta-analysis pooled 19 randomized trials with 135,967 participants taking 16.5-2,000 IU/day of vitamin E. Doses of 400 IU/day or more raised deaths by 39 per 10,000 people, with risk starting to climb above about 150 IU/day. Many high-dose trials enrolled people with chronic disease, so the size of the harm in healthy adults is uncertain, but no trial shows a benefit that would justify the risk.
studies.quote: High-dosage (> or =400 IU/d) vitamin E supplements may increase all-cause mortality and should be avoided.

studies.title: Effect of vitamin K on bone mineral density and fractures in adults: an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials
studies.authors: Mott A, Bradley T, Wright K, et al.
studies.summary: This updated systematic review identified 36 randomized trials of oral vitamin K (K1 and K2 forms) on bone mineral density and fractures in adults. In postmenopausal or osteoporotic patients, vitamin K was linked to lower odds of clinical fracture (OR 0.72), but this weakened to a non-significant OR 0.76 when restricted to low risk-of-bias trials, and vertebral fractures were unchanged. The authors conclude there is no evidence vitamin K improves bone density and the fracture signal is insufficient to confirm.
studies.quote: For post-menopausal or osteoporotic patients, there is no evidence that vitamin K affects bone mineral density or vertebral fractures

studies.title: Three-year low-dose menaquinone-7 supplementation helps decrease bone loss in healthy postmenopausal women
studies.authors: Knapen MH, Drummen NE, Smit E, et al.
studies.summary: This 3-year randomized placebo-controlled trial gave 244 healthy postmenopausal women 180 µg/day of vitamin K2 as MK-7 or placebo, measuring bone density by DXA. MK-7 improved vitamin K status and slowed the age-related decline in bone density and bone mineral content at the lumbar spine and femoral neck, but not at the total hip. It is a single trial in one population measuring bone density rather than fractures, so it supports but does not prove a fracture benefit.
studies.quote: MK-7 intake significantly improved vitamin K status and decreased the age-related decline in BMC and BMD at the lumbar spine and femoral neck

studies.title: Vitamin K supplementation and vascular calcification: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
studies.authors: Li T, Wang Y, Tu WP
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 14 randomized trials (1,533 patients, many with kidney or cardiovascular disease) testing vitamin K supplementation on vascular calcification. Vitamin K slowed coronary artery calcification score progression (mean difference -17.37, p = 0.04) and lowered dp-ucMGP, a marker of poor vitamin K status, with no excess adverse events. The calcification effect was small and borderline, came largely from patient populations, and the authors call for more rigorous trials.
studies.quote: VK supplementation has a significant effect on CAC scores, slowing down the progression of CAC

studies.title: Effects of Magnesium Supplementation on Blood Pressure: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Double-Blind Placebo-Controlled Trials
studies.authors: Zhang X, Li Y, Del Gobbo LC, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 34 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials (2,028 adults) of oral magnesium and blood pressure. A median 368 mg/day for about 3 months lowered systolic pressure by 2.00 mm Hg and diastolic by 1.78 mm Hg, and about 300 mg/day for a month was enough to see an effect. The drop is modest, and the trials varied enough that results differ across studies.
studies.quote: Our findings indicate a causal effect of Mg supplementation on lowering BPs in adults.

studies.title: Oral magnesium supplementation for insomnia in older adults: a Systematic Review & Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Mah J, Pitre T
studies.summary: This systematic review found only three randomized trials (151 older adults) comparing oral magnesium with placebo for insomnia. Magnesium cut the time to fall asleep by about 17 minutes, while the 16-minute gain in total sleep time was not statistically significant. All trials had moderate-to-high risk of bias and the evidence was rated low to very low quality, so the sleep claims for magnesium rest on thin evidence.
studies.quote: Pooled analysis showed that post-intervention sleep onset latency time was 17.36

studies.title: Oral Magnesium Supplementation for Treating Glucose Metabolism Parameters in People with or at Risk of Diabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Double-Blind Randomized Controlled Trials
studies.authors: Veronese N, Dominguez LJ, Pizzol D, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled double-blind randomized trials of oral magnesium versus placebo in people with diabetes or at high risk of it. Magnesium lowered fasting glucose in people with diabetes, and in at-risk people it improved glucose after a 2-hour glucose tolerance test and markers of insulin sensitivity. The benefit is clearest in people with diabetes or prediabetes, who often have low magnesium; it says little about healthy people with normal levels.
studies.quote: Mg supplementation may improve insulin-sensitivity parameters in those at high risk of diabetes

studies.title: Zinc lozenges and the common cold: a meta-analysis comparing zinc acetate and zinc gluconate, and the role of zinc dosage.
studies.authors: Hemilä H
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled seven placebo-controlled trials (575 people with natural colds) that used zinc lozenges at more than 75 mg/day. Colds were 33% shorter on average with zinc, with acetate and gluconate lozenges performing similarly. The benefit applies to short courses started at the first sign of a cold, and doses above 100 mg/day added nothing.
studies.quote: The mean common cold duration was 33% (95% CI 21% to 45%) shorter for the zinc groups of the seven included trials.

studies.title: A randomized, placebo-controlled, clinical trial of high-dose supplementation with vitamins C and E, beta carotene, and zinc for age-related macular degeneration and vision loss: AREDS report no. 8.
studies.authors: Age-Related Eye Disease Study Research Group
studies.summary: AREDS randomized 3,640 adults aged 55-80 to antioxidants, zinc 80 mg plus copper 2 mg, both, or placebo for an average of 6.3 years. Antioxidants plus zinc cut the odds of progressing to advanced macular degeneration (OR 0.72), with the clearest benefit in people already at higher risk. Copper was added specifically to prevent zinc-induced copper deficiency, and the benefit was not shown in people with only early AMD.
studies.quote: demonstrated a statistically significant odds reduction for the development of advanced AMD with antioxidants plus zinc

studies.title: Zinc-Induced Hematologic Toxicities: A Systematic Review of Descriptive Studies.
studies.authors: Dutta A, Chaudhary V, Kumari S, et al.
studies.summary: This systematic review collected 37 published cases (1972-2025) of blood disorders caused by excess zinc from supplements, denture creams, or swallowed coins. Serum copper was low in every patient, with anemia and neutropenia common at doses from about 50 mg/day up to over 1,500 mg/day. It is case-level evidence and rare, but it is the reason long-term zinc should be paired with copper; stopping zinc and adding copper usually fixed the blood counts, while nerve damage recovered slowly or incompletely.
studies.quote: Zinc-induced hematologic toxicity is an uncommon but underrecognized and largely reversible condition.

studies.title: Effect of selenium and vitamin E on risk of prostate cancer and other cancers: the Selenium and Vitamin E Cancer Prevention Trial (SELECT).
studies.authors: Lippman SM, Klein EA, Goodman PJ, et al.
studies.summary: SELECT randomized 35,533 healthy men to 200 mcg/day selenium, vitamin E, both, or placebo, with a median follow-up of 5.5 years. Selenium did not reduce prostate cancer (HR 1.04) or any other prespecified cancer. There was a non-significant uptick in type 2 diabetes with selenium, so in people who already get enough, extra selenium offers no cancer protection.
studies.quote: Selenium or vitamin E, alone or in combination at the doses and formulations used, did not prevent prostate cancer

studies.title: Selenium Supplementation in Patients with Hashimoto Thyroiditis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
studies.authors: Huwiler VV, Maissen-Abgottspon S, Stanga Z, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis of 35 randomized trials looked at selenium supplements in people with Hashimoto thyroiditis. Selenium modestly lowered TSH in people not on thyroid hormone (SMD -0.21) and lowered TPO antibodies more clearly (SMD -0.96), with side effects similar to placebo. These are lab markers rather than symptoms or disease progression, and the antibody results varied a lot between trials (I2 = 90%).
studies.quote: In people with HT without THRT, selenium was effective and safe in lowering TSH, TPOAb, and MDA levels.

studies.title: Selenium intake, status, and health: a complex relationship.
studies.authors: Rayman MP
studies.summary: This review by a leading selenium researcher covers how both too little and too much selenium affect health worldwide. Many outcomes, including mortality, follow a U-shaped curve, with harm at both low and high selenium status. The practical point is that selenium helps people who are low and may harm people who are already replete, so baseline status and dose matter more than the supplement itself.
studies.quote: Some health effects, such as increased mortality, are associated with both low and high Se status.

studies.title: Iodine deficiency and thyroid disorders.
studies.authors: Zimmermann MB, Boelaert K
studies.summary: This review summarizes how population iodine intake shapes thyroid disease in adults. Severe deficiency causes goitre and hypothyroidism, while milder deficiency drives nodular goitre and hyperthyroidism over time; correcting it brings a small, possibly temporary rise in subclinical hypothyroidism and thyroid autoimmunity. The goal is adequate intake, not more, and the review is narrative rather than a pooled analysis.
studies.quote: Iodine deficiency early in life impairs cognition and growth, but iodine status is also a key determinant of thyroid disorders in adults.

studies.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of iodine nutrition in modern vegan and vegetarian diets.
studies.authors: Eveleigh ER, Coneyworth L, Welham SJM
studies.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 11 observational studies covering 4,421 adults on vegan, vegetarian, or omnivorous diets. Vegans had the lowest iodine intake (about 17 mcg/day versus a 150 mcg/day adult target) and none of the diet groups reached the optimal urinary iodine range. Risk was worst where salt is not routinely iodized, so plant-based eaters should use iodized salt or a modest supplement rather than rely on food.
studies.quote: Vegetarians and particularly vegans living in countries with no current USI programme continue to have increased risk of low iodine status

studies.title: Effect of inadequate iodine status in UK pregnant women on cognitive outcomes in their children: results from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC).
studies.authors: Bath SC, Steer CD, Golding J, et al.
studies.summary: This cohort study measured iodine in first-trimester urine from 1,040 UK pregnant women and followed their children's IQ and reading into school age. Children of mothers with low iodine were more likely to score in the bottom quarter for verbal IQ (OR 1.58) and reading accuracy (OR 1.69). It is observational, so it shows association rather than proof, but it shows that even mild deficiency in a wealthy country can matter.
studies.quote: Our results show the importance of adequate iodine status during early gestation and emphasise the risk that iodine deficiency can pose to the developing infant

studies.title: Calcium intake and risk of fracture: systematic review.
studies.authors: Bolland MJ, Leung W, Tai V, et al.
studies.summary: This systematic review covered 44 cohort studies of dietary calcium and 26 randomized trials of calcium supplements in adults over 50. Supplements cut total fractures by about 11% (RR 0.89) across all trials, but the best-quality trials (44,505 people) showed no effect at any site, and dietary calcium was not linked to fracture risk. High-dose calcium is a weak fracture strategy; a low dose that fills a dietary gap is the defensible use.
studies.quote: Evidence that calcium supplements prevent fractures is weak and inconsistent.

studies.title: Effect of calcium supplements on risk of myocardial infarction and cardiovascular events: meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Bolland MJ, Avenell A, Baron JA, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 15 placebo-controlled trials of calcium supplements (500 mg/day or more) without vitamin D, using patient-level data from 8,151 people and trial-level data from 11,921. People on calcium had about 30% more heart attacks (HR 1.31). The finding is still debated and the trials were not designed to measure heart outcomes, but it argues for getting calcium mostly from food and keeping supplement doses low.
studies.quote: Calcium supplements (without coadministered vitamin D) are associated with an increased risk of myocardial infarction.

studies.title: Nutritional aspects of manganese homeostasis.
studies.authors: Aschner JL, Aschner M
studies.summary: This narrative review covers manganese as an essential mineral: where it occurs in food, how it is absorbed and excreted, and when it becomes toxic. The body tightly regulates manganese levels, and ordinary diets supply enough, while excess exposure can build up in the brain and cause a Parkinson-like syndrome (manganism). There are no trials showing benefit from supplementing manganese, so only a small dose, if any, makes sense.
studies.quote: Humans maintain stable tissue levels of Mn. This is achieved via tight homeostatic control of both absorption and excretion.

studies.title: Nothing Boring About Boron.
studies.authors: Pizzorno L
studies.summary: This narrative review collects animal, cell and small human studies on boron's roles in bone, hormones, vitamin D, magnesium and inflammation. It reports benefits for bone maintenance and lower inflammatory markers such as hs-CRP and TNF-α, and suggests 3 mg/day for people eating few fruits and vegetables or at risk of osteoporosis. It is written for an integrative-medicine audience and is more enthusiastic than the thin human trial base supports.
studies.quote: In none of the numerous studies conducted to date, however, do boron's beneficial effects appear at intakes > 3 mg/d.

studies.title: Comparative effects of daily and weekly boron supplementation on plasma steroid hormones and proinflammatory cytokines.
studies.authors: Naghii MR, Mofid M, Asgari AR, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of Trace Elements in Medicine and Biology
studies.summary: Eight healthy men took 10 mg of boron daily for one week, with blood drawn before and after in an uncontrolled, placebo-day comparison. Free testosterone rose, estradiol fell, and hs-CRP and TNF-α decreased after one week. With only eight subjects, no parallel control group and a dose well above typical intake, this is a pilot signal, not evidence of lasting benefit.
studies.quote: After one week (in samples taken at 8.00 A.M, only), the mean plasma free testosterone increased and the mean plasma estradiol decreased significantly.

studies.title: Dietary Lithium, Silicon, and Boron: An Updated Critical Review of Their Roles in Metabolic Regulation, Neurobiology, Bone Health, and the Gut Microbiome.
studies.authors: Melenikioti E, Pavlidou E, Dakanalis A, et al.
studies.summary: This critical narrative review searched three databases through January 2025 and graded evidence for boron, lithium and silicon by human, animal and cell tiers. For boron, human support comes from metabolic, inflammatory and cognitive studies of modest size. The authors conclude current human data are insufficient to justify supplementation, which is the more sober counterweight to enthusiastic reviews.
studies.quote: current human data are insufficient to justify dietary recommendations or supplementation

studies.title: Lithium deficiency and the onset of Alzheimer's disease.
studies.authors: Aron L, Ngian ZK, Qiu C, et al.
studies.summary: This study measured metals in human post-mortem brain tissue and then depleted or replaced dietary lithium in wild-type and Alzheimer's mouse models. Lithium was the only metal significantly reduced in brains of people with mild cognitive impairment, and halving cortical lithium in mice accelerated amyloid, tau pathology and memory loss, while low-dose lithium orotate prevented them. It is a striking mechanistic result but the treatment evidence is entirely in mice; no human trial of lithium orotate has yet shown benefit.
studies.quote: Of the metals we analysed, Li was the only one that was significantly reduced in the brain in individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI)

studies.title: Association between naturally occurring lithium in drinking water and suicide rates: systematic review and meta-analysis of ecological studies.
studies.authors: Memon A, Rogers I, Fitzsimmons SMDD, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 15 ecological studies comparing natural lithium levels in public drinking water with regional suicide rates. Higher water lithium was consistently associated with lower total suicide mortality (pooled β -0.27), with high heterogeneity. Ecological data compare regions, not individuals, so confounding is likely and the authors call for randomized community trials before any recommendation.
studies.quote: The random-effects meta-analysis showed a consistent protective (or inverse) association between lithium levels/concentration in publicly available drinking water and total

studies.title: Microdose lithium treatment stabilized cognitive impairment in patients with Alzheimer's disease.
studies.authors: Nunes MA, Viel TA, Buck HS
studies.summary: This small controlled trial gave Alzheimer's patients a microdose of 300 μg lithium daily or placebo for 15 months and tracked Mini-Mental State Examination scores. The lithium group showed no decline while controls worsened, with differences appearing from three months onward. It was a small single-center study that has not been replicated, so supplement-dose lithium for brain health remains preliminary.
studies.quote: the treated group showed no decreased performance in the mini-mental state examination test, in opposition to the lower scores observed for the control group

studies.title: Alpha-Ketoglutarate, an Endogenous Metabolite, Extends Lifespan and Compresses Morbidity in Aging Mice
studies.authors: Asadi Shahmirzadi A, Edgar D, Liao CY, et al.
studies.summary: This study fed middle-aged C57BL/6 mice calcium alpha-ketoglutarate (CaAKG) in their diet and tracked lifespan alongside longitudinal frailty and healthspan measures. CaAKG extended lifespan, reduced frailty and lowered systemic inflammatory cytokines, an effect the authors tie to induction of IL-10. These are mouse results only; no human lifespan or hard-outcome data exist for CaAKG.
studies.quote: We find that CaAKG promotes a longer, healthier life associated with a decrease in levels of systemic inflammatory cytokines.

studies.title: Rejuvant, a potential life-extending compound formulation with alpha-ketoglutarate and vitamins, conferred an average 8 year reduction in biological aging, after an average of 7 months of use, in the TruAge DNA methylation test
studies.authors: Demidenko O, Barardo D, Budovskii V, et al.
studies.summary: This retrospective analysis looked at DNA methylation age in 42 people who took Rejuvant, a CaAKG-plus-vitamin formulation, for an average of 7 months. Their measured biological age fell by an average of about 8 years. There was no placebo or control group, the sample was small and self-selected, and the authors themselves state placebo-controlled testing is required, so this is very weak evidence.
studies.quote: individuals showed an average decrease in biological aging of 8 years (p-value=6.538x10-12)

studies.title: Alpha-ketoglutarate supplementation and BiologicaL agE in middle-aged adults (ABLE)-intervention study protocol
studies.authors: Sandalova E, Goh J, Lim ZX, et al.
studies.summary: This paper describes the ABLE trial, a double-blind placebo-controlled RCT of 1 g/day sustained-release CaAKG for 6 months in 120 healthy 40-60-year-olds whose DNA methylation age exceeds their chronological age. The primary outcome is change in DNA methylation age, with secondary outcomes including inflammation, strength, arterial stiffness and aerobic capacity. It is a protocol, not results, and its existence underlines that properly controlled human evidence for CaAKG is still pending.
studies.quote: Alpha-Ketoglutarate (AKG) has been studied widely in model animals, but there are few studies testing its geroprotective properties in humans.

studies.title: Randomized controlled trial of oral glutathione supplementation on body stores of glutathione
studies.authors: Richie JP, Nichenametla S, Neidig W, et al.
studies.summary: This 6-month randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial gave 54 healthy non-smoking adults 250 or 1,000 mg/day of oral glutathione and measured glutathione in blood and tissue cells. At 6 months the high dose raised glutathione 30-35% in erythrocytes, plasma and lymphocytes, and natural killer cell activity more than doubled at 3 months. Levels fell back to baseline within a month of stopping, and the study measured biomarkers rather than any health outcome.
studies.quote: daily consumption of GSH supplements was effective at increasing body compartment stores of GSH

studies.title: Effects of oral glutathione supplementation on systemic oxidative stress biomarkers in human volunteers
studies.authors: Allen J, Bradley RD
studies.journal: Journal of Alternative and Complementary Medicine
studies.summary: This randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial gave 40 healthy adults 500 mg of oral glutathione twice daily for 4 weeks. It found no change in urinary oxidative stress markers (F2-isoprostanes, 8-OHdG) or in red blood cell glutathione status. Together with the longer Richie trial, it suggests any effect of oral glutathione is slow, modest, and not reliably detectable over a short course.
studies.quote: No significant changes were observed in biomarkers of oxidative stress, including glutathione status, in this clinical trial of oral glutathione supplementation in healthy adults.

studies.title: Efficacy of glutathione for the treatment of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease: an open-label, single-arm, multicenter, pilot study
studies.authors: Honda Y, Kessoku T, Sumida Y, et al.
studies.summary: This open-label, single-arm pilot study gave 34 patients with fatty liver disease 300 mg/day of oral glutathione for 4 months after 3 months of lifestyle changes. ALT (a liver enzyme) fell significantly, along with triglycerides and ferritin, and liver fat dropped in the responders. With no control group and only 29 completers, this is hypothesis-generating; the authors themselves call for large trials.
studies.quote: This pilot study demonstrates the potential therapeutic effects of oral administration of glutathione in practical dose for patients with NAFLD.

studies.title: Lysine for Herpes Simplex Prophylaxis: A Review of the Evidence
studies.authors: Mailoo VJ, Rampes S
studies.summary: Two reviewers searched four databases and summarized the clinical trials of oral L-lysine for preventing herpes simplex recurrences. Lysine looked ineffective below 1 g/day unless paired with a low-arginine diet, while doses above 3 g/day seemed to improve patients' subjective experience of outbreaks. The trials are small, old and heterogeneous, so dose matters and the evidence is weak.
studies.quote: L-lysine supplementation appears to be ineffective for prophylaxis or treatment of herpes simplex lesions with doses of less than 1 g/d without low-arginine diets.

studies.title: Interventions for prevention of herpes simplex labialis (cold sores on the lips)
studies.authors: Chi CC, Wang SH, Delamere FM, et al.
studies.summary: This Cochrane review pooled 32 randomized trials (2,640 people) covering 19 different ways to prevent cold sores. Long-term oral antivirals such as aciclovir or valaciclovir modestly reduced recurrences, but the reviewers found no evidence of efficacy for lysine. If cold-sore prevention is the goal, prescription antivirals have better evidence than lysine.
studies.quote: We failed to find any evidence of efficacy for lysine, LongoVital® supplementation, gamma globulin

studies.title: Lysine fortification reduces anxiety and lessens stress in family members in economically weak communities in Northwest Syria
studies.authors: Smriga M, Ghosh S, Mouneimne Y, et al.
studies.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
studies.summary: This 3-month randomized double-blind study fortified wheat flour with lysine for families in poor Syrian communities whose diets relied on wheat, which is low in lysine. Fortification lowered trait anxiety in men and blunted stress responses (cortisol in women, skin conductance in men). The people studied likely had low lysine intake, so the result may not carry over to well-fed adults eating plenty of protein.
studies.quote: Lysine fortification also significantly reduced chronic anxiety as measured by the trait anxiety inventory in males.
