studies.title: Effect of oral L-arginine supplementation on blood pressure: a meta-analysis of randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials.
studies.authors: Dong JY, Qin LQ, Zhang Z, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 11 double-blind, placebo-controlled trials with 387 people taking 4-24 g/day of oral L-arginine. Arginine lowered systolic blood pressure by 5.4 mmHg and diastolic by 2.7 mmHg compared with placebo. The trials were small and short, and the doses are large, so this is a modest effect on a lab number rather than proof of fewer heart attacks.
studies.quote: This meta-analysis provides further evidence that oral L-arginine supplementation significantly lowers both systolic and diastolic BP.

studies.title: Association of l-Arginine Supplementation with Markers of Endothelial Function in Patients with Cardiovascular or Metabolic Disorders: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
studies.authors: Rodrigues-Krause J, Krause M, Rocha IMGD, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 13 randomized trials of oral L-arginine versus placebo in people with heart disease, obesity, or diabetes, with flow-mediated dilation as the main outcome. Overall there was no significant improvement in endothelial function (SMD 0.30, 95% CI -0.85 to 1.46), and nitric oxide markers did not change. Results were extremely inconsistent between trials (I2 = 96%), so the endothelial-function rationale for arginine is not well supported.
studies.quote: Overall, the results indicated that oral l-arginine supplementation was not associated with improvements on selected variables in these patients

studies.title: L-arginine therapy in acute myocardial infarction: the Vascular Interaction With Age in Myocardial Infarction (VINTAGE MI) randomized clinical trial.
studies.authors: Schulman SP, Becker LC, Kass DA, et al.
studies.summary: This randomized, double-blind trial gave 153 heart attack survivors L-arginine (goal 9 g/day) or placebo for 6 months. Arginine did not improve vascular stiffness or heart pumping function, and 6 people (8.6%) on arginine died versus none on placebo, so the trial was stopped early. It is a single small trial in a specific group, but it is a clear warning against using arginine after a heart attack.
studies.quote: L-arginine, when added to standard postinfarction therapies, does not improve vascular stiffness measurements or ejection fraction and may be associated with higher postinfarction mortality.

studies.title: Effects of L-Theanine Administration on Stress-Related Symptoms and Cognitive Functions in Healthy Adults: A Randomized Controlled Trial
studies.authors: Hidese S, Ogawa S, Ota M, et al.
studies.summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial gave 30 healthy adults 200 mg/day of L-theanine for four weeks. Depression, trait-anxiety and sleep-quality (PSQI) scores improved, with shorter sleep latency and less sleep disturbance versus placebo, and verbal fluency and executive function scores rose. It is a small study, so treat the results as encouraging rather than settled.
studies.quote: The PSQI subscale scores for sleep latency, sleep disturbance, and use of sleep medication reduced after L-theanine administration, compared to the placebo administration

studies.title: The Effects of Green Tea Amino Acid L-Theanine Consumption on the Ability to Manage Stress and Anxiety Levels: a Systematic Review
studies.authors: Williams JL, Everett JM, D'Cunha NM, et al.
studies.summary: This PRISMA systematic review gathered 9 randomized controlled trials of pure L-theanine supplements on stress and anxiety. It concluded that 200-400 mg/day may help reduce stress and anxiety in people under stressful conditions. The trials were small and short, and the authors say longer, larger studies are needed before calling it a therapy.
studies.quote: may assist in the reduction of stress and anxiety in people exposed to stressful conditions

studies.title: Acute effects of tea constituents L-theanine, caffeine, and epigallocatechin gallate on cognitive function and mood: a systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Camfield DA, Stough C, Farrimond J, Scholey AB
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 11 randomized placebo-controlled studies of single doses of L-theanine, EGCG and caffeine on mood and attention. Caffeine plus L-theanine produced moderate improvements in alertness and attention-switching accuracy in the first 2 hours. Effect size tracked the caffeine dose more than the theanine dose, so much of the attention boost may come from the caffeine.
studies.quote: Evidence of moderate effect sizes in favor of combined caffeine and L-theanine in the first 2 hours postdose were found

studies.title: The effect of coenzyme Q10 on morbidity and mortality in chronic heart failure: results from Q-SYMBIO: a randomized double-blind trial.
studies.authors: Mortensen SA, Rosenfeldt F, Kumar A, et al.
studies.summary: Q-SYMBIO randomized 420 patients with moderate to severe heart failure to CoQ10 100 mg three times daily or placebo on top of standard therapy for 2 years. Major adverse cardiovascular events occurred in 15% on CoQ10 versus 26% on placebo (hazard ratio 0.50), with lower all-cause mortality (10% vs 18%). Short-term endpoints did not change, the trial was modest in size and slow to recruit, and it has not been replicated by a large independent trial.
studies.quote: The primary long-term endpoint was reached by 15% of the patients in the CoQ10 group versus 26% in the placebo group

studies.title: Effects of Coenzyme Q10 on Statin-Induced Myopathy: An Updated Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
studies.authors: Qu H, Guo M, Chai H, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Heart Association
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 12 randomized trials with 575 statin users to test whether CoQ10 eases statin-associated muscle symptoms. CoQ10 reduced muscle pain scores (weighted mean difference -1.60), plus weakness, cramps and tiredness, but did not change creatine kinase. The trials were small and heterogeneous, and an earlier meta-analysis (Banach 2015) and a later one (Kennedy 2020) found no clear benefit, so the evidence is genuinely mixed.
studies.quote: Compared with placebo, CoQ10 supplementation ameliorated statin-associated muscle symptoms, such as muscle pain

studies.title: Dose-Response Effect of Coenzyme Q10 Supplementation on Blood Pressure among Patients with Cardiometabolic Disorders: A Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE)-Assessed Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
studies.authors: Zhao D, Liang Y, Dai S, et al.
studies.summary: This GRADE-assessed dose-response meta-analysis pooled 26 randomized trials with 1,831 people with cardiometabolic disease. CoQ10 lowered systolic blood pressure by about 4.8 mmHg, with the largest effect around 100-200 mg/day and longer use beyond 12 weeks. Evidence certainty was moderate for systolic and low for diastolic pressure, so it is an adjunct at best, not a replacement for blood pressure drugs.
studies.quote: 100-200 mg/d of CoQ10 supplementation may achieve the greatest benefit on SBP in patients with cardiometabolic diseases

studies.title: Cardioprotection and lifespan extension by the natural polyamine spermidine.
studies.authors: Eisenberg T, Abdellatif M, Schroeder S, et al.
studies.summary: This mostly preclinical study fed spermidine to aging mice and salt-sensitive rats and paired it with dietary questionnaire data from a human cohort. Spermidine extended mouse lifespan, preserved heart function via autophagy, and lowered blood pressure in rats, while higher dietary intake in humans tracked with lower blood pressure and cardiovascular disease. The core evidence is animal data plus observational human correlation, so it shows a plausible mechanism, not proof that supplements help people.
studies.quote: oral supplementation of the natural polyamine spermidine extends the lifespan of mice and exerts cardioprotective effects

studies.title: Higher spermidine intake is linked to lower mortality: a prospective population-based study.
studies.authors: Kiechl S, Pechlaner R, Willeit P, et al.
studies.journal: The American Journal of Clinical Nutrition
studies.summary: The Bruneck Study followed 829 adults aged 45-84 for 20 years, estimating dietary spermidine with repeated food-frequency questionnaires. Each 1-SD higher spermidine intake was linked to 24% lower all-cause mortality (adjusted HR 0.76), a finding replicated in the SAPHIR cohort. This is observational: spermidine-rich foods like whole grains, legumes and mushrooms mark a healthier diet overall, so residual confounding is likely.
studies.quote: The age-, sex- and caloric ratio-adjusted HR for all-cause death per 1-SD higher spermidine intake was 0.74

studies.title: Effects of Spermidine Supplementation on Cognition and Biomarkers in Older Adults With Subjective Cognitive Decline: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
studies.authors: Schwarz C, Benson GS, Horn N, et al.
studies.summary: The SmartAge trial randomized 100 adults aged 60-90 with subjective memory complaints to a wheat-germ spermidine supplement (0.9 mg/day) or placebo for 12 months. Memory performance did not differ from placebo (between-group difference -0.03, P = .47), nor did secondary outcomes. This is the best human trial so far and it was null, though the dose was low; any hints on inflammation or verbal memory were exploratory.
studies.quote: longer-term spermidine supplementation in participants with subjective cognitive decline did not modify memory and biomarkers compared with placebo

studies.title: Rapid and sustainable detoxication of airborne pollutants by broccoli sprout beverage: results of a randomized clinical trial in China.
studies.authors: Egner PA, Chen JG, Zarth AT, et al.
studies.summary: A 12-week randomized placebo-controlled trial gave 291 adults in a heavily polluted region of Qidong, China a daily broccoli sprout beverage (600 μmol glucoraphanin plus 40 μmol sulforaphane). Urinary excretion of detoxified benzene rose 61% and acrolein 23% versus placebo, and the effect did not fade over 12 weeks. It measured detox biomarkers, not cancer or lung disease outcomes, so the long-term health payoff is assumed rather than shown.
studies.quote: Rapid and sustained, statistically significant (P ≤ 0.01) increases in the levels of excretion of the glutathione-derived conjugates of benzene (61%), acrolein (23%)

studies.title: Effect of broccoli sprout extract and baseline gut microbiota on fasting blood glucose in prediabetes: a randomized, placebo-controlled trial.
studies.authors: Dwibedi C, Axelsson AS, Abrahamsson B, et al.
studies.summary: A double-blind trial randomized 74 drug-naive adults with prediabetes to broccoli sprout extract or placebo once daily for 12 weeks. Fasting glucose fell 0.2 mmol/L versus placebo, missing the prespecified 0.3 mmol/L target, though a subgroup whose gut bacteria better converted glucoraphanin to sulforaphane responded more strongly. The overall effect is small, and the responder finding is exploratory until replicated.
studies.quote: Gastro-intestinal side effects but no severe adverse events were observed in response to treatment. BSE did not meet the prespecified primary outcome

studies.title: Broccoli or Sulforaphane: Is It the Source or Dose That Matters?
studies.authors: Yagishita Y, Fahey JW, Dinkova-Kostova AT, et al.
studies.summary: This narrative review surveys more than 50 clinical trials of glucoraphanin and sulforaphane and compares formulations such as whole broccoli, sprouts, beverages and supplements. It finds that bioavailability varies widely by formulation, largely depending on whether active myrosinase or gut bacteria convert glucoraphanin into sulforaphane. Doses and products differ so much across studies that firm dosing advice is not yet possible, and validated human biomarkers are still lacking.
studies.quote: This review evaluates the current state of knowledge regarding the relationships between formulation (e.g., plants, sprouts, beverages, supplements), bioavailability and efficacy

studies.title: The Effect of Lutein/Zeaxanthin Intake on Human Macular Pigment Optical Density: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Wilson LM, Tharmarajah S, Jia Y, et al.
studies.summary: This systematic review and meta-analysis pooled 46 studies (3,189 adults with healthy eyes) testing lutein/zeaxanthin from supplements or food on macular pigment optical density (MPOD). Intakes under 5 mg/day showed no significant change, while 5 to under 20 mg/day raised MPOD by 0.04 units and 20 mg/day or more raised it by 0.11 units over 3-12 months. MPOD is a surrogate marker, and the authors note it is still unclear what dose or duration produces a clinically meaningful change in vision.
studies.quote: MPOD increased with lutein/zeaxanthin intake, particularly at higher doses, among adults with healthy eyes.

studies.title: Tomato and lycopene supplementation and cardiovascular risk factors: A systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Cheng HM, Koutsidis G, Lodge JK, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 21 intervention trials in adults testing tomato products or lycopene supplements on blood lipids, endothelial function, blood pressure and inflammation markers. Lycopene supplements lowered systolic blood pressure by 5.66 mmHg, while tomato products lowered LDL cholesterol by 0.22 mmol/L and improved flow-mediated dilation by 2.53%. Most other outcomes were unchanged, the trials were small and short, and these are risk-factor changes, not proof of fewer heart attacks or strokes.
studies.quote: increasing the intake of these has positive effects on blood lipids, blood pressure and endothelial function

studies.title: Lutein + zeaxanthin and omega-3 fatty acids for age-related macular degeneration: the Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 (AREDS2) randomized clinical trial
studies.authors: Age-Related Eye Disease Study 2 Research Group
studies.summary: AREDS2 was a multicenter, double-masked, placebo-controlled factorial trial of 4,203 adults aged 50-85 at risk of advanced macular degeneration, testing lutein 10 mg plus zeaxanthin 2 mg (and/or fish oil) on top of the AREDS vitamin formula. Over a median 5 years, adding lutein/zeaxanthin did not significantly cut progression to advanced AMD in the primary analysis (31% placebo vs 29%; HR 0.90, 98.7% CI 0.76-1.07). The useful takeaway is narrower: lutein/zeaxanthin is a reasonable replacement for beta carotene in the AREDS formula because beta carotene was linked to more lung cancers in former smokers, and the benefit applies to people who already have intermediate AMD, not the general population.
studies.quote: lutein + zeaxanthin could be an appropriate carotenoid substitute in the AREDS formulation

studies.title: Garlic lowers blood pressure in hypertensive subjects, improves arterial stiffness and gut microbiota: A review and meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Ried K
studies.summary: This review and meta-analysis pooled 12 randomized trials with 553 people with high blood pressure who took garlic supplements, mostly aged garlic extract. Garlic lowered systolic pressure by about 8.3 mmHg and diastolic by 5.5 mmHg, comparable to a first-line blood pressure drug. The trials were small and much of the aged-garlic evidence comes from the author's own Kyolic studies, so an independent large trial would strengthen the case.
studies.quote: The meta-analysis of 12 trials and 553 hypertensive participants confirmed that garlic supplements lower systolic blood pressure (SBP)

studies.title: Effects of Garlic on Glucose Parameters and Lipid Profile: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis on Randomized Controlled Trials.
studies.authors: Zhao X, Cheng T, Xia H, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled randomized trials through February 2024 testing garlic or garlic supplements on blood sugar and lipids. Garlic lowered total cholesterol by about 14 mg/dL and LDL by about 8 mg/dL, raised HDL slightly, and reduced fasting glucose and HbA1c, but did not change triglycerides. The garlic forms and doses varied widely and heterogeneity was high, so the effect is modest and product-dependent.
studies.quote: The intervention of garlic is beneficial to control blood glucose and blood lipids in humans.

studies.title: Garlic for the common cold.
studies.authors: Lissiman E, Bhasale AL, Cohen M
studies.summary: This Cochrane review searched for randomized trials of garlic to prevent or treat colds and found only one eligible trial, of 146 people taking an allicin supplement or placebo for 12 weeks. That trial reported 24 colds on garlic versus 65 on placebo, but recovery time was similar. One self-reported trial is not enough, and the authors conclude claims of effectiveness rely largely on poor-quality evidence.
studies.quote: There is insufficient clinical trial evidence regarding the effects of garlic in preventing or treating the common cold.

studies.title: Effect of Chlorella supplementation on cardiovascular risk factors: A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
studies.authors: Fallah AA, Sarmast E, Habibian Dehkordi S, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 19 randomized trials with 797 participants testing Chlorella on cardiovascular risk factors. Chlorella lowered total cholesterol by about 9 mg/dL, LDL by 8 mg/dL, systolic blood pressure by 4.5 mmHg and fasting glucose by 4 mg/dL, with no change in triglycerides, HDL or BMI. Benefits appeared mainly at 4 g/day or more for at least 8 weeks and in people with existing risk factors; trials were small.
studies.quote: Chlorella supplementation improved levels of TC, LDL-C, SBP, DBP, and FBG but the changes in TG, HDL-C, and BMI were not satisfactory

studies.title: Beneficial effects of Chlorella species supplementation in the general population: a GRADE-assessed systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Mardani H, Karimi MA, Sharifi M, et al.
studies.summary: This GRADE-assessed meta-analysis pooled 24 studies of Chlorella in the general population, searched through February 2025. Chlorella produced small reductions in LDL (about 6 mg/dL), total cholesterol (8 mg/dL), body weight (1.3 kg), insulin resistance and hs-CRP. Certainty of evidence was rated low to very low for nearly every outcome, so these are hints, not established effects.
studies.quote: given the overall very low certainty of evidence based on the GRADE assessment, these results should be interpreted cautiously

studies.title: The Role of Chlorella and Spirulina as Adjuvants of Cardiovascular Risk Factor Control: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomised Controlled Trials.
studies.authors: Pinto-Leite M, Martins D, Ferreira AC, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 12 randomized trials of Chlorella (168-279 participants per outcome) and 9 of Spirulina on blood pressure, lipids and glucose. It found Chlorella had a neutral effect on blood pressure and blood lipids, while Spirulina modestly lowered diastolic pressure. This contradicts earlier positive pooled results and shows the Chlorella evidence is small and inconsistent.
studies.quote: Our analysis showed that Chlorella supplementation had a neutral effect on BP and lipemia.

studies.title: Effect of fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum L.) intake on glycemia: a meta-analysis of clinical trials.
studies.authors: Neelakantan N, Narayanan M, de Souza RJ, et al.
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 10 clinical trials lasting at least a week that compared fenugreek seed with a control. Fenugreek lowered fasting glucose by 0.96 mmol/L and HbA1c by 0.85 percentage points, but only in people with diabetes taking medium or high doses. Most trials were of low quality and results varied widely, so the effect in people with normal blood sugar is unproven.
studies.quote: Results from clinical trials support beneficial effects of fenugreek seeds on glycemic control in persons with diabetes.

studies.title: The Effect of Fenugreek in Type 2 Diabetes and Prediabetes: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials.
studies.authors: Kim J, Noh W, Kim A, et al.
studies.summary: This newer meta-analysis pooled 10 randomized trials (706 people) of fenugreek in type 2 diabetes and prediabetes. Fenugreek lowered fasting glucose, 2-hour glucose, and HbA1c, and improved total cholesterol, triglycerides, and HDL, with only mild stomach side effects. It did not improve insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and the trials were small, so it is an add-on for people with high blood sugar, not a treatment on its own.
studies.quote: Fenugreek significantly reduced FBG, 2-hPG, and HbA1c, but it did not significantly decrease HOMA-IR.

studies.title: Effects of oral fenugreek-derived preparations on testosterone-related outcomes in adult men: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized placebo-controlled trials.
studies.authors: Yang P, Niu Z, Guo J, et al.
studies.summary: This 2026 meta-analysis reviewed 13 randomized placebo-controlled trials of fenugreek products in adult men, with 6 contributing to the total-testosterone analysis. It found a small rise in total testosterone (SMD 0.25) and no reliable change in free testosterone. No trial was at low risk of bias and certainty was rated very low, and many trials were industry-sponsored extracts, so testosterone claims are not supported.
studies.quote: Current evidence does not support clinical or commercial testosterone-boosting claims.

studies.title: Efficacy of Turmeric Extracts and Curcumin for Alleviating the Symptoms of Joint Arthritis: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials.
studies.authors: Daily JW, Yang M, Park S
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 8 randomized trials of turmeric extract or curcumin (about 1,000 mg/day of curcumin) for arthritis, mostly knee osteoarthritis. Curcumin cut pain scores by about 2 points on a 10-point scale versus placebo and performed about the same as pain medication. The trials were few and small, so the authors say the evidence is promising but not definitive.
studies.quote: these RCTs provide scientific evidence that supports the efficacy of turmeric extract (about 1000 mg/day of curcumin) in the treatment of arthritis.

studies.title: Anti-inflammatory effects of oral supplementation with curcumin: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
studies.authors: Ferguson JJA, Abbott KA, Garg ML
studies.summary: This meta-analysis reviewed 32 randomized trials (2,038 people) of oral curcumin and blood markers of inflammation, pooling 28 of them. Curcumin lowered CRP by 1.55 mg/L and also reduced IL-6 and TNF-alpha. These are biomarker changes rather than disease outcomes, and the best dose, duration, and formulation remain unsettled.
studies.quote: These findings provide evidence for the anti-inflammatory effects of curcumin and support further investigation to confirm dose, duration, and formulation

studies.title: Curcumin: A Review of Its Effects on Human Health.
studies.authors: Hewlings SJ, Kalman DS
studies.summary: This narrative review surveys human research on curcumin for inflammation, arthritis, metabolic syndrome, and exercise recovery. Its key practical point is that plain curcumin is poorly absorbed and quickly cleared, and that pairing it with piperine from black pepper raised bioavailability by about 2,000% in early studies. It is a broad, positive overview rather than a systematic review, so treat its benefit claims as less rigorous than the bioavailability caveat.
studies.quote: Ingesting curcumin by itself does not lead to the associated health benefits due to its poor bioavailability

studies.title: Association between muscular strength and mortality in men: prospective cohort study
studies.authors: Ruiz JR, Sui X, Lobelo F, et al.
studies.summary: Prospective cohort of 8,762 men aged 20-80 in the Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study, with strength measured by 1-rep max leg press and bench press and followed for about 19 years. Men in the middle and top thirds of strength had roughly 23-28% lower all-cause mortality than the weakest third, and the link held after adjusting for cardiorespiratory fitness. It is observational, men only, and combines leg and upper-body strength, so it shows strength tracks with survival rather than proving leg training causes it.
studies.quote: Muscular strength is inversely and independently associated with death from all causes and cancer in men

studies.title: Exercise for preventing falls in older people living in the community
studies.authors: Sherrington C, Fairhall NJ, Wallbank GK, et al.
studies.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
studies.summary: Cochrane review of 108 randomised trials with 23,407 community-dwelling adults aged 60 and over, testing exercise programmes for fall prevention. Exercise cut the rate of falls by 23% (high-certainty evidence), and programmes combining balance and functional work with resistance training cut falls by about 34%. Resistance training alone had uncertain effects on falls, so leg strength work pays off most when paired with balance training.
studies.quote: Exercise programmes reduce the rate of falls and the number of people experiencing falls in older people living in the community

studies.title: Progressive resistance strength training for improving physical function in older adults
studies.authors: Liu CJ, Latham NK
studies.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
studies.summary: Cochrane review of 121 randomised trials with 6,700 older adults doing progressive resistance training, usually 2-3 times a week at high intensity. Training produced a large gain in muscle strength (SMD 0.84) and a moderate-to-large improvement in getting out of a chair, with a smaller gain in gait speed. Effects on broad physical ability were small and adverse events were poorly reported, so the clearest benefit is strength and basic lower-body function.
studies.quote: This review provides evidence that PRT is an effective intervention for improving physical functioning in older people

studies.title: Muscle-strengthening activities are associated with lower risk and mortality in major non-communicable diseases: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies
studies.authors: Momma H, Kawakami R, Honda T, et al.
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 prospective cohort studies on muscle-strengthening activity and disease and death, independent of aerobic activity. Muscle-strengthening was linked to 10-17% lower risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease, total cancer and diabetes, with the biggest benefit at about 30-60 minutes per week. The curve was J-shaped, so more than an hour or so a week showed no added mortality benefit, and all included data are observational.
studies.quote: Muscle-strengthening activities were associated with a 10-17% lower risk of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular disease (CVD), total cancer, diabetes and lung cancer

studies.title: Dose-response relationship between weekly resistance training volume and increases in muscle mass: A systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
studies.summary: Meta-regression of 15 training studies (34 treatment groups) testing how weekly resistance training volume affects muscle growth. Each additional weekly set was associated with about 0.37% more muscle gain, and higher-volume groups gained about 3.9% more than lower-volume groups. The studies were small and short, and the three-level comparison (under 5, 5-9, 10+ sets per muscle) only trended toward significance.
studies.quote: The findings indicate a graded dose-response relationship whereby increases in RT volume produce greater gains in muscle hypertrophy

studies.title: Effects of Resistance Training Frequency on Measures of Muscle Hypertrophy: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Schoenfeld BJ, Ogborn D, Krieger JW
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 10 trials comparing how often a muscle group is trained per week, with volume equated. Training a muscle twice a week produced a larger hypertrophy effect size than once a week (0.49 vs 0.30). Whether three times a week beats twice is unknown, and the evidence base is small, but hitting arms and back at least twice weekly is a reasonable target.
studies.quote: frequencies of training twice a week promote superior hypertrophic outcomes to once a week

studies.title: Efficacy of Split Versus Full-Body Resistance Training on Strength and Muscle Growth: A Systematic Review With Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Ramos-Campo DJ, Benito-Peinado PJ, Andreu-Caravaca L, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of strength and conditioning research
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies (392 healthy adults) comparing split routines with full-body routines. Strength gains in bench press and lower limbs, and muscle growth in arms, thighs and lean mass, were statistically similar between the two approaches. The studies were small and volume was matched, so the practical point is that full-body sessions work as well as splits and the choice can rest on schedule and preference.
studies.quote: does not significantly impact either strength gains or muscle hypertrophy when volume is equated

studies.title: American College of Sports Medicine position stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults
studies.authors: American College of Sports Medicine
studies.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise
studies.summary: ACSM position stand setting out evidence-based progression models for resistance training in healthy adults. It recommends 2-3 sessions a week for novices, 8-12 rep loads to start, large-muscle and multi-joint exercises before small ones, and emphasis on multi-joint lifts involving the whole body. It is a consensus document built largely on short training studies, and it is now dated (2009), though its core advice has held up.
studies.quote: It is also recommended that emphasis be placed on multiple-joint exercises especially those involving the total body

studies.title: World Health Organization 2020 guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour
studies.authors: Bull FC, Al-Ansari SS, Biddle S, et al.
studies.summary: WHO 2020 physical activity guidelines, built by an expert group from updated systematic reviews across all ages and several special populations. Adults are advised to do 150-300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly plus muscle-strengthening activity involving all major muscle groups on two or more days. This is a population-level minimum rather than an optimal program, but a full-body session twice a week satisfies the strength part in one go.
studies.quote: These guidelines highlight the importance of regularly undertaking both aerobic and muscle strengthening activities

studies.title: Is running associated with a lower risk of all-cause, cardiovascular and cancer mortality, and is the more the better? A systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.authors: Pedisic Z, Shrestha N, Kovalchik S, et al.
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 14 studies from six prospective cohorts with 232,149 participants and 25,951 deaths. Any running was associated with 27% lower all-cause, 30% lower cardiovascular and 23% lower cancer mortality compared with no running. No dose-response was found for frequency, duration, pace or volume, so a single weekly run captures much of the benefit and more is not clearly better.
studies.quote: Any amount of running, even just once a week, is better than no running

studies.title: Leisure-time running reduces all-cause and cardiovascular mortality risk
studies.authors: Lee DC, Pate RR, Lavie CJ, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
studies.summary: Prospective cohort of 55,137 adults in the Aerobics Center Longitudinal Study followed for a mean of 15 years. Runners had 30% lower all-cause and 45% lower cardiovascular mortality than non-runners, about 3 extra years of life expectancy, and even under 6 miles a week was enough. It is observational and runners may differ from non-runners in other ways, but persistent runners over time saw the largest benefit.
studies.quote: Compared with nonrunners, runners had 30% and 45% lower adjusted risks of all-cause and cardiovascular mortality, respectively, with a 3-year life expectancy benefit

studies.title: Cardiorespiratory fitness as a quantitative predictor of all-cause mortality and cardiovascular events in healthy men and women: a meta-analysis
studies.authors: Kodama S, Saito K, Tanaka S, et al.
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of 33 cohort studies with about 103,000 healthy adults linking measured cardiorespiratory fitness to mortality and heart disease. Each 1-MET higher fitness level, roughly a 1 km/h faster running speed, was associated with 13% lower all-cause mortality and 15% lower cardiovascular events. Low-fit people (under 7.9 METs) had 70% higher mortality than high-fit people, so regular running is a practical way to move up the fitness scale.
studies.quote: Better CRF was associated with lower risk of all-cause mortality and CHD/CVD

studies.title: Leisure time physical activity and mortality: a detailed pooled analysis of the dose-response relationship
studies.authors: Arem H, Moore SC, Patel A, Hartge P, et al.
studies.summary: This pooled six US and European cohorts covering 661,137 adults and 116,686 deaths over a median of 14 years of follow-up. Meeting the 150-minute moderate-activity minimum was linked to 31% lower mortality, with the benefit leveling off at 3-5 times that amount (39% lower) and no sign of harm at 10 times or more. It is observational and self-reported, so fitter, healthier people may simply exercise more, but the dose-response shape is consistent.
studies.quote: An upper threshold for mortality benefit occurred at 3 to 5 times the physical activity recommendation

studies.title: Long-Term Leisure-Time Physical Activity Intensity and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality: A Prospective Cohort of US Adults
studies.authors: Lee DH, Rezende LFM, Joh HK, Keum N, et al.
studies.summary: This study followed 116,221 US nurses and health professionals for 30 years, with activity reassessed up to 15 times, and recorded 47,596 deaths. Meeting the moderate-activity guideline (150-299 min/week) was tied to 19-25% lower mortality, and the near-maximum benefit came at about 300-600 min/week of moderate activity. Above that there was no clear extra benefit or harm, and the cohort is mostly white health professionals, so causation and generalizability are limited.
studies.quote: Meeting the long-term leisure-time MPA guideline (150-299 min/wk) was similarly associated with lower mortality

studies.title: Much Ado About Zone 2: A Narrative Review Assessing the Efficacy of Zone 2 Training for Improving Mitochondrial Capacity and Cardiorespiratory Fitness in the General Population
studies.authors: Storoschuk KL, Moran-MacDonald A, Gibala MJ, Gurd BJ
studies.summary: This narrative review examines the training-study evidence behind the popular claim that Zone 2 (below lactate threshold) is the best intensity for mitochondria and fat oxidation. It concludes the evidence does not support Zone 2 as optimal, and that higher intensities matter more when weekly training time is limited. Zone 2 is still useful as volume, but the specific mitochondrial hype comes mostly from observations of elite athletes, not trials in ordinary people.
studies.quote: We conclude that current evidence does not support Zone 2 training as the optimal intensity for improving mitochondrial or fatty acid oxidative capacity.

studies.title: Superior cardiovascular effect of aerobic interval training versus moderate continuous training in heart failure patients: a randomized study
studies.authors: Wisløff U, Støylen A, Loennechen JP, Bruvold M, et al.
studies.summary: This trial randomized 27 elderly patients with post-heart-attack heart failure to 4x4-minute intervals at 95% of peak heart rate, moderate continuous training at 70%, or usual care, three times a week for 12 weeks. VO2peak rose 46% with intervals versus 14% with moderate training, and only the interval group showed reverse remodeling of the heart. It is the founding study of the Norwegian 4x4, but it was very small and a much larger later trial (SMARTEX-HF) did not confirm intervals were superior.
studies.quote: VO2peak increased more with aerobic interval training than moderate continuous training (46% versus 14%, P<0.001)

studies.title: Effect of exercise training for five years on all cause mortality in older adults-the Generation 100 study: randomised controlled trial
studies.authors: Stensvold D, Viken H, Steinshamn SL, Dalen H, et al.
studies.summary: Generation 100 randomized 1,567 Norwegians aged 70-77 to twice-weekly 4x4 intervals at about 90% of peak heart rate, moderate continuous training, or national activity guidelines for five years. Overall mortality did not differ between exercise and control groups, though HIIT trended lower (HR 0.63 vs control; 0.51 vs moderate training, confidence intervals crossing 1). The result is a trend, not proof, and the participants were already healthy and active, which made differences hard to detect.
studies.quote: we observed a lower all cause mortality trend after HIIT compared with controls and MICT

studies.title: Effectiveness of High-Intensity Interval Training (HIT) and Continuous Endurance Training for VO2max Improvements: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Controlled Trials
studies.authors: Milanović Z, Sporiš G, Weston M
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 28 controlled trials (723 healthy adults aged 18-45) comparing interval training, continuous endurance training and no exercise on VO2max. Both raised VO2max substantially (about 5.5 and 4.9 mL/kg/min versus controls), with intervals adding a small extra gain of about 1.2 mL/kg/min over continuous training. The edge for intervals is real but small, and the trials were short and mostly in young people.
studies.quote: Endurance training and HIT both elicit large improvements in the VO2max of healthy, young to middle-aged adults

studies.title: Number of Sprint Repetitions in a Sprint Interval Training Session Does Not Moderate Improvements in V̇O2max With Training: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
studies.authors: Hutchinson M, Kinghorn DJ, Hall ECR, Metcalfe RS, et al.
studies.journal: Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 93 trials from 78 studies (1,188 mostly untrained people) of at least two weeks of all-out cycling sprint training. Sprint interval training raised VO2max by about 8.3%, and adding more sprints per session made essentially no difference. A few sprints per session is enough for fitness, but the data come from cycle-ergometer studies in untrained people, so gains in already-fit people will be smaller.
studies.quote: SIT produced an 8.3% increase in V̇O2max (95% CrI: 7.0 to 9.5%).

studies.title: Twelve Weeks of Sprint Interval Training Improves Indices of Cardiometabolic Health Similar to Traditional Endurance Training despite a Five-Fold Lower Exercise Volume and Time Commitment
studies.authors: Gillen JB, Martin BJ, MacInnis MJ, Skelly LE, et al.
studies.summary: Sedentary men were randomized to 12 weeks of sprint intervals (3 x 20-second all-out sprints, 10 minutes total), 45 minutes of moderate continuous cycling, or no training, three times a week. Both training groups improved peak oxygen uptake by 19% and improved insulin sensitivity and muscle mitochondrial content to a similar degree. The trial is small (25 men, 9 in the sprint group), so it shows sprints can match longer cardio on these markers, not that they beat it.
studies.quote: Peak oxygen uptake increased after training by 19% in both groups

studies.title: Skeletal muscle power: a critical determinant of physical functioning in older adults
studies.authors: Reid KF, Fielding RA
studies.summary: This review summarizes cross-sectional, longitudinal and training studies on muscle power (force times speed) in older adults. It reports that power falls earlier and faster with age than strength and predicts functional limitations better than strength does. It supports keeping some fast, explosive work like sprints as you age, but it is a narrative review and does not test sprinting itself.
studies.quote: Muscle power declines earlier and more precipitously with advancing age compared with muscle strength.

studies.title: Social relationships and mortality risk: a meta-analytic review
studies.authors: Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Layton JB
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of 148 prospective studies (308,849 people, average follow-up about 7.5 years) on social relationships and mortality. People with stronger social relationships had 50% greater odds of survival (OR 1.50), and complex measures of social integration showed an even larger effect (OR 1.91). The authors compare the effect to smoking and exceeding obesity and inactivity, but these are observational data that cannot fully separate cause from confounding by health.
studies.quote: The influence of social relationships on risk for mortality is comparable with well-established risk factors for mortality

studies.title: Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review
studies.authors: Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Baker M, et al.
studies.journal: Perspectives on psychological science : a journal of the Association for Psychological Science
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of prospective studies (70 studies, about 3.4 million people) on objective social isolation, subjective loneliness and living alone as predictors of death. After adjusting for confounders, social isolation raised the odds of death by 29%, loneliness by 26%, and living alone by 32%. Effects were stronger in people under 65, and like all such data it is observational, but it shows both being alone and feeling alone carry risk.
studies.quote: social isolation odds ratio (OR) = 1.29, loneliness OR = 1.26, and living alone OR = 1.32

studies.title: Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for coronary heart disease and stroke: systematic review and meta-analysis of longitudinal observational studies
studies.authors: Valtorta NK, Kanaan M, Gilbody S, et al.
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 16 longitudinal datasets (4,628 coronary heart disease and 3,002 stroke events over 3-21 years) in high-income countries. Poor social relationships were linked to a 29% higher risk of coronary heart disease (RR 1.29) and a 32% higher risk of stroke (RR 1.32). Confidence intervals were wide and it is unknown whether interventions that reduce loneliness lower these risks, but it points to cardiovascular disease as one pathway.
studies.quote: Poor social relationships were associated with a 29% increase in risk of incident CHD

studies.title: Spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is associated with good health and wellbeing
studies.authors: White MP, Alcock I, Grellier J, et al.
studies.summary: Cross-sectional analysis of 19,806 adults from England's nationally representative MENE survey, relating time spent in nature in the past 7 days to self-reported health and wellbeing. People with at least 120 minutes of nature contact per week were more likely to report good health (OR 1.59) and high wellbeing (OR 1.23), with benefits peaking at 200-300 minutes and no gain below 120. It is cross-sectional and self-reported, so reverse causation is possible, but the 120 min/week threshold is a practical target and can be split across several visits.
studies.quote: Compared to no nature contact last week, the likelihood of reporting good health or high well-being became significantly greater with contact

studies.title: The health benefits of the great outdoors: A systematic review and meta-analysis of greenspace exposure and health outcomes
studies.authors: Twohig-Bennett C, Jones A
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 143 studies (103 observational, 40 interventional) covering about 100 health outcomes and greenspace exposure. Greater greenspace exposure was associated with lower cortisol, heart rate and diastolic blood pressure, 28% lower type 2 diabetes risk, and lower all-cause (OR 0.69) and cardiovascular mortality. Many pooled results came from poor-quality, highly heterogeneous studies, so the direction is consistent but the effect sizes are uncertain.
studies.quote: Greenspace exposure is associated with numerous health benefits in intervention and observational studies

studies.title: Green spaces and mortality: a systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies
studies.authors: Rojas-Rueda D, Nieuwenhuijsen MJ, Gascon M, et al.
studies.summary: WHO-funded meta-analysis of 9 cohort studies (over 8.3 million people in seven countries) relating satellite-measured greenness around the home (NDVI) to all-cause mortality. Each 0.1 increase in greenness within 500 m of home was associated with a 4% lower risk of death (HR 0.96). This measures living near green space, not deliberately spending time in it, and heterogeneity was high, so it supports the general idea rather than a specific weekly dose.
studies.quote: We found evidence of an inverse association between surrounding greenness and all-cause mortality

studies.title: Seafood Long-Chain n-3 Polyunsaturated Fatty Acids and Cardiovascular Disease: A Science Advisory From the American Heart Association
studies.authors: Rimm EB, Appel LJ, Chiuve SE, et al.
studies.summary: American Heart Association science advisory reviewing observational studies and trials on seafood omega-3 fats and cardiovascular disease. It concludes that 1-2 seafood meals per week lower the risk of heart failure, coronary heart disease, ischemic stroke and sudden cardiac death. The benefit is clearest when fish replaces less healthy foods, and the authors note longer dietary trials are still needed.
studies.quote: We conclude that 1 to 2 seafood meals per week be included to reduce the risk of congestive heart failure, coronary heart disease

studies.title: Fish intake, contaminants, and human health: evaluating the risks and the benefits
studies.authors: Mozaffarian D, Rimm EB
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis in JAMA weighing the cardiovascular benefits of fish against risks from mercury, dioxins and PCBs. Eating 1-2 servings a week, especially oily fish, was associated with 36% lower coronary death and 17% lower total mortality. Benefits outweigh contaminant risks for most adults, but very high eaters and women of childbearing age should limit high-mercury species.
studies.quote: reduces risk of coronary death by 36% (95% confidence interval, 20%-50%; P<.001) and total mortality by 17%

studies.title: Fish Consumption and the Risk of Chronic Disease: An Umbrella Review of Meta-Analyses of Prospective Cohort Studies
studies.authors: Jayedi A, Shab-Bidar S
studies.summary: Umbrella review of 34 meta-analyses covering 298 prospective cohort studies on fish intake and 40 chronic disease outcomes. Each extra 100 g/day of fish was linked to 8% lower all-cause mortality and 25% lower cardiovascular mortality, with lower risk of heart attack, stroke, heart failure and depression. The evidence is observational and rated moderate at best, and there was no clear link with most cancers.
studies.quote: evidence of moderate quality suggests that fish consumption is associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease, depression, and mortality

studies.title: Meat nutritional composition and nutritive role in the human diet
studies.authors: Pereira PM, Vicente AF
studies.summary: Narrative review of the nutritional composition of meat and its role in the human diet. It describes meat as a rich source of high-quality protein, iron, vitamin B12 and other B vitamins, zinc, selenium and phosphorus. It is a composition review rather than an outcome study, and it explicitly advises moderation and separating fresh meat cuts from processed products.
studies.quote: Meat is a valuable source of high biological value protein, iron, vitamin B12 as well as other B complex vitamins, zinc, selenium and phosphorus

studies.title: Red and Processed Meat Consumption and Risk for All-Cause Mortality and Cardiometabolic Outcomes: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis of Cohort Studies
studies.authors: Zeraatkar D, Han MA, Guyatt GH, et al.
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 55 cohorts with over 4 million participants on red and processed meat and mortality and cardiometabolic disease. Cutting unprocessed red meat by 3 servings a week was associated with a very small reduction in cardiovascular death, stroke, heart attack and type 2 diabetes, with similar small effects for processed meat. The evidence was low certainty, which supports eating unprocessed red meat in moderation but does not show high intake is harmless.
studies.quote: between red and processed meat consumption and all-cause mortality and adverse cardiometabolic outcomes is very small, and the evidence is of low certainty

studies.title: Meat consumption and risk of 25 common conditions: outcome-wide analyses in 475,000 men and women in the UK Biobank study
studies.authors: Papier K, Fensom GK, Knuppel A, et al.
studies.summary: UK Biobank cohort of about 475,000 adults followed for 8 years, testing meat intake against 25 common non-cancer conditions. Each extra 70 g/day of red and processed meat was linked to 15% higher heart disease risk and 30% higher diabetes risk, while unprocessed red meat was linked to 20% lower iron-deficiency anaemia per 50 g/day. Much of the excess risk shrank after adjusting for BMI, so the honest read is that a modest amount supplies iron while high intake carries risk.
studies.quote: Higher consumption of unprocessed red meat alone was associated with a lower risk of iron deficiency anaemia

studies.title: Priority Micronutrient Density in Foods
studies.authors: Beal T, Ortenzi F
studies.summary: Analysis of an aggregated global food composition database ranking foods by density of six commonly lacking micronutrients: iron, zinc, folate, vitamin A, calcium and vitamin B12. Organ meats ranked as the top source of these priority micronutrients, ahead of small fish, leafy greens, shellfish and beef. This is a nutrient-density ranking, not a health outcome study, so it shows what organ meat supplies rather than proving it improves health.
studies.quote: the top sources of priority micronutrients are organs, small fish, dark green leafy vegetables, bivalves, crustaceans, goat, beef, eggs

studies.title: Characterization of Hanwoo Bovine By-products by Means of Yield, Physicochemical and Nutritional Compositions
studies.authors: Seong PN, Kang GH, Park KM, et al.
studies.journal: Korean journal for food science of animal resources
studies.summary: Laboratory analysis of yield and nutrient composition across edible by-products of Korean Hanwoo cattle, including liver, kidney, heart and spleen. Liver had the highest vitamin A, riboflavin, niacin and copper content of the organs tested, and most by-products were good sources of essential amino acids and minerals. It is a single-breed composition study with no health outcomes, so it supports liver as nutrient-dense but nothing more.
studies.quote: Liver had the highest vitamin A, B2 and niacin contents whereas the highest B1 and B5 contents were found in kidney

studies.title: The acute and chronic toxic effects of vitamin A
studies.authors: Penniston KL, Tanumihardjo SA
studies.journal: The American journal of clinical nutrition
studies.summary: Review in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition of the acute and chronic toxic effects of preformed vitamin A from liver and supplements. It notes that preformed vitamin A intake often exceeds the RDA in developed countries and that intakes only about twice the RDA have been linked to osteoporosis and hip fracture. Liver is very high in preformed vitamin A, so a small weekly portion is sensible, and pregnant women and supplement users should be especially careful.
studies.quote: Osteoporosis and hip fracture are associated with preformed vitamin A intakes that are only twice the current RDA

studies.title: Effect of forest bathing trips on human immune function
studies.authors: Li Q
studies.summary: Review of a series of small Japanese studies in which adults took 3-day/2-night forest trips and had natural killer (NK) cell activity, anticancer proteins and urinary adrenaline measured before, during and up to 30 days after. NK activity and NK cell counts rose on forest days, adrenaline fell, and the NK boost lasted over 30 days, while a city tourist trip had no such effect. The studies are small, unblinded and measure immune markers rather than cancer outcomes, so the anticancer framing is a hypothesis.
studies.quote: suggesting that a forest bathing trip once a month would enable individuals to maintain a higher level of NK activity

studies.title: Spending at least 120 minutes a week in nature is associated with good health and wellbeing
studies.authors: White MP, Alcock I, Grellier J, et al.
studies.summary: Nationally representative English survey of 19,806 adults linking minutes of recreational nature contact in the past week to self-rated health and wellbeing. People with 120-179 minutes a week were about 59% more likely to report good health than those with none, with benefits plateauing at 200-300 minutes. It is cross-sectional and self-reported, but it gives a practical weekly target and found it did not matter whether the time came in one visit or several.
studies.quote: Compared to no nature contact last week, the likelihood of reporting good health or high well-being became significantly greater with contact

studies.title: The health benefits of the great outdoors: A systematic review and meta-analysis of greenspace exposure and health outcomes
studies.authors: Twohig-Bennett C, Jones A
studies.summary: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 103 observational and 40 interventional studies covering about 100 health outcomes related to greenspace exposure. More greenspace was linked to lower cortisol, heart rate and diastolic blood pressure, and to lower type 2 diabetes risk (OR 0.72) and all-cause mortality (OR 0.69). The authors flag poor study quality and high heterogeneity, and most data are about living near greenery, not scheduled forest visits.
studies.quote: Greenspace exposure is associated with numerous health benefits in intervention and observational studies

studies.title: Mushroom Consumption and Incident Dementia in Elderly Japanese: The Ohsaki Cohort 2006 Study
studies.authors: Zhang S, Tomata Y, Sugiyama K, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Geriatrics Society
studies.summary: Prospective cohort of 13,230 Japanese adults aged 65 and older followed for 5.7 years for incident dementia. People eating mushrooms three or more times a week had a 19% lower dementia risk (HR 0.81) than those eating them less than once a week, while 1-2 times a week showed no clear benefit. It is observational and diet was self-reported once, so mushroom eaters may differ in other ways, and the paper is not open access.
studies.quote: This cohort study suggests that frequent mushroom consumption is significantly associated with a lower risk of incident dementia

studies.title: Higher Mushroom Consumption Is Associated with Lower Risk of Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies
studies.authors: Ba DM, Ssentongo P, Beelman RB, et al.
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of 17 observational studies comparing the highest and lowest mushroom intakes against cancer risk. Higher intake was associated with 34% lower total cancer risk (RR 0.66) and 35% lower breast cancer risk. Eleven of the 17 studies were case-control designs prone to recall bias, and only breast cancer held up on a site-by-site basis.
studies.quote: Higher mushroom consumption was associated with lower risk of total cancer (pooled RR for the highest compared with the lowest consumption groups: 0.66

studies.title: Mushroom consumption and cardiometabolic health outcomes in the general population: a systematic review
studies.authors: Hong JY, Kim MK, Yang N
studies.summary: Systematic review of 5 prospective cohorts and 4 clinical trials on mushroom intake and cardiometabolic outcomes in the general population. It found suggestive improvements in blood glucose, HDL-related indices, hs-CRP and body weight measures, but no association with cardiovascular disease, stroke or type 2 diabetes. The honest takeaway is that mushrooms look like a good food rather than a proven heart-disease intervention, because there are only one or two studies per outcome.
studies.quote: Due to the scarcity of available studies, drawing definitive conclusions is premature

studies.title: Frequency of nut consumption and mortality risk in the PREDIMED nutrition intervention trial
studies.authors: Guasch-Ferré M, Bulló M, Martínez-González MÁ, et al.
studies.summary: Analysis of 7,216 Spanish adults aged 55-80 at high cardiovascular risk in the PREDIMED trial, followed for a median of 4.8 years. People eating more than three servings of nuts a week had 39% lower all-cause mortality (HR 0.61) than non-consumers, with similar reductions in cardiovascular and cancer deaths. The nut-frequency comparison is observational within a trial population, so healthier habits among nut eaters could explain part of it.
studies.quote: Compared to non-consumers, subjects consuming nuts>3 servings/week (32% of the cohort) had a 39% lower mortality risk

studies.title: Association of nut consumption with total and cause-specific mortality
studies.authors: Bao Y, Han J, Hu FB, et al.
studies.journal: The New England Journal of Medicine
studies.summary: Two large US cohorts (76,464 women and 42,498 men) were followed for up to 30 years with repeated diet questionnaires. Compared with non-eaters, death risk was 13% lower at two to four servings a week and 20% lower at seven or more, a steady dose-response. It is observational and part-funded by a tree-nut industry foundation, though the findings match other independent cohorts.
studies.quote: the frequency of nut consumption was inversely associated with total and cause-specific mortality, independently of other predictors of death

studies.title: Nut consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer, all-cause and cause-specific mortality: a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies
studies.authors: Aune D, Keum N, Giovannucci E, et al.
studies.summary: Dose-response meta-analysis of 20 prospective studies on nut intake and cardiovascular disease, cancer and death. Each extra 28 g a day was linked to 29% lower coronary heart disease risk, 15% lower total cancer risk and 22% lower all-cause mortality, with tree nuts and peanuts performing similarly. Heterogeneity was moderate and all included studies are observational, so the 4.4 million attributable deaths figure assumes causality.
studies.quote: Higher nut intake is associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality

studies.title: Foods and food groups associated with the incidence of colorectal polyps: the Adventist Health Study
studies.authors: Tantamango YM, Knutsen SF, Beeson WL, et al.
studies.summary: Analysis of 2,818 Adventist Health Study participants who had a colonoscopy, comparing diet frequency against 441 self-reported colorectal polyp cases. Eating brown rice at least once a week was linked to 40% lower polyp risk, and legumes three or more times a week to 33% lower risk. Polyps were self-reported and the cohort is unusually health-conscious, so this is a hypothesis-level signal, not proof.
studies.quote: Consumption of brown rice at least 1 time/wk reduced the risk by 40%

studies.title: White rice, brown rice, and risk of type 2 diabetes in US men and women
studies.authors: Sun Q, Spiegelman D, van Dam RM, et al.
studies.summary: Three US cohorts covering 39,765 men and 157,463 women tracked white and brown rice intake against new type 2 diabetes. Two or more servings of brown rice a week was linked to 11% lower diabetes risk, while five or more servings of white rice a week was linked to 17% higher risk. Brown rice eaters were few and health-conscious, and swapping white rice for whole grains in general showed a larger (36%) estimated benefit than brown rice alone.
studies.quote: Substitution of whole grains, including brown rice, for white rice may lower risk of type 2 diabetes

studies.title: Arsenic in cooked rice foods: Assessing health risks and mitigation options
studies.authors: Kumarathilaka P, Seneweera S, Ok YS, et al.
studies.summary: Review of why cooked rice can carry high inorganic arsenic and which post-harvest and cooking methods reduce it. Washing rice and cooking it in excess water, or in percolating water, lowers arsenic, though some methods also strip nutrients. This is the main caveat to a rice habit: brown rice keeps more arsenic in its bran than white, so keep portions moderate, cook it like pasta, and vary your grains.
studies.quote: Sequential washing of raw rice grains and use of an excess volume of water for cooking also decrease As content in cooked rice

studies.title: Blood docosahexaenoic acid and eicosapentaenoic acid in vegans: Associations with age and gender and effects of an algal-derived omega-3 fatty acid supplement
studies.authors: Sarter B, Kelsey KS, Schwartz TA, et al.
studies.summary: Cross-sectional measurement of the omega-3 index in 165 long-term vegans, plus an uncontrolled 4-month trial giving 254 mg/day of algal DHA+EPA to 46 vegans with an index below 4%. The average vegan index was 3.7%, and supplementation raised it from 3.1% to 4.8%. There was no placebo group and the dose was daily, so the weekly schedule is an extrapolation from how slowly red-cell omega-3 levels change.
studies.quote: The vegans responded robustly to a relatively low dose of a vegetarian omega-3 supplement

studies.title: Algal-oil capsules and cooked salmon: nutritionally equivalent sources of docosahexaenoic acid
studies.authors: Arterburn LM, Oken HA, Bailey Hall E, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American Dietetic Association
studies.summary: Randomized open-label trial in 32 healthy adults comparing 600 mg/day DHA from algal-oil capsules with the same DHA from cooked salmon for two weeks. DHA rose about 80% in plasma phospholipids and about 25% in red blood cells in both groups, with no meaningful difference between them. It shows algae DHA is absorbed as well as fish DHA, but it is short, small and was run by an algal-oil manufacturer.
studies.quote: algal-oil DHA capsules represent a safe and convenient source of non-fish-derived DHA

studies.title: Omega-3 fatty acids for the primary and secondary prevention of cardiovascular disease
studies.authors: Abdelhamid AS, Brown TJ, Brainard JS, et al.
studies.journal: The Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews
studies.summary: Cochrane review of 86 randomized trials (162,796 people) lasting at least a year that raised long-chain omega-3 or ALA intake. Long-chain omega-3 had little or no effect on all-cause mortality (RR 0.97) but slightly reduced coronary heart disease events (RR 0.91) and lowered triglycerides about 15%. This is the honest ceiling: algae DHA fills a nutrient gap for plant-based eaters, but don't expect large heart-protection effects.
studies.quote: Moderate- and low-certainty evidence suggests that increasing LCn3 slightly reduces risk of coronary heart disease mortality and events

studies.title: Association of Cardiorespiratory Fitness With Long-term Mortality Among Adults Undergoing Exercise Treadmill Testing
studies.authors: Mandsager K, Harb S, Cremer P, et al.
studies.summary: Retrospective cohort of 122,007 patients who had treadmill exercise testing at the Cleveland Clinic, followed for a median 8.4 years. Elite fitness was associated with 80% lower mortality than low fitness, and being unfit carried as much or more risk than smoking, diabetes or coronary disease. The cohort was patients referred for testing, not the general public, but no upper limit of benefit was seen for fitness.
studies.quote: Cardiorespiratory fitness is inversely associated with long-term mortality with no observed upper limit of benefit

studies.title: Cardiorespiratory Fitness and Mortality Risk Across the Spectra of Age, Race, and Sex
studies.authors: Kokkinos P, Faselis C, Samuel IBH, et al.
studies.journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology
studies.summary: Cohort of 750,302 US veterans aged 30-95 with treadmill-measured fitness, followed for a median 10.2 years. The least fit 20% had about 4-fold higher mortality than the most fit, and the lowest risk was around 14 METs with no increase at extremely high fitness. The population was mostly older men, but the graded benefit held across age, sex and race.
studies.quote: Being unfit carried a greater risk than any of the cardiac risk factors examined

studies.title: Cardiac arrest during long-distance running races
studies.authors: Kim JH, Malhotra R, Chiampas G, et al.
studies.journal: The New England journal of medicine
studies.summary: Registry study of cardiac arrests among 10.9 million runners in US marathons and half-marathons from 2000 to 2010. Cardiac arrest occurred in 0.54 per 100,000 participants, higher in marathons (1.01 per 100,000) than half-marathons and mostly in men, often from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy or coronary disease. The absolute risk of long-distance running is very low, but it is not zero, so training up gradually and checking heart risk factors is sensible.
studies.quote: Marathons and half-marathons are associated with a low overall risk of cardiac arrest and sudden death

studies.title: Effect of training on lactate/ventilatory thresholds: a meta-analysis
studies.authors: Londeree BR
studies.summary: This meta-analysis combined 85 study groups from 34 studies to see how training intensity affects oxygen uptake at the lactate or ventilatory threshold. Sedentary people improved their threshold strongly (effect size 2.32), while already-trained people gained less and tended to respond better to higher intensity (effect size 1.1 vs 0.4). It is old and small by modern standards, but it supports threshold work for beginners and suggests trained people need harder sessions too.
studies.quote: training at an intensity near the lactate or ventilatory threshold is an adequate training stimulus for improving the thresholds for sedentary subjects

studies.title: Polarized training has greater impact on key endurance variables than threshold, high intensity, or high volume training
studies.authors: Stöggl T, Sperlich B
studies.summary: Forty-eight well-trained runners, cyclists, triathletes and skiers were randomized to nine weeks of polarized, threshold, high-intensity, or high-volume training. Polarized training produced the largest gains (VO2peak up 11.7%), while the threshold-focused group showed no further improvement in most performance measures. This argues against making threshold the bulk of your training, while still allowing it as an occasional session or test; groups were small (about 12 each) and short.
studies.quote: THR or HVT did not lead to further improvements in performance related variables.

studies.title: Comparison of Polarized Versus Other Types of Endurance Training Intensity Distribution on Athletes' Endurance Performance: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis
studies.authors: Silva Oliveira P, Boppre G, Fonseca H
studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 17 studies (437 athletes) comparing polarized training with other intensity distributions, including threshold-heavy plans, for at least four weeks. Polarized training gave a small edge in VO2peak (SMD 0.24), but time-trial results and speed or power at threshold improved about the same either way. In practice, how you spread intensity matters less than people claim, and a periodic threshold session or time trial is a reasonable way to track progress.
studies.quote: However, the effect of POL was similar to that of other TIDs on the remaining surrogates of endurance performance.

studies.title: Health effects of voluntary exposure to cold water - a continuing subject of debate
studies.authors: Esperland D, de Weerd L, Mercer JB
studies.summary: Literature review of 104 studies on the health effects of voluntary cold-water immersion and winter swimming in humans. Cold water appears to reduce or brown body fat and improve insulin sensitivity, and some studies report benefits for mood and immunity. Most studies were small, often single-sex, and used different temperatures and protocols, so the authors conclude benefits remain unproven and a subject of debate.
studies.quote: Some of the studies indicate that voluntary exposure to cold water has some beneficial health effects

studies.title: The Effect of Cold Showering on Health and Work: A Randomized Controlled Trial
studies.authors: Buijze GA, Sierevelt IN, van der Heijden BC, et al.
studies.summary: Randomized trial of 3,018 Dutch adults assigned to finish daily showers with 30, 60 or 90 seconds of cold water, or a usual-shower control, for 30 days then at their discretion for 60 more days. The cold-shower groups had 29% fewer sickness-absence days from work (IRR 0.71), but no reduction in the number of days actually ill. The trial was unblinded and outcomes were self-reported, so the effect may reflect perception or resilience more than immunity; duration of cold did not matter.
studies.quote: A routine (hot-to-) cold shower resulted in a statistical reduction of self-reported sickness absence but not illness days

studies.title: Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training
studies.authors: Roberts LA, Raastad T, Markworth JF, et al.
studies.summary: Two linked experiments: 21 active men strength trained for 12 weeks with either 10 minutes of cold-water immersion or active recovery after each session, plus a 9-man biopsy study of acute muscle signalling. The cold-water group gained less strength and muscle; type II fibre size rose 17% and myonuclei 26% with active recovery but not with cold immersion, and anabolic signalling was blunted. If building muscle is a goal, keep cold plunges away from lifting sessions (separate by several hours or do them on non-lifting days).
studies.quote: CWI attenuates the acute changes in satellite cell numbers and activity of kinases that regulate muscle hypertrophy

studies.title: Randomized controlled trial of once-per-week intermittent fasting for health improvement: the WONDERFUL trial
studies.authors: Bartholomew CL, Muhlestein JB, May HT, et al.
studies.summary: Intermountain researchers randomized 103 adults with metabolic syndrome features and modestly high LDL to 24-hour water-only fasts (twice weekly for 4 weeks, then once weekly for 22 weeks) or normal eating. The fasting did not lower LDL (the primary outcome) but did improve insulin resistance (HOMA-IR -0.75 vs -0.10) and metabolic syndrome score. Dropout was high (only 71 of 103 finished) and the schedule was weekly, so a once-a-month 24-hour fast is a much smaller dose than what was tested.
studies.quote: A low-frequency intermittent fasting regimen did not reduce LDL-C or improve cognitive function but significantly reduced both HOMA-IR and MSS.

studies.title: Relation of routine, periodic fasting to risk of diabetes mellitus, and coronary artery disease in patients undergoing coronary angiography
studies.authors: Horne BD, Muhlestein JB, May HT, et al.
studies.summary: Intermountain surveyed 200 patients having coronary angiography about routine periodic fasting (largely the monthly Latter-day Saint fast) and pooled them with 448 patients from an earlier study. Routine fasters had less diabetes (10.3% vs 22.0%, OR 0.41) and less coronary artery disease (63.2% vs 75.0%, OR 0.42). This is observational and fasters in Utah differ in religion and lifestyle from non-fasters, so it shows association, not that monthly fasting causes the benefit.
studies.quote: prospective hypothesis testing showed that routine periodic fasting was associated with a lower prevalence of DM in patients undergoing coronary angiography

studies.title: Flipping the Metabolic Switch: Understanding and Applying the Health Benefits of Fasting
studies.authors: Anton SD, Moehl K, Donahoo WT, et al.
studies.summary: This narrative review (Anton, Mattson and colleagues) describes what happens physiologically when a fast runs long enough to deplete liver glycogen and shift the body to burning fat and ketones. That 'metabolic switch' typically begins beyond about 12 hours without food, so a 24-hour fast clearly crosses it, and the authors argue it triggers stress-resistance and repair pathways. Much of the mechanistic support comes from animal studies, and the review itself calls for human trials that measure ketones to confirm dose and effect.
studies.quote: the point of negative energy balance at which liver glycogen stores are depleted and fatty acids are mobilized (typically beyond 12 hours after cessation of food intake)

studies.title: A single consumption of high amounts of the Brazil nuts improves lipid profile of healthy volunteers
studies.authors: Colpo E, Vilanova CD, Brenner Reetz LG, et al.
studies.summary: Ten healthy adults ate 0, 5, 20 or 50 g of Brazil nuts in a single sitting in a randomized crossover design, with blood drawn over the following 30 days. LDL fell and HDL rose within 9 hours of the 20 g and 50 g servings, and the full paper reports the lipid shift was still visible at 30 days. With only ten people this is the source of the 'once a month' idea, so treat it as intriguing pilot data, not proof.
studies.quote: the ingestion of a single serving of Brazil nut can acutely improve the serum lipid profile of healthy volunteers

studies.title: Effect of Brazil Nuts on Selenium Status, Blood Lipids, and Biomarkers of Oxidative Stress and Inflammation: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Clinical Trials
studies.authors: Godos J, Giampieri F, Micek A, et al.
studies.summary: Meta-analysis of eight randomized trials that fed people Brazil nuts and measured selenium, blood lipids and oxidative-stress markers. Brazil nuts reliably raised blood selenium (SMD 6.93) and glutathione peroxidase activity, but pooled changes in total, LDL and HDL cholesterol were not significant. The selenium benefit is solid; the cholesterol benefit that inspired the monthly habit is not confirmed by pooled trials.
studies.quote: a significant positive effect of Brazil nuts on selenium blood concentration (SMD = 6.93, 95% CI: 3.99; 9.87) was found

studies.title: Improving the selenium supply of vegans and omnivores with Brazil nut butter compared to a dietary supplement in a randomized controlled trial
studies.authors: Simon R, Lossow K, Pellowski D, et al.
studies.summary: Randomized trial of 44 vegans and 42 omnivores given placebo, Brazil nut butter, or a supplement each adding 55 µg selenium a day for two weeks. Vegans had lower selenium intake at baseline, and nut butter raised serum selenium and selenoprotein P as well as the supplement did, with a stronger effect in vegans. It supports Brazil nuts as an occasional selenium top-up for plant-based eaters, though the trial was short and measured biomarkers, not health outcomes.
studies.quote: Brazil nuts are a plant-based source of selenium suitable for vegans and omnivores to improve their selenium status when consumed once in a while

studies.title: Routine scale and polish for periodontal health in adults
studies.authors: Lamont T, Worthington HV, Clarkson JE, et al.
studies.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
studies.summary: Cochrane review of two UK general-practice randomized trials (1,711 adults without severe periodontitis who were regular dental attenders) comparing 6- or 12-monthly scale and polish versus no scheduled cleanings over 2-3 years. Routine scaling and polishing made little or no difference to gingivitis, pocket depth or oral-health quality of life (high-certainty evidence), though it modestly reduced tartar. The value of a checkup for low-risk people lies more in early detection than the cleaning itself; people with gum disease or high risk likely benefit more.
studies.quote: routine scale and polish treatment makes little or no difference to gingivitis, probing depths and oral health-related quality of life

studies.title: Treatment of periodontitis for glycaemic control in people with diabetes mellitus
studies.authors: Simpson TC, Clarkson JE, Worthington HV, et al.
studies.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
studies.summary: Cochrane review of 35 randomized trials (3,249 people with diabetes and periodontitis) comparing professional periodontal treatment below the gumline with no treatment or usual care. Treatment lowered HbA1c by about 0.43 percentage points at 3-4 months and 0.30 at 6 months (moderate-certainty evidence), a clinically meaningful drop similar to adding a second diabetes drug. This applies to people who already have gum disease and diabetes, and most trials lasted 12 months or less.
studies.quote: periodontal treatment using subgingival instrumentation improves glycaemic control in people with both periodontitis and diabetes by a clinically significant amount

studies.title: Oral care measures for preventing nursing home-acquired pneumonia
studies.authors: Cao Y, Liu C, Lin J, et al.
studies.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
studies.summary: Cochrane review of six randomized trials (6,244 nursing home residents) comparing professional oral care with usual self-administered oral care for preventing pneumonia. Professional care did not clearly reduce pneumonia incidence, but two trials found it may cut pneumonia-related deaths by more than half at 24 months (RR 0.43). All trials were at high risk of bias and the evidence is low certainty, and it applies to frail older adults rather than healthy people.
studies.quote: professional oral care may reduce the risk of pneumonia-associated mortality compared with usual oral care at 24 months' follow-up

studies.title: Ivermectin versus albendazole or thiabendazole for Strongyloides stercoralis infection.
studies.authors: Henriquez-Camacho C, Gotuzzo E, Echevarria J, et al.
studies.summary: This Cochrane review pooled seven randomized trials (1147 participants) comparing ivermectin with albendazole or thiabendazole in people with confirmed chronic Strongyloides infection. Ivermectin cured more people than albendazole (risk ratio 1.79, moderate-quality evidence) and was at least as well tolerated, with no serious adverse events reported. It applies only to diagnosed infection, ivermectin is prescription-only in the US, and nothing here supports taking it as a routine yearly cleanse.
studies.quote: Ivermectin results in more people cured than albendazole, and is at least as well tolerated.

studies.title: Efficacy of current drugs against soil-transmitted helminth infections: systematic review and meta-analysis.
studies.authors: Keiser J, Utzinger J
