studies.summary: This meta-analysis pooled 20 randomized trials of single-dose albendazole, mebendazole, levamisole and pyrantel pamoate against roundworm, hookworm and whipworm, mostly in children in highly endemic regions. Single-dose pyrantel pamoate, the main over-the-counter dewormer in the US, cured 88% of roundworm infections but only 31% of hookworm infections, and no pooled estimate was possible for whipworm. The pyrantel data are thin (131 and 152 patients), it does not cover many parasites, and the trials treated infected people rather than testing a yearly cleanse in healthy adults.
studies.quote: Single-dose oral albendazole, mebendazole, and pyrantel pamoate show high cure rates against A lumbricoides.

studies.title: Effectiveness of dried Carica papaya seeds against human intestinal parasitosis: a pilot study.
studies.authors: Okeniyi JA, Ogunlesi TA, Oyelami OA, Adeyemi LA
studies.summary: This small randomized pilot trial gave 60 Nigerian children with parasites confirmed on stool microscopy a single 20 mL dose of either air-dried papaya seed and honey elixir or honey alone. Stools cleared of parasites in 77% of the papaya group versus 17% of the honey group at 7 days, with no harmful effects reported. It is one small, short trial in infected children in a high-prevalence setting with no comparison to standard drugs, so it does not show that papaya seeds work as a cleanse for people without an infection.
studies.quote: Significantly more subjects given CPH elixir than those given honey had their stools cleared of parasites

studies.title: Usefulness of pumpkin seeds combined with areca nut extract in community-based treatment of human taeniasis in northwest Sichuan Province, China.
studies.authors: Li T, Ito A, Chen X, et al.
studies.summary: This non-randomized community study in Sichuan, China, treated 115 suspected tapeworm cases with pumpkin seeds plus areca nut extract and compared small groups given either one alone. In the 45 confirmed cases, 89% expelled intact worms after the combination, usually within about 2 hours, while pumpkin seeds alone worked in 9 of 12 confirmed cases but took about 14 hours. The groups were small and not randomized, nearly half of patients had nausea or dizziness, and areca nut is a known carcinogen, so this is not support for eating pumpkin seeds as a routine cleanse.
studies.quote: The pumpkin seed/areca combined treatment was indicated to be safe and highly effective (89%) for human taeniasis.

studies.title: General health checks in adults for reducing morbidity and mortality from disease
studies.authors: Krogsbøll LT, Jørgensen KJ, Gøtzsche PC
studies.journal: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews
studies.summary: Cochrane review of 17 randomised trials with about 252,000 adults comparing general health checks with no checks. Health checks had little or no effect on total mortality (RR 1.00), cancer mortality or cardiovascular mortality, based mostly on high-certainty evidence. This means broad untargeted checkups do not save lives on their own, so the value of a yearly blood test lies in specific, evidence-backed markers acted on when abnormal.
studies.quote: Health checks have little or no effect on total mortality (risk ratio (RR) 1.00, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.97 to 1.03

studies.title: Screening for Prediabetes and Type 2 Diabetes: US Preventive Services Task Force Recommendation Statement
studies.authors: US Preventive Services Task Force, Davidson KW, Barry MJ, et al.
studies.summary: USPSTF recommendation statement based on a commissioned systematic review of screening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in asymptomatic adults. It concludes with moderate certainty that screening adults aged 35-70 with overweight or obesity, and referring those with prediabetes to prevention programs, has a moderate net benefit (B grade). The recommendation is targeted to a risk group rather than everyone, which is how screening tends to earn its benefit.
studies.quote: The USPSTF recommends screening for prediabetes and type 2 diabetes in adults aged 35 to 70 years who have overweight or obesity

studies.title: Apolipoprotein B Particles and Cardiovascular Disease: A Narrative Review
studies.authors: Sniderman AD, Thanassoulis G, Glavinovic T, et al.
studies.summary: Narrative review in JAMA Cardiology of the biology and evidence behind apolipoprotein B as a measure of atherogenic lipoprotein particles. It argues apoB counts the particles that actually drive plaque and captures cardiovascular risk more accurately than LDL cholesterol or non-HDL cholesterol. It is a narrative review by advocates rather than a trial, but it makes a solid case for adding apoB to a routine lipid panel.
studies.quote: Apolipoprotein B unifies, amplifies, and simplifies the information from the conventional lipid markers as to the atherogenic risk attributable to the apoB lipoproteins

studies.title: Fasting-mimicking diet and markers/risk factors for aging, diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease
studies.authors: Wei M, Brandhorst S, Shelehchi M, et al.
studies.summary: 100 generally healthy US adults were randomized to normal eating or a 5-day low-calorie, low-protein fasting-mimicking diet (FMD) once a month for 3 months, with controls later crossed over. Three FMD cycles reduced body weight, trunk fat, blood pressure and IGF-1, with no serious adverse effects, and benefits were larger in people already at risk. It was short, unblinded, had notable dropout, and was run by the diet's inventor (Longo, who holds equity in the company selling it), so the results need independent confirmation.
studies.quote: Three FMD cycles reduced body weight, trunk, and total body fat; lowered blood pressure; and decreased insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1).

studies.title: Fasting-mimicking diet causes hepatic and blood markers changes indicating reduced biological age and disease risk
studies.authors: Brandhorst S, Levine ME, Wei M, et al.
studies.summary: This is a secondary, exploratory analysis of blood samples and liver MRI from FMD trial participants, replicated in a second clinical study. Three monthly 5-day FMD cycles were linked to lower insulin resistance, less liver fat, a younger immune profile, and a 2.5-year drop in median biological age independent of weight loss. Biological-age scores are surrogate markers, not lived years, and the work comes from the same group with a commercial stake in the product.
studies.quote: 3 FMD cycles were associated with a decrease of 2.5 years in median biological age, independent of weight loss

studies.title: Safety, health improvement and well-being during a 4 to 21-day fasting period in an observational study including 1422 subjects
studies.authors: Wilhelmi de Toledo F, Grundler F, Bergouignan A, et al.
studies.summary: This one-year observational study followed 1,422 people doing Buchinger fasts of 4 to 21 days (about 200-250 kcal/day of juice and broth) under daily medical supervision in a German clinic. Weight, waist and blood pressure fell, ketones rose, 93.2% reported no hunger, and adverse effects occurred in under 1%. There was no control group, the clinic ran the study, and participants were screened and supervised; people on insulin or blood-pressure drugs, those with eating disorders, and anyone fasting at home without guidance on medications and gradual refeeding should not assume the same safety record.
studies.quote: Adverse effects were reported in less than 1% of the participants.

policies.name: Free Trade
policies.why: Dropping every tariff and quota on your own, without waiting for anyone else, returns about $90 to $2,800 per dollar of adjustment cost. Countries that liberalise grow about 1.5 percentage points a year faster. The tariffs still in place in 2026 cost US households $760 to $940 a year each.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-edited Copenhagen Consensus benefit-cost estimates (Anderson 2012, 2015; Cambridge UP 2018 chapter) backed by peer-reviewed quasi-experimental and instrumental-variable evidence on growth (Wacziarg & Welch 2008 WBER; Frankel & Romer 1999 AER; Fajgelbaum et al. 2020 QJE). Even the narrowest peer-reviewed estimate (Feyrer et al. 2023, JBCA) is above 1.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: one country acting alone needs only ordinary tariff legislation, with working precedents in Hong Kong (no tariff on any import or export, HK Trade and Industry Department), Singapore, New Zealand's unilateral tariff cuts and Britain's 1846 Corn Law repeal.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Anderson (2015) finds developing-country BCRs of 2,100-4,700 versus 1,300-2,800 globally and ~160 million fewer people in extreme poverty by 2030; Feyrer et al. (2023) find ~100 for low/lower-middle-income countries versus ~5 for high-income; Fajgelbaum et al. (2020) show 2018 US tariffs fell fully on domestic buyers.
policies.summary: Unilaterally abolishing all tariffs and quotas, repealing anti-dumping duties, and simplifying border paperwork is among the best-evidenced policies in economics. Copenhagen Consensus estimates for full trade liberalisation, counting growth effects, return about $90 to $2,800 per $1 of adjustment cost, and liberalisers grow about 1.5 percentage points a year faster. The sub-policies also pay: anti-dumping repeal returns about 2-14 to 1 and trade facilitation about 11-640 to 1.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 4
policies.evidence: Free trade is among the best-evidenced policies in economics. The Copenhagen Consensus has asked the same question three times: what is the return on full global trade liberalisation? Each time, counting growth effects, the answer has been in the hundreds or thousands of dollars per dollar of cost.
policies.ratio: Both ends use Copenhagen Consensus estimates of full global liberalisation that include growth effects. Low end: 90. - Anderson (2012): "The net present value of the future benefits of a Doha agreement ranges from $12 trillion to $64 trillion. The costs are less than $400 billion in present value terms." - His reported global benefit-cost ratio is 90 to 180 (140 to 250 for developing countries). - The floor, 90, is the low end.
policies.counter: Feyrer et al. (2023) give the narrowest estimate. They model a 5% rise in world trade, static and first-year only, and find benefits of $700bn against costs of $100bn, a ratio of 11 globally and about 5 for high-income countries.

policies.name: Innovation Prizes
policies.why: Prizes and advance market commitments pay only when someone delivers a defined result, so donors buy outcomes rather than promises. The research they would fund has some of the best returns anywhere, about $11.80 to $348 per dollar when clean energy, farm and geoengineering research are weighted equally. It costs taxpayers nothing, which is the best price of all.
policies.grade_reason: The weighted range rests mainly on Galiana & Green's Copenhagen Consensus models (published in the Cambridge University Press volume 'Global Problems, Smart Solutions'), with a peer-reviewed JBCA estimate for ag R&D (Rosegrant et al. 2023) and peer-reviewed evidence that prizes and AMCs induce innovation (Brunt et al. 2012; Kremer et al. 2020). Not A-: no study measures the return on prize money itself, and the geoengineering figures are contested think-tank estimates.
policies.difficulty_reason: Easy: a single philanthropic or corporate funder can do it under existing law, and it has been done many times (Ansari X Prize, XPRIZE Carbon Removal 2025, Frontier AMC 2022, pneumococcal AMC).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Agricultural-yield prizes are pro-poor (Rosegrant et al. 2023 project 35% less hunger and 16% lower food prices in the Global South after 35 years, 2022-2056), while cheaper clean energy and climate-risk research benefit everyone; no source measures the distribution across the combined programme.
policies.summary: Privately funded prizes and advance market commitments pay out only when someone delivers a defined result: higher crop yields, cheaper clean energy, or answers about geoengineering. No study measures the return on prize money itself, but the research they would fund has some of the best returns in the literature: about $3-11 per dollar for clean-energy R&D (Copenhagen Consensus), $9-33 for agricultural R&D, and very high but contested figures for geoengineering research. Weighting the three areas equally, on the view that prize money flows to the highest-return results, gives about $11.80 to $348 of benefit per dollar, with no cost to taxpayers; weighting by the size of each research programme gives about $3 to $13.
policies.selected_by: Mission Innovation (governments' clean-energy R&D pledge, Paris 2015); Copenhagen Consensus R&D findings
policies.evidence: No study measures the return on prize money itself. The research these prizes would buy, however, has some of the highest returns in the literature. Galiana and Green (2012) find that more low-carbon energy research yields "benefits ranging from 3 to 11 times higher than cost, depending on rate of success and time horizon." Agricultural research does better.
policies.ratio: Each area takes the best published return on research spending. Low end: $11.80 per $1. - Energy technology: 3 (Galiana and Green 2012). - Agricultural yields: 7.5, the lowest ratio for a heat-resilient-crop advance market commitment aimed at West African maize or East African sorghum, the two most cost-effective targets (Glennerster et al. 2024). - Geoengineering: 25, for stratospheric aerosols (Bickel and Lane 2009, as reported by Pielke 2009). - Ratio: (3 + 7.5 + 25) ÷ 3 = 11.8. High end: $348 per $1. - Energy technology: 11.
policies.counter: The case against rests on the geoengineering figure. Goes, Tuana and Keller (2011) find that fully substituting aerosol geoengineering for emission cuts fails a cost-benefit test over a wide range of scenarios, because of the risk of stopping abruptly and the damage the aerosols do themselves.

policies.name: Maternal and Newborn Care
policies.why: Trained staff, clean delivery, drugs to stop bleeding, antibiotics and newborn resuscitation could prevent most newborn deaths in poor countries. Basic hospital upgrades return $62 to $80 per dollar on a full cost of about $4.7 billion a year, or $28.50 to $66.50 once the cost of raising the taxes that fund them is counted. Few things on this list save lives so cheaply, and private funders could carry much of the bill.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis (Madise et al. 2023, JBCA; Lomborg 2023 JBCA summary) whose intervention effects come from the trial-based Lives Saved Tool evidence summarised in the Lancet Every Newborn series (Bhutta et al. 2014).
policies.difficulty_reason: Needs a sustained government/donor scale-up to staff, equip and supply birth facilities in 55 countries (Madise et al. 2023), plus demand-generation payments for facility births on the model of India's Janani Suraksha Yojana, which Madise et al. use for costing.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The 55 low- and lower-middle-income countries modelled carry about 90% of global maternal and neonatal deaths; the welfare loss from these deaths is ~5.5% of their GDP (Madise et al. 2023).
policies.summary: Upgrade basic hospitals and health centres in poor countries so every birth has trained staff, clean delivery, drugs to stop bleeding, antibiotics, newborn resuscitation and steroids for preterm labour. Peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus analysis finds $65-83 of benefit per $1 for these facility packages, mainly from newborn lives saved, at roughly $2.4bn a year in public cost. Existing interventions could prevent about 71% of newborn deaths, most of them through better care at birth.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3
policies.evidence: Most of the gain is newborn lives. The best estimate comes from a peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis across 55 low- and lower-middle-income countries (Madise et al. 2023). It finds $83 of benefit per $1 for basic emergency obstetric and newborn care alone.
policies.ratio: Low end. Madise et al. (2023) give 65 for comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care. The source cost already includes country-level delivery and management, so only the international donor channel's overhead is added.
policies.counter: Broader packages score lower. Madise et al. (2023) find 36 for the entire continuum of care, 7 for antenatal care and 6 for care around conception.

policies.name: End the Fed & Implement Neutral Reserve Currency
policies.why: Before 1914 most of the world ran on gold, prices held steady for decades, and countries sharing the standard traded 18 to 60% more with each other. Ending the Fed and backing money with gold, bitcoin or a commodity basket removes the inflation tax and halves the rate of banking crises, at a small cost for holding the reserve. It returns about $6.40 to $144 per dollar, and the main risk is a rigid money supply in a deep slump.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed historical estimates of the gold standard's effects on trade (Lopez-Cordova & Meissner 2003 AER; Estevadeordal, Frantz & Taylor 2003 QJE), borrowing costs (Bordo & Rockoff 1996 JEH), crises (Bordo et al. 2001) and inflation (Lagos & Wright 2005 JPE; Lucas 2000 Econometrica). Not tried in a modern economy, and the Depression-era evidence cuts the other way, so B.
policies.difficulty_reason: It dismantles a major entrenched institution with no modern precedent.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Inflation is a tax on all money holders (Lucas 2000).
policies.summary: This policy would abolish the Federal Reserve and return money to a neutral standard (gold, bitcoin or a basket of commodities) issued by competing banks, the system most major economies used before 1914. Stable money removes the hidden tax of inflation and its interaction with the tax code, banking crises under the classical gold standard were half as frequent as since 1973, and countries sharing gold traded 18-60% more with each other, which raises incomes; governments that kept to gold also borrowed more cheaply. Counting those gains against the cost of holding gold or running free banks gives about $6.40 to $144 of benefit per dollar.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 3
policies.evidence: Money tied to a commodity brought stable prices for a long time. A consumer basket costing $100 in 1790 cost $108 in 1913; prices then rose about 24-fold under the Fed by 2008, an average inflation of about 3.4% a year (Selgin, Lastrapes and White 2012). Inflation is a tax on money holders.
policies.ratio: All figures are a percentage of United States GDP a year. The view is global, so the extra return the United States earns on dollar reserves is a transfer between countries, not a gain or cost to the world. Benefits come through four channels. 1.
policies.counter: Three findings point the other way. An International Monetary Fund study finds that any harm to trade from exchange-rate volatility "would appear to be fairly small and is by no means a robust, universal finding" (Clark, Tamirisa and Wei 2004).

policies.name: Contraception & Family Planning
policies.why: About 214 million women in poor countries want to avoid pregnancy and lack modern contraception, and reaching them costs about $3.6 billion a year. The return is about $20 to $112 per dollar, or $6.79 to $84 once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, with health benefits alone worth about $40. A 15-year trial in Ghana adds that paying for girls to finish secondary school delayed childbearing, raised their earnings and halved infant deaths among their children.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimate including family planning (Madise et al. 2023, JBCA) consistent with Copenhagen Post-2015 and Ghana Priorities BCRs, backed by quasi-experimental evidence (Matlab, Bangladesh: Joshi & Schultz 2013 Demography; Colombia: Miller 2010 Economic Journal). The girls'-education sub-policy rests on a 15-year randomized trial with a peer-reviewed BCR (Duflo et al. 2026, AER).
policies.difficulty_reason: Needs a sustained donor/government funding scale-up (~$3.6bn a year vs ~$1.27bn donor funding in 2017; Lomborg 2019) with working precedents, e.g.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Unmet need is concentrated among poorer women in high-fertility low-income countries (Kohler & Behrman; Madise et al. 2023 cover 55 LICs/LMICs).
policies.summary: Fund modern contraception (pills, injectables, implants, IUDs, counselling) for the roughly 214 million women in poor countries who want to avoid pregnancy but lack access, at about $3.6bn a year. Copenhagen Consensus estimates $22-120 of benefit per $1, depending on how much of the 'demographic dividend' from smaller families is counted; health benefits alone give about $40. A sub-policy, paying for girls to finish secondary school, is backed by a 15-year randomized trial in Ghana (Duflo, Dupas, Kremer and co-authors): it delayed childbearing, raised women's earnings and halved infant mortality among their children, returning at least $4 per $1 of government cost, more if targeted at girls.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3
policies.evidence: Kohler and Behrman (2015) estimate that universal access to contraception would mean 640,000 fewer newborn deaths, 150,000 fewer maternal deaths and 600,000 fewer children losing their mothers each year (Lomborg 2019). Counting health alone, each dollar returns about $40. Adding a demographic dividend from smaller families, worth $288 billion a year, brings the total to $120 per $1.
policies.ratio: Low end. Madise et al. (2023) give a benefit-cost ratio of 22 for the family planning package alone. The programme cost already includes country-level delivery and management, so only the overhead of the international donor channel is added.
policies.counter: Pritchett (1994) argues that women's desired family size, not access to contraception, explains most of the difference in fertility between countries. If so, supplying contraception would do less to cut births, and the demographic dividend would shrink.

policies.name: Tuberculosis Treatment
policies.why: Tuberculosis is curable, yet it still kills on a huge scale in poor countries. Rapid tests, screening and full treatment courses would save close to a million lives a year at roughly $2,000 per death averted. The return is $26 to $79 per dollar on about $6.7 billion a year, or $9.54 to $62 after the cost of raising the taxes that fund it, one of the best places on the list for a philanthropist's money.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus benefit-cost analysis (Pretorius et al. 2023, JBCA), consistent with Post-2015 (43) and with positive older World Bank estimates, built on the trial-established efficacy of standard TB treatment and diagnostics.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with precedent: national TB programmes already treat 8.3m people a year with 88% success for drug-susceptible TB, but only US$5.9bn was available in 2024 against a US$22bn annual target for 2027 (WHO 2025).
policies.who_benefits_reason: TB deaths (over 1.2m in 2024; WHO 2025) are concentrated in low- and lower-middle-income countries, and the modelled ~1m deaths averted a year are in LICs/LMICs (Pretorius et al. 2023).
policies.summary: Find and treat far more TB cases in poor countries: rapid molecular tests, screening of high-risk groups, full treatment courses, prevention for contacts, and work with private clinics. A peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus study puts the return at about $46 per $1 (range 28-84), saving close to a million lives a year at roughly $2,000 per death averted. Governments and donors would need to find about $5.2bn a year (about $6.2bn including patients' non-financial costs).
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3
policies.evidence: TB still kills over 1.2 million people a year (World Health Organization 2025). Standard diagnosis and treatment work: national programmes already cure 88% of drug-susceptible cases. The problem is reach and money.

policies.name: Childhood Immunization
policies.why: Routine childhood vaccines in poor countries return about $14 to $94 per dollar on full cost, or $4.81 to $72 once the cost of raising the taxes that fund them is counted, still one of the best-documented bargains in health. The core package costs about $1.5 billion a year in programme spending and saves about 523,000 lives a year. The hard part is reaching the last 10 to 15% of children, and private donors are well placed to pay for it.
policies.grade_reason: Several independent peer-reviewed benefit-cost/ROI studies (Patenaude et al. 2023 JBCA; Ozawa et al. 2016 and Sim et al. 2020 in Health Affairs) agree that benefits are many times costs, and each vaccine's efficacy rests on randomized controlled trials. The results are consistent across methods, datasets and decades.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: a sustained donor and government funding scale-up through national immunization programmes on the proven Gavi model.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Zero-dose children are concentrated in the poorest households and fragile states (WHO/UNICEF 2025).
policies.summary: Paying for routine childhood vaccines (measles, pneumococcal, rotavirus, HPV and others) in poor countries is one of the best-documented high-return investments in health. Every major study finds benefits far above costs: about 17-26 times when only medical costs and lost work are counted, and 45-101 times when lives saved are valued. The Copenhagen Consensus 2023 package costs about $1.5bn a year in programme spending and saves about 523,000 lives a year.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3 + WHO/GiveWell
policies.evidence: Few policies have been studied as often, and few studies agree as well. Patenaude, Sriudomporn and Mak (2023) cost a scale-up of nine vaccines in 80 countries for 2023-2030 and find benefits of $762.2 billion against costs of $7.58 billion. That is about $101 of benefit per $1, the figure the Copenhagen Consensus uses.
policies.ratio: The ratio compares the value of illness and deaths averted with the cost of buying and delivering the vaccines. The source costs already include delivery inside each country, so only the overhead of the international funding channel is added. Overhead rates.
policies.counter: The case for a lower verdict rests on how lives are valued and where. Counting only medical costs and lost work, Ozawa et al. (2016) find a ratio of about 17, and Sim et al. (2020) find 19.8 for 2021-30, against 101 when lives saved are valued (Patenaude, Sriudomporn and Mak 2023).

policies.name: Malaria Prevention
policies.why: Malaria still kills about 610,000 people a year, mostly African children, and bed nets, seasonal preventive drugs and cheap treatment return $17 to $45 per dollar on full cost, or $5.81 to $33.60 once the cost of raising the taxes that fund them is counted. GiveWell puts the price of a life saved at $4,000 to $5,500. The global funding gap is about $5.4 billion a year, an easy target for private philanthropy.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Shretta & Anye 2023 in JBCA; Hallett et al. 2025 in the Lancet) built on randomized-trial evidence for nets, SMC and ACTs, with large-scale observational confirmation (Bhatt et al. 2015; ACCESS-SMC 2020). It is not A+ because there is essentially one BCA per component rather than several independent BCAs.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: a sustained donor funding scale-up (only 42% of the required funding was attained in 2024) through proven channels: the Global Fund, PMI, national malaria programmes, AMF and Malaria Consortium.
policies.who_benefits_reason: About 95% of malaria deaths are in the WHO African Region and about 75% of those are children under five (World Malaria Report 2025).
policies.summary: Insecticide-treated bed nets, seasonal preventive drugs for young children in the Sahel, and cheap combination treatment are the core tools against malaria, which still kills about 610,000 people a year, mostly African children. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies put the return at about $19-48 per dollar when lives saved are valued, and GiveWell estimates $4,000-5,500 per life saved. Costed scale-ups need about $1.4bn a year, while the global funding gap is about $5.4bn a year.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3 + GiveWell
policies.evidence: Malaria still killed about 610,000 people in 2024, mostly African children (WHO 2025). The tools to stop it are proven. Bhatt et al. (2015) estimate that control efforts "averted 663 (542–753 credible interval) million clinical cases since 2000," and that insecticide-treated nets "were by far the largest contributor (68% of cases averted)." Shretta and Anye (2023) cost a 10-point rise in net coverage in 29 African countries at $5.7 billion over 2023-2030.
policies.ratio: The ratio compares lives saved, work days regained and health spending avoided with the cost of nets, drugs and their delivery. The source costs already include delivery inside each country, so only the overhead of the international funding channel is added. The Global Fund's operating expenses were 9.0% of grant spending in 2023 and 6.7% in 2024.
policies.counter: The narrowest reading of the evidence is the main counter-case. Hallett et al. (2025) find $3.50 of direct economic benefit per $1 when no value is placed on lives saved.

policies.name: Tobacco and Alcohol Taxes
policies.why: Higher prices cut smoking and heavy drinking, especially among the young and poor, and doubling real cigarette prices could cut smoking by about a third. Estimates run from about $3 to $100 per dollar of social cost, after counting tax collection, smuggling enforcement and a 10% loss to illicit cigarettes, and from $1.47 to $98 once the cost of raising the taxes that pay for collection and enforcement is counted. Of all the taxes a government can levy, one on a product that kills its users is among the easiest to defend.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Watkins et al. 2023 in JBCA; Bertram et al. 2018 in the Lancet, underlying WHO's ROI figures), built on price elasticities from meta-analyses of many quasi-experimental and econometric studies (Wagenaar et al. 2009; Jha & Peto 2014). It is not A+ because the BCR depends heavily on how lost consumer surplus is treated (100 vs 1,300) and no RCTs exist.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs ordinary tax legislation in each country, with many precedents (the Philippines, Turkey, South Africa and others have raised tobacco excise sharply).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Global Tobacco Economics Consortium (2018, BMJ): in 13 middle-income countries, a 50% cigarette price rise gives the poorest 20% 6.7 times more life-years than the richest 20%, averts 8.8 million men's falls into extreme poverty, and the poorest pay only about 10% of the extra tax.
policies.summary: Raising excise taxes on cigarettes and alcohol pushes up prices, which cuts smoking and heavy drinking, especially among the young and the poor, and raises revenue. Copenhagen Consensus analysis puts the return at about 53-100 per dollar of social cost; WHO's narrower economic-only estimates are $7.43 for tobacco and $9.13 for alcohol. Counting the full cost of collecting the tax, policing smuggling and secure tax stamps (up to about $2.47bn a year across poor countries) a 10% loss of benefit to illicit cigarettes, and the excess burden of the taxes that pay the public collection and enforcement costs, lowers the bottom of the range to about 1.5; the top is about 98.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3 + WHO Best Buys
policies.evidence: Price is the strongest lever on tobacco use. Jha and Peto (2014) put the price elasticity of cigarettes at about -0.4: doubling the real price cuts smoking by about a third and still raises revenue. For alcohol, a meta-analysis of 112 studies finds an elasticity of -0.51 (Wagenaar, Salois and Komro 2009).
policies.ratio: The ratio compares health gains with the real resource costs of the tax. Tax revenue itself is a transfer from smokers and drinkers to government, not a benefit or a cost. High end (100).
policies.counter: The counter-evidence suggests the ratio could be higher still. Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill (2023) report tobacco tax ratios of 620 in low-income and 1,300 in lower-middle-income countries when smokers' lost enjoyment is not counted as a cost.

policies.name: School Deworming
policies.why: A pill once or twice a year clears worms that sap children's nutrition and school attendance, at about 30 cents a child. A 20-year randomized follow-up in Kenya found treated children earned and consumed more as adults, a 37% annual social return. The wider evidence is disputed, so the range runs from $6 to $100 per dollar, or $2 to $75 once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, on a programme costing under $0.3 billion a year.
policies.grade_reason: Built on a long-run cluster-randomized trial with peer-reviewed economic returns (Baird et al. 2016, QJE; Hamory et al. 2021, PNAS) and a Copenhagen Consensus best-practice paper, but the wider trial evidence is contested (Cochrane review), so B+ rather than A.
policies.difficulty_reason: Delivered through existing schools once or twice a year with cheap, largely donated drugs.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Children in poor, high-infection areas; the Kenyan trial's long-run gains in earnings and consumption accrue to them as adults.
policies.summary: Giving schoolchildren a cheap pill once or twice a year clears intestinal worms that sap nutrition and school attendance. A long-running randomized trial in Kenya found the treated children earned and consumed more as adults twenty years later, an annual social return of 37%, and the development-economics handbook DCP3 puts the long-run benefits at more than 100 times the cost. Copenhagen Consensus's conservative figure is about $6 per $1.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3
policies.evidence: Intestinal worms sap children's nutrition and keep them out of school. The best evidence comes from the Primary School Deworming Project in Kenya, a randomized trial that phased treatment into schools and then followed the children for two decades. Ten years on, Baird et al. (2016) found that men who had been eligible as boys "work 17% more hours each week, spend more time in non-agricultural self-employment, are more likely to hold manufacturing jobs, and miss one fewer meal per week." The twenty-year follow-up by Hamory et al. (2021) puts the annualised social internal rate of return at 37%.
policies.ratio: Low end. Hall and Horton (2008) find that for pre-school children "each dollar spent results in about $6 of benefits." Ratio: 6. High end.
policies.counter: The Cochrane review is the main counter-evidence. Taylor-Robinson et al. (2015) conclude that "there is quite substantial evidence that deworming programmes do not show benefit in terms of average nutritional status, haemoglobin, cognition, school performance, or death." The review covers short-run outcomes, so it is left out of the range.

policies.name: HIV Prevention
policies.why: Three randomized trials found voluntary medical circumcision cuts men's risk of acquiring HIV by about 60%, for a one-off procedure costing under $100. The programme in the hardest-hit Southern African countries costs only $30 to $35 million a year and saves more in future HIV treatment than it costs. Returns of $6.80 to $53 per dollar, or $2.26 to $39 after the cost of raising the taxes that fund it, are falling where HIV is declining, which is a nice problem to have.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed economic evaluations (Njeuhmeli 2011 and Haacker 2016, PLOS Medicine; Bansi-Matharu 2023, Lancet Global Health) and a Copenhagen Consensus BCR, all built on randomized controlled trials showing ~60% protection against HIV acquisition (Auvert et al. 2005, ANRS 1265; Kenya and Uganda trials).
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained donor-funded scale-up with precedent (national VMMC programmes across 13 eastern and southern African countries modelled by Njeuhmeli et al. 2011).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Targets hyperendemic Southern African countries (adult HIV prevalence >15%) where HIV is a leading cause of lost life and income; women also benefit over time as fewer male partners are infected (Geldsetzer et al. 2015).
policies.summary: Offer free, voluntary medical circumcision to HIV-negative adult men in the Southern African countries with the highest HIV rates. Three randomized trials found it cuts men's risk of acquiring HIV by about 60%, and it is a one-off procedure costing under $100. Copenhagen Consensus puts the return at about $28 per $1 (range 7-56 depending on discount rate and how a life-year is valued), for only $30-35 million a year; it also saves more on future HIV treatment than it costs.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + GiveWell
policies.evidence: The core evidence is experimental. Three randomized trials, in South Africa, Kenya and Uganda, found that circumcision cuts a man's risk of acquiring HIV by about 60%. In the South African trial of 3,274 young men, HIV incidence was 0.85 per 100 person-years in the circumcised group against 2.1 in the control group (Auvert et al. 2005).
policies.ratio: Low end. Geldsetzer et al. (2015) find 7.4 at a 5% discount rate, valuing a year of life at $1,000. The cost already includes country-level delivery and management, so only the overhead of the international donor channel is added.
policies.counter: Falling HIV incidence is the main counter-evidence. Bansi-Matharu et al. (2023) compare five models across sub-Saharan Africa and find continued circumcision cost-effective in 68% of setting scenarios: 62% where incidence is below 0.1 per 100 person-years, rising to 95% above 1.0.

policies.name: Blood Pressure and Heart Drugs
policies.why: Aspirin at the time of a heart attack returns about $63 per dollar and blood-pressure pills about $47, and both are cheap generics. Heart attacks and strokes are now the leading killers in many poor countries, and a primary-care scale-up costs roughly $2.4 billion a year. Estimates run from about $3 to $59 per dollar, or $1.02 to $44 once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Watkins et al. 2023 in JBCA; Bertram et al. 2018 in the Lancet; Nugent & Brouwer 2015 in Global Heart), with effect sizes taken from randomized-trial meta-analyses of aspirin, antihypertensives and statins, and polypill RCTs (TIPS-3, PolyIran). It is not A+ because the published BCRs for each component vary by an order of magnitude and depend heavily on the DALY value.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs a sustained funding scale-up of primary-care hypertension and CVD treatment, with precedent in the WHO HEARTS programme in dozens of countries.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Benefits go to adults with hypertension or heart disease across all income groups in LICs and LMICs.
policies.summary: Cheap generic drugs (aspirin at the time of a heart attack, blood-pressure pills, and combination 'polypills' with a statin) prevent heart attacks and strokes, now the leading killers in many poor countries. Copenhagen Consensus panels put aspirin for heart attacks at about $63 per $1 and blood-pressure medication at about $47. WHO's narrower economic-only estimate is $3.29, and long-term multi-drug regimens score lower (about 3-17).
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + DCP3 + WHO Best Buys
policies.evidence: The drugs work, and they cost little. In the TIPS-3 trial, a polypill plus aspirin lowered major cardiovascular events against placebo, with a hazard ratio of 0.69 (Yusuf et al. 2021). Watkins, Ahmed and Pickersgill (2023) rank aspirin for a suspected heart attack as a "best investment", with a ratio above 15 in both low-income and lower-middle-income countries.
policies.ratio: The ratio compares health and economic gains with the cost of drugs, screening and follow-up. The source costs already include delivery inside each country, so only the overhead of the international funding channel is added. United Nations (UN) agencies charge 8% on earmarked donor funds and 7% on thematic funds (Executive Boards 2018).
policies.counter: The counter-evidence cuts both ways. Nugent (2015) puts aspirin for heart attacks at 153 per $1.

policies.name: Micronutrient Supplementation
policies.why: Iron, zinc and vitamin A in flour, salt and oil, plus prenatal tablets and vitamin A capsules for young children, cost cents to a few dollars per person a year. Vitamin A capsules cut child deaths by about 12% in trials, and iodized salt alone returns about $30 per dollar. The whole package costs about half a billion dollars a year for $5.60 to $35 back per dollar, or $1.85 to $26 once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost estimates (Larsen et al. 2023 in JBCA; Horton & Ross 2003 in Food Policy) backed by randomized trials and meta-analyses (Cochrane review of vitamin A supplementation, 19 trials, 1.2 million children, high-certainty evidence). It is not A+ because a large trial (DEVTA) found a non-significant mortality effect for vitamin A, and no BCA covers the exact iron-zinc-vitamin A fortification bundle.
policies.difficulty_reason: Easy: one health ministry or food regulator can mandate fortification under existing food-standards law, and over 60 countries already have 70%+ household coverage of iodized salt.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Micronutrient deficiency is concentrated among poor households that rely on cheap, nutrient-poor staples. 80% of undernourished children are in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa (Copenhagen Consensus), and vitamin A and pregnancy supplements are delivered through public programmes that reach low-income mothers and children.
policies.summary: Adding iron, zinc and vitamin A to flour, salt and oil, giving pregnant women a daily multiple-micronutrient tablet, and giving young children vitamin A capsules all cost cents to a few dollars per person a year. Peer-reviewed benefit-cost studies put the return at about 6-8 per dollar for iron fortification counting only productivity, about 30 for iodized salt, and about 37 for prenatal multiple micronutrients. Vitamin A capsules cut child deaths by about 12% in trials and are among GiveWell's most cost-effective programmes.
policies.selected_by: Copenhagen Consensus + GiveWell (+DCP3)
policies.evidence: Micronutrients cost cents to a few dollars per person a year, and the returns are large. Larsen, Hoddinott and Razvi (2023) find that switching pregnant women from iron and folic acid to multiple micronutrients returns 37.5 per $1 at an 8% discount rate. Adding calcium gives 18.6 to 23.9.
policies.ratio: The ratio compares gains in survival, health and future earnings with the cost of nutrients and their delivery. The source costs already include delivery inside each country, so only the overhead of the international funding channel is added. United Nations (UN) agencies charge 8% on earmarked donor funds and 7% on thematic funds (Executive Boards 2018).
policies.counter: The largest single trial is the main counter-evidence. DEVTA, which gave vitamin A to preschool children in north India, found a mortality ratio of 0.96, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.89 to 1.03, which is not statistically significant (Awasthi et al. 2013).

policies.name: Secure Property Rights
policies.why: About 1.1 billion adults say their rights to their land or home are insecure, which makes it hard to borrow against, sell or safely improve what they hold. Titling costs $5 to $25 a parcel, and titled families in Peru and Argentina worked more, built more and kept their kids in school longer. It returns about $6 to $23 per dollar, or $1.97 to $17.50 once the cost of raising the taxes that pay for titling is counted, a cheap way to turn dead capital into wealth.
policies.grade_reason: One peer-reviewed benefit-cost analysis (Byamugisha & Dubosse 2023, JBCA) backed by quasi-experimental and natural-experiment studies (Field 2007; Galiani & Schargrodsky 2010; Ali, Deininger & Goldstein 2014); systematic reviews find mixed income effects, so A-.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with working precedents: Rwanda's nationwide land tenure regularisation demarcated 4.8 million parcels in its first year (Ali et al. 2014), and Peru's urban titling programme issued titles to over a million households in the 1990s (Field 2007).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Targets squatters, smallholders and female-headed households, who gained most in Rwanda; about 1.1 billion adults report insecure land or property rights (Prindex).
policies.summary: Giving the world's poor formal, tradable titles to the land and homes they already occupy lets them invest, borrow against and sell what they own. A peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus analysis for Sub-Saharan Africa finds $18 back per dollar for rural titling and $30-45 for urban titling, at costs of $5-25 a parcel, and field studies find titled families work more, build more and keep children in school longer. Because reviews find weaker effects on rural incomes, the range runs from about $6 to $23 per dollar.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 2
policies.evidence: About 1.1 billion adults, 23% of adults worldwide, report that they feel insecure about their land or property rights (Prindex 2024). The best cost-benefit study is a peer-reviewed Copenhagen Consensus analysis for Sub-Saharan Africa (Byamugisha and Dubosse 2023). It finds $18 back per dollar for rural titling and $30 to $45 for urban titling, at costs of $5 to $25 a parcel.
policies.ratio: The base is Byamugisha and Dubosse (2023): Sub-Saharan Africa, an 8% discount rate and a 30-year horizon. Benefits rest on a 15% household wealth effect for rural land and a 25% rise in urban property values. Inputs (present values). - Rural titling: benefits $395.71bn, costs $21.72bn.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-evidence concerns rural titling in Africa. Jacoby and Minten (2007) find that in rural Madagascar a title had no significant effect on plot investment and little effect on productivity or land values.

policies.name: Deregulate the Economy (Top Ten)
policies.why: Ten rules come off the books at once: occupational licensing, minimum wages, restrictive zoning, slow FDA approvals, the sugar program, community-bank compliance, the Jones Act, EPA rules that fail their own cost test, compulsory collective bargaining and antitrust enforcement. Licensing alone costs consumers up to $203 billion a year, and the most favourable published estimate puts the growth cost of federal regulation since 1980 at nearly a quarter of GDP. Net of the health and environmental benefits those rules buy, the package returns about $1.28 to $26.37 per dollar, with zoning's true size and that growth estimate the big unknowns.
policies.grade_reason: Most items rest on peer-reviewed natural experiments or structural models that measure the gain (Kleiner & Soltas 2023; Cengiz et al. 2019; Hsieh & Moretti 2019; Peltzman 1973; Philipson et al. 2008), with official estimates for the sugar program, bank compliance, the EPA rules and antitrust (GAO, CBO, OMB, FTC, DOJ). The high end rests on a peer-reviewed growth model (Coffey et al. 2020) whose regulation measure has been challenged (Goldschlag & Tabarrok 2018), on Hsieh & Moretti's perfect-mobility case, which a replication and a separate calculation put far lower, and on a 1985 estimate of lives lost to drug delay.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each item needs ordinary legislation, rule repeal or federal pre-emption of state licensing and local zoning, with strong precedents: the airline, trucking and rail deregulation of 1978-80, Arizona's 2019 universal licence recognition, Auckland's 2016 upzoning, 26 state right-to-work laws, and repeal of rules under the Congressional Review Act.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Zoning and licensing reform favour lower-income entrants and renters; FDA, sugar and Jones Act reform help consumers widely; minimum-wage repeal and NLRA reform lower some wages, and ending antitrust enforcement may raise some prices.
policies.summary: Ten federal, state and local regulations are removed or scaled back: occupational licensing, minimum wages, restrictive zoning, slow FDA drug approval, the sugar program, community-bank compliance rules, the Jones Act's limits on coastal shipping, EPA rules whose own cost estimates exceed their benefits, compulsory collective bargaining, and antitrust enforcement. Licensing sets the low end; at the high end, zoning and an aggregate estimate of the growth cost of federal regulation since 1980 carry the gain, net of the lowest credible estimate of the health and environmental benefits those rules provide. The package gives $1.28 to $26.37 of benefit per dollar of cost.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 5
policies.evidence: Most items rest on strong evidence. Occupational licensing costs consumers $184 billion to $203 billion a year (Kleiner and Vorotnikov 2018; Kleiner 2015). Licensing does buy some quality: Kleiner and Soltas (2023) find that higher willingness to pay offsets 80% of the higher prices, and that cost sets the low end.
policies.ratio: The package is treated as one reform. The ratio is total yearly benefits over total yearly full costs, in billions of 2025 dollars. The low end pairs the lowest credible benefits with the highest costs; the high end uses the most favourable credible published estimates.
policies.counter: Repealing EPA rules wholesale would lower the ratio, not raise it. On the Office of Management and Budget's (2017) tally, the 39 major EPA rules of 2007-2016 bring benefits of $195.8 billion to $705.7 billion a year against costs of $54.1 billion to $64.8 billion (2015 dollars).

policies.name: Privatize Government Land
policies.why: Four western states earn $14.51 per dollar of management cost on their trust lands, while the Forest Service and BLM earn 73 cents. Selling federal land and giving radio spectrum full, tradable property rights returns about $1.66 to $10 per dollar, and 60 MHz more mobile spectrum alone is worth about $8.8 billion a year to consumers. The open question is recreation and conservation value, which for the national parks alone is put at about $92 billion a year.
policies.grade_reason: The low end comes from a peer-reviewed fiscal model (Jakus et al. 2017, Land Economics) and the high end from PERC's think-tank comparison of official agency accounts. Property-rights theory of resource management in academic books (Anderson & Leal) and peer-reviewed spectrum welfare estimates (Hazlett & Munoz 2009, RAND J.
policies.difficulty_reason: It dismantles the federal land agencies, which manage about one-third of US land, with no modern precedent; Cato's own blueprint phases auctions over 20-40 years (Anderson, Smith & Simmons 1999).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Under the Anderson-Smith-Simmons (Cato 1999) design, every citizen gets equal 'public land share certificates', spreading the gains.
policies.summary: This policy would sell or transfer federal land, parks and natural resources to private (or trust) owners and give radio spectrum full, tradable property rights. Land run for income earns far more than federal land: four western states earn $14.51 per $1 of management cost on trust lands, against 73 cents for the Forest Service and BLM. Counting the cost of running the sales (3.3% of proceeds in BLM's recent land sales) as well as management, the ratio is about 1.7 (a Utah takeover bearing every federal cost, high energy prices) to 10.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 2
policies.evidence: Land run for income earns far more than land run by federal agencies. Fretwell and Regan (2015) compare 2009-2013 accounts across four western states. State trust lands earned $14.51 for every $1 of management cost; the Forest Service and the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) earned 73 cents.
policies.ratio: No study computes a full welfare ratio for selling federal land. The range uses published revenue-per-management-dollar ratios for land run for income, then adds the one-time cost of selling it. Land value.
policies.counter: The largest uncounted cost is non-market value. Haefele, Loomis and Bilmes (2016) put the total economic value of the National Park Service at about $92 billion a year.

policies.name: Tradable Fishing Quotas
policies.why: Tradable quotas give fishers a secure, sellable share of the catch and end the race to empty the sea. Across more than 11,000 fisheries, those with catch shares were about half as likely to collapse. Each dollar of cost, including temporary catch cuts, returns about $2.80 to $16, or 93 cents to $15.60 when governments pay the management bill from taxes instead of charging fishers.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed natural comparisons measure the gain from catch shares: Costello, Gaines & Lynham 2008, Science, on collapse across 11,000+ fisheries; Grafton, Squires & Fox 2000, J. Law & Econ., on the BC halibut natural experiment.
policies.difficulty_reason: Ordinary legislation or regulation in one country, with many precedents (New Zealand, Iceland, US catch-share programmes such as BC/Alaska halibut).
policies.who_benefits_reason: The World Bank (2017) notes the benefits concentrate on the relatively few fishers who stay in, while displaced vessel owners and crews bear most adjustment costs and the public sector bears much of the management cost.
policies.summary: Tradable fishing quotas give fishers a secure, sellable share of the total allowed catch, ending the race to fish. Across more than 11,000 fisheries, those with catch shares were about half as likely to collapse. The World Bank estimates that cutting global fishing effort to a sustainable level would raise fishery net benefits by about $83bn a year.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 2
policies.evidence: Open-access fisheries are overfished, and the losses are large. The World Bank (2017a) estimates that the world's marine fisheries forgo about $83.3 billion a year in net benefits. In the bank's words, reform would boost the sector's profits "from an estimated $3 billion a year to $86 billion" (World Bank 2017b).
policies.ratio: The ratio uses the World Bank's (2017a) global model, at a 5% discount rate over 20 years. Benefits are the present value of fishery net benefits on a reform path, compared with the current path. On the current path, with 2012 effort held constant, that present value is $514 billion.
policies.counter: Essington (2010) finds that catch shares in North American fisheries markedly reduced year-to-year swings in exploitation, landings and discards. Yet "The average levels of most indicators were unaffected by catch share implementation", apart from discards.

key_studies.authors: Costello, C.; Gaines, S. D.; Lynham, J.
key_studies.title: Can Catch Shares Prevent Fisheries Collapse?
key_studies.finding: Data on 11,000+ fisheries: nearly a third of open-access fisheries have collapsed, about half that rate under catch shares.

policies.name: Open Borders
policies.why: Letting people live and work in any country moves workers to where they are several times more productive; identical low-skill workers earn about four times as much in the US as at home. Published models put the gain at 35 to 57% of world output before moving costs, the biggest total gain of any policy on this list. Moving billions of people costs about $18 to $19 trillion a year, so each dollar returns about $2.14 to $3.34, with most of the gain going to migrants and poor countries.
policies.grade_reason: The range comes from a peer-reviewed general-equilibrium model (Borjas 2015, JEL) that prices both the gain and the moving cost, cross-checked by peer-reviewed estimates (Clemens 2011, JEP; Kennan 2013, RED; Docquier, Machado & Sekkat 2015, SJE). All are calibrated simulations of a policy never tried at world scale, and the result depends on how much productivity migrants carry, so B.
policies.difficulty_reason: Requires every high-income country to repeal entry and work restrictions, with no modern precedent outside regional zones such as the EU single market.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Most of the gain goes to migrants and their origin countries: Borjas (2015) finds Southern wages rise 143% while Northern wages fall 39.3% and capital owners gain $12.0tn; Docquier, Machado & Sekkat (2015) find sending-country natives gain 26-79% and natives of the US and EU 0.3-2.1%.
policies.summary: Letting people live and work in any country moves workers to where they are far more productive; identical low-skill workers earn about four times as much in the US as at home. Published models put the gain at roughly 35-57% of world output before moving costs, the largest of any policy on this list. Moving several billion people is also very costly, about $19-20 trillion a year, so each $1 spent returns about $2.14 to $3.34.
policies.selected_by: Gallup World Poll 2021: nearly 900 million adults would like to migrate permanently (opposite view: CES 2024, 79% of Americans backed more border patrols)
policies.evidence: The same worker produces far more in a rich country than in a poor one. Identical low-skill workers from the median country earn at least 3.95 times as much in the United States as at home, a gain of at least PPP$13,600 a year in purchasing-power terms (Clemens, Montenegro, and Pritchett 2019). Removing migration barriers therefore promises the largest gain of any policy studied.
policies.ratio: The benefit is the rise in world output when workers move to where they are most productive. The cost is the real resources spent on moving. Borjas (2015, Table 2) gives both from one model.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-evidence is Clemens and Pritchett (2019), who model productivity carried from home, slow assimilation and congestion. They conclude: "On current evidence about the magnitudes of these parameters, dynamically efficient policy would not imply open borders but would imply relaxations on current restrictions." The study gives no dollar ratio, so it bounds the policy from above rather than setting a number.

key_studies.title: Economics and Emigration: Trillion-Dollar Bills on the Sidewalk?
key_studies.venue: Journal of Economic Perspectives 25(3):83-106 (CGD Working Paper 264, Aug 2011)
key_studies.finding: Table 1 (efficiency gain from eliminating barriers, % of world GDP). Labour mobility, all barriers: Hamilton & Whalley (1984) 147.3; Moses & Letnes (2004) 96.5; Iregui (2005) 67; Klein & Ventura (2007) 122. Text: full-removal gains 'often in the range of 50-150 percent of world GDP'. Tables at pp. 27-28 of the CGD WP version (identical text to JEP article).

key_studies.authors: Borjas, G.J.
key_studies.title: Immigration and Globalization: A Review Essay
key_studies.finding: Premigration world GDP $70tn. Table 1 (costless open borders, elasticity -0.3): world GDP gain $9.4tn / $40.1tn / $62.4tn for North/South productivity ratio R = 2/4/6; at R=4, 2.6bn workers (5.6bn people) move, Northern wages -39.3%, Southern +143.0%, capitalists +$12.0tn. key_studies.authors: Docquier, F.; Machado, J.; Sekkat, K.
key_studies.title: Efficiency Gains from Liberalizing Labor Mobility
key_studies.finding: Calibrated GE model with empirically estimated migration and visa costs: about 400 million people want to migrate; liberalizing migration raises world GDP by 11.5-12.5% in the medium term; gains range from 7.0% (with schooling externalities, i.e. brain-drain effects) to 17.9% (with network effects). WP version: natives' income USA +0.3%, EU27 +2.1%, GCC -0.7%; sending-country natives +26% (SSA) to +79.3%.

key_studies.authors: Kennan, J.
key_studies.title: Open Borders
key_studies.finding: Net gain from open borders (static model with migration costs), averaged over all workers incl. non-migrants in less-developed countries: $11,046 per worker per year (PPP 2012$) vs average income $8,382 (+132%) for 40 countries; $10,369 vs $8,903 (+116%) for all non-frontier PWT countries (NBER WP pp. 15-16). Real-wage fall in rich countries small and disappears as capital adjusts.

key_studies.authors: Clemens, M.A.; Montenegro, C.E.; Pritchett, L.
key_studies.title: The Place Premium: Bounding the Price Equivalent of Migration Barriers
key_studies.finding: Lower-bound US/home real-wage ratio for identical low-skill workers: Mexico 2.557, median country 3.95; lower-bound gain PPP$10,523 (Mexico) to 13,600 (median) per year. (Carried over from evidence/16.json.)

key_studies.authors: Docquier, F.; Rapoport, H.
key_studies.title: Globalization, Brain Drain, and Development
key_studies.finding: Survey finding: high-skill emigration 'need not deplete a country's human capital stock' and 'can generate positive network externalities'. Effects on sending countries depend on context. Used to set the brain-drain term to zero for low-skill flows in the strict-border mirror-image score.

quotes.text: For labor mobility barriers, the estimated gains are often in the range of 50–150 percent of world GDP.
high skill U.S. workers lose $21 (0.04%) a year, whereas low skill U.S. workers gain $9 (0.02%) a year due to the increased scarcity of low-skilled workers.
On current evidence about the magnitudes of these parameters, dynamically efficient policy would not imply open borders but would imply relaxations on current restrictions.

policies.name: Climate Adaptation
policies.why: Early-warning systems, flood defences, mangroves and marshes protect people from storms and floods, and official reviews find about $1.70 to $10 back per dollar, or 58 cents to $7.46 once the cost of raising the taxes that fund them is counted. Early warnings alone return $4 to $36 per dollar, and covering every developing country costs about $1 billion a year. Helping people cope with the weather they already get is the most practical climate spending there is.
policies.grade_reason: The central value comes from a peer-reviewed review of risk-based BCAs (Mechler 2016) and is consistent with peer-reviewed coastal (Hinkel et al. 2014 PNAS) and nature-based-defence (Narayan et al. 2016) studies; the range end points are official estimates (GCA, World Bank, NIBS). No randomized or quasi-experimental BCR for the package.
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with clear precedents: Bangladesh's cyclone warning and shelter programme, FEMA mitigation grants, and the UN Early Warnings for All initiative endorsed by 50 countries.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Disaster mortality falls hardest on low-income countries; the UN notes countries with limited early-warning coverage have disaster mortality eight times higher than those with high coverage, and Hallegatte's estimate targets developing countries.
policies.summary: Early-warning systems and flood defences, including mangroves and marshes, protect people and property from storms and floods. Official and peer-reviewed reviews consistently find benefits of about $2 to $10 per $1 spent, with around $4 typical. Early warnings alone score higher, $4 to $36 per $1, because they are cheap (about $1bn a year for all developing countries).
policies.selected_by: Peoples' Climate Vote 45% + 45% (Protecting People group)
policies.evidence: Early warnings and flood defences protect people and property, and the evidence that they pay is consistent. The Global Commission on Adaptation (2019) finds benefits of $2 to $10 per $1 across its five priority adaptation investments. It estimates $1.8 trillion invested over 2020 to 2030 would yield $7.1 trillion in net benefits.
policies.ratio: The package combines early warnings and flood defences. Both sit inside the range found by the Global Commission on Adaptation (2019): $2 to $10 per $1 across its five priority investments, with an average of almost 4. The Commission finds early warnings save lives and assets worth at least ten times their cost, and mangrove benefits run up to 10 times costs.
policies.counter: The case against rests on how the published ratios are made. Kelman and Shreve (2014) find that many studies of disaster risk reduction lack sensitivity analysis, ignore climate change and its downsides, and give results that depend heavily on context.

key_studies.authors: Mechler, R.
key_studies.title: Reviewing estimates of the economic efficiency of disaster risk management: opportunities and limitations of using risk-based cost-benefit analysis
key_studies.finding: Disaster risk management benefits outweigh costs on average by about four times (risk-based studies); evidence base limited.

key_studies.authors: Hinkel, J.; Lincke, D.; Vafeidis, A. T.; Perrette, M.; Nicholls, R. J.; Tol, R. S. J.; Marzeion, B.; Fettweis, X.; Ionescu, C.; Levermann, A.
key_studies.title: Coastal flood damage and adaptation costs under 21st century sea-level rise

key_studies.finding: Without adaptation 0.2-4.6% of world population flooded annually in 2100 and losses 0.3-9.3% of GDP; dike investment and maintenance $12-71bn/yr in 2100, much smaller than avoided damages.

key_studies.authors: Narayan, S.; Beck, M. W.; Reguero, B. G.; Losada, I. J.; van Wesenbeeck, B.; Pontee, N.; Sanchirico, J. N.; Ingram, J. C.; Lange, G.-M.; Burks-Copes, K. A.
key_studies.title: The Effectiveness, Costs and Coastal Protection Benefits of Natural and Nature-Based Defences
key_studies.finding: Salt marshes and mangroves are 2-5 times cheaper than submerged breakwaters for wave heights up to 0.5 m; coral reefs and marshes have the highest wave-reduction potential.

key_studies.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
key_studies.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
key_studies.finding: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue, range 17-56 cents (per Fullerton & Henderson 1987, NBER w2353).

key_studies.authors: Feldstein, M.
key_studies.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
key_studies.finding: Deadweight loss of nearly $2 per extra $1 of revenue from a proportional rise in all personal income tax rates.

key_studies.authors: Hallegatte, S.
key_studies.title: A Cost Effective Solution to Reduce Disaster Losses in Developing Countries: Hydro-Meteorological Services, Early Warning, and Evacuation (Policy Research Working Paper 6058)
key_studies.finding: Upgrading hydro-met and EWS in all developing countries: avoided asset losses $0.3-2bn/yr, ~23,000 lives/yr ($0.7-3.5bn), wider benefits $3-30bn/yr; total $4-36bn/yr for ~$1bn/yr; BCR 4-36.

policies.name: Abolish the Income Tax
policies.why: Each dollar of income tax costs somewhere between 13 cents and $2 extra in lost work, saving and investment, and filing adds another $329 to $501 billion a year. Repeal means replacing about $3.1 trillion a year, mostly by shrinking government. The return is about $1.24 to $3.20 per dollar of revenue given up, and nobody will miss tax day.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed welfare-cost estimates: natural-experiment MVPFs (Hendren & Sprung-Keyser 2020, QJE); a quasi-experimental study of the 2017 corporate cut (Chodorow-Reich, Zidar & Zwick 2024, JEP); Feldstein's TAXSIM deadweight-loss estimate (1999, REStat); and Ballard-Shoven-Whalley general-equilibrium results (AER 1985). These are converted into a BCR and extrapolated to full repeal, which no study observes, so it is not A-range.
policies.difficulty_reason: Ordinary federal legislation can abolish the personal and corporate income taxes: the 16th Amendment permits an income tax but does not require one, and repealing it would only stop a future reinstatement.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The income tax is the progressive part of the federal system.
policies.summary: This policy would abolish the personal income tax (via repeal of the 16th Amendment) and the corporate income tax, replacing about $3.1 trillion a year mainly by shrinking government. Economists estimate that each dollar of income tax costs between about 13 cents and 2 dollars extra in lost work, saving and investment. Filing and paperwork add another $329-501bn a year (11-16 cents per dollar raised), and the IRS spends about $11bn a year on the income taxes; repeal removes both.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 1
policies.evidence: Every dollar raised by income tax costs the economy more than a dollar. People work, save and invest less, and they spend time and money on filing. Estimates of that extra loss run from 13 cents per dollar (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1982) to about $2 per extra dollar raised (Feldstein 1999).
policies.ratio: The ratio is the benefit to taxpayers per $1 of income tax given up. The revenue is replaced by cutting government, and the forgone spending is valued at $1 per $1. Three parts add up: Ratio = 1 + deadweight loss removed per $ + compliance cost removed per $ + administration removed per $.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is on the spending side. Hendren and Sprung-Keyser (2020) show that some programmes, especially direct investment in children's health and education, return far more than $1 per $1.

key_studies.authors: Feldstein, M.
key_studies.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
key_studies.finding: Deadweight loss >12x Harberger's classic estimate; raising revenue via proportional rate increases costs ~$2 of deadweight loss per $1 of extra revenue

key_studies.authors: Hendren, N.; Sprung-Keyser, B.
key_studies.title: A Unified Welfare Analysis of Government Policies
key_studies.finding: MVPFs of top-income-tax-rate changes: 1981 cut infinite (95% CI 0.94-inf; conventional BCR 1.67), 1986 44.27 (CI 2.37-inf), 1993 increase 1.85 (CI 1.19-4.07), 2013 increase 1.16

key_studies.authors: Saez, E.; Slemrod, J.B.; Giertz, S.H.
key_studies.title: The Elasticity of Taxable Income with Respect to Marginal Tax Rates: A Critical Review
key_studies.finding: Elasticity estimates vary considerably by method and period; frames deadweight-loss calculations (counterweight to high-elasticity estimates)

key_studies.authors: Chodorow-Reich, G.; Zidar, O.; Zwick, E.
key_studies.title: Lessons from the Biggest Business Tax Cut in US History
key_studies.finding: TCJA corporate provisions: corporate revenue fell ~40% (0.63% of GDP/yr over first decade); corporate investment +8-14%; long-run domestic corporate capital +7%; long-run GDP +0.9% (first-decade average +0.44%); labour income up < $1,000 per worker vs CEA's $4,000-9,000; individual-tax offsets only 1.5-6.3% of the revenue loss.

key_studies.authors: Bergh, A.; Henrekson, M.
key_studies.title: Government Size and Growth: A Survey and Interpretation of the Evidence
key_studies.finding: In rich countries, a 10-percentage-point increase in government size is associated with 0.5-1% lower annual growth; authors warn of pitfalls in a causal reading.

key_studies.authors: Altig, D.; Auerbach, A.J.; Kotlikoff, L.J.; Smetters, K.A.; Walliser, J.
key_studies.title: Simulating Fundamental Tax Reform in the United States
key_studies.finding: Significant long-run output increases for some reforms replacing the income tax (e.g., consumption taxes); smaller gains for reforms protecting low-income and older generations
