13 cents to 22 cents per dollar of revenue.

policies.name: End Bailouts and Deposit Insurance
policies.why: Deposit insurance and bailouts let banks take risks with someone else's money, and explicit insurance makes crises more likely where institutions are weak. Bank-run models still value the first dollars of cover highly, so the range is wide, at about 50 cents to $5.50 per dollar. Private replacement insurance would cost about $2.9 billion a year, and depositors would finally know who carries the risk.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed cross-country panel (Demirgüç-Kunt & Detragiache 2002, JME), peer-reviewed historical studies (Calomiris & Jaremski 2019, JF; Calomiris 1990, JEH) and peer-reviewed models (Diamond & Dybvig 1983; Dávila & Goldstein 2023, JPE) quantify each input. The ratio itself is assembled here rather than published, and the inputs disagree on sign, so it cannot rate B+ or above.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: it dismantles a major federal institution in place since 1933 and ends the implicit too-big-to-fail guarantee (worth up to $70bn a year to US banks, IMF 2014).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Mixed.
policies.summary: This policy would close federal deposit insurance and bar government rescues of failed banks, so that depositors and creditors carry their own risk. Cross-country evidence finds explicit deposit insurance makes banking crises more likely where institutions are weak, and historical US state schemes encouraged risk-taking that ended in collapse. Bank-run theory and a recent calibrated model, however, find deposit insurance very valuable, especially its first dollars of cover.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 3/5
policies.evidence: The case for abolition rests on market discipline. Demirgüç-Kunt and Detragiache (2002) studied 61 countries from 1980 to 1997, with 40 systemic crises. They find that explicit deposit insurance makes banking crises more likely, and that "the adverse impact of deposit insurance on bank stability tends to be stronger the more extensive is the coverage offered to depositors, and where the scheme is funded and run by the government rather than the private sector." The effect fades where institutions are strong.
policies.ratio: No published study gives a benefit-cost ratio for abolishing deposit insurance. The ratio is built from published inputs. The benefit is crises avoided because guarantees no longer weaken market discipline.
policies.counter: The strongest evidence against abolition is Dávila and Goldstein (2023). They put optimal US coverage in 2008 at about $381,000 and find that "the welfare gains from having a deposit insurance system at all are very large." On its own, their estimate implies a ratio below 1 for full abolition.

key_studies.authors: Demirgüç-Kunt, A.; Detragiache, E.
key_studies.title: Does deposit insurance increase banking system stability? An empirical investigation
key_studies.finding: 61 countries 1980-97, 40 systemic crises (4.4% of observations): explicit deposit insurance raises crisis probability, more so with wide coverage, government-run funded schemes, deregulated rates and weak institutions. The effect becomes insignificant at high institutional quality. Cutting US coverage to Swiss levels would have lowered the predicted probability of the 1980 US crisis from 4.3% to 2.5% (IMF WP 00/3 version, p.15).

key_studies.authors: Calomiris, C. W.; Jaremski, M.
key_studies.title: Stealing Deposits: Deposit Insurance, Risk-Taking, and the Removal of Market Discipline in Early 20th-Century Banks
key_studies.finding: Early-1900s state deposit-insurance laws removed the market discipline that had constrained uninsured banks. Insured banks took more insolvency risk during the WWI farm boom, and the insurance systems collapsed with high losses when prices fell.

key_studies.authors: Calomiris, C. W.
key_studies.title: Is Deposit Insurance Necessary? A Historical Perspective
key_studies.finding: Antebellum and 1920s US experience: self-regulating mutual-liability schemes succeeded and compulsory state insurance systems failed. Branch banking improved stability.

key_studies.authors: Anginer, D.; Demirgüç-Kunt, A.; Zhu, M.
key_studies.title: How does deposit insurance affect bank risk? Evidence from the recent crisis
key_studies.finding: Generous deposit insurance raised bank risk and systemic fragility in 2004-06 (log z-score coefficient -0.472) and lowered it during 2007-09 (+0.221). 'The overall effect of deposit insurance over the full sample remains negative' (WB PRWP 6289 version).

key_studies.authors: Lucas, D.
key_studies.title: Measuring the Cost of Bailouts
key_studies.finding: Total direct cost of 2008 crisis-related US bailouts 'on the order of $500 billion, or 3.5% of GDP in 2009'.

key_studies.authors: Correia, S.; Luck, S.; Verner, E.
key_studies.title: Why Do Banks Fail? Bank Runs Versus Solvency (summary of 'Failing Banks', NBER WP 32907)
key_studies.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Liberty Street Economics
key_studies.finding: 5,000+ US bank failures 1865-2023. Insolvency is almost always the root cause, and runs can be ruled out as a plausible cause in >80% of pre-FDIC failures. Depositors lost ~30% in a typical pre-FDIC failure.

quotes.text: the adverse impact of deposit insurance on bank stability tends to be stronger the more extensive is the coverage offered to depositors, and where the scheme is funded and run by the government rather than the private sector.
the welfare gains from having a deposit insurance system at all are very large.
an increase in coverage of $100,000 is associated with a welfare gain of $13.2 billion for the whole banking sector.

policies.name: Privatize Social Security
policies.why: Funded personal accounts let workers own their retirement savings, and about 2% of payroll eventually replaces the 12.4% payroll tax. Capital and wages rise, though today's workers must also keep paying for the benefits already promised. Counting both sides, each dollar of transition cost returns about $1 to $2.
policies.grade_reason: The numbers come from published theory quantified in peer-reviewed or academic-press models: Feldstein (1996, AER P&P); Feldstein & Samwick and Kotlikoff (1998, University of Chicago Press/NBER); Kotlikoff, Smetters & Walliser and Cooley & Soares (1999, Review of Economic Dynamics). They are supported by a historical case (Chile 1981; Schmidt-Hebbel 1998 credits the reform with about a quarter of Chile's growth increase).
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate under the rubric: it needs ordinary federal legislation, and full or partial privatization has precedents (Chile 1981 and other Latin American countries, World Bank 2005).
policies.who_benefits_reason: In the long run, gains reach all income classes.
policies.summary: This policy would replace pay-as-you-go Social Security with funded personal retirement accounts, phasing the old system out. Simulation studies find large long-run gains: about 2% of payroll in accounts eventually replaces the 12.4% payroll tax, and the economy's capital stock and wages rise. Those gains go mostly to young and future workers, while today's workers must also keep paying for benefits already promised.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Area 1
policies.evidence: The best evidence comes from simulation models of the United States economy, not from field experiments. Feldstein and Samwick (1998) find that, in the long run, accounts funded with about 2.04% of payroll can replace the 12.4% payroll tax. The reason is simple: invested savings earn the return on capital, while a pay-as-you-go system earns only the growth of the wage base.
policies.ratio: The ratio compares what later generations gain with what the transition generations pay to keep honouring promised benefits. High end (2.0). Feldstein and Samwick (1998) model a shift to Mandatory Individual Retirement Accounts.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is that personal accounts create little new value. Diamond and Orszag (2005) argue that costs will rise by about 2.5% of GDP over 75 years and that modest benefit cuts and revenue increases can restore solvency.

key_studies.authors: Feldstein, M.
key_studies.title: The Missing Piece in Policy Analysis: Social Security Reform (Richard T. Ely Lecture)
key_studies.finding: Deadweight loss of the unfunded system about 1% of GDP a year; shifting to a funded system has a net present-value gain of more than $15 trillion, about 3% of future GDP each year.

key_studies.authors: Kotlikoff, L. J.; Smetters, K.; Walliser, J.
key_studies.title: Privatizing Social Security in the United States: Comparing the Options
key_studies.finding: Privatization 'can substantially raise long-run living standards' but imposes welfare losses on transition generations and takes a long time to pay off.

key_studies.authors: Cooley, T. F.; Soares, J.
key_studies.title: Privatizing Social Security
key_studies.finding: Privatizing is long-run welfare-improving, but every feasible transition uses debt that shifts cost to unborn generations; a majority never supports transition in the first two periods.

key_studies.authors: Schmidt-Hebbel, K.
key_studies.title: Does Pension Reform Really Spur Productivity, Saving, and Growth?
key_studies.venue: Central Bank of Chile Working Paper No. 33
key_studies.finding: Chile's 1981 funded-account reform improved labour markets and raised saving, investment and productivity; it accounts for about a quarter of Chile's growth increase.

key_studies.authors: Diamond, P. A.
key_studies.title: Administrative Costs and Equilibrium Charges with Individual Accounts
key_studies.finding: A government-organised individual-account system might cost $40-50 per worker per year; privately organised accounts would cost considerably more.

policies.name: Energy Without Subsidies
policies.why: Governments spend $634 billion to $1.4 trillion a year subsidising energy, mostly fossil fuels, and those subsidies waste about 40 cents of every dollar while raising emissions. Ending all of them, renewables and nuclear included, and clearing the way to license reactors, drill, build pipelines and export gas returns about 78 cents to $2.16 per dollar, counting every subsidy removed as money moved from recipients back to taxpayers. The low end reflects losing the emission cuts that renewable subsidies buy; faster nuclear licensing and letting development banks fund gas plants in poor countries add gains no study has yet priced.
policies.grade_reason: The priced parts rest on peer-reviewed estimates (Davis 2014 AER; Jewell et al. 2018 Nature; Abrell et al. 2019 J. Public Econ; Prest 2022 JAERE) with a Copenhagen Consensus ratio of 15 for fossil-subsidy phase-out as a cross-check, combined with official and think-tank figures for LNG exports, subsidy totals and the GDP effect of ending clean-energy credits (DOE, NERA, IRENA, Energy Innovation).
policies.difficulty_reason: Each country can act alone through ordinary legislation, and fuel-subsidy reform has precedents in Indonesia (2015) and India (2014).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Ending subsidies removes transfers that go mostly to better-off households (about 60% of US clean-energy tax credits went to the top income quintile, Borenstein & Davis 2016), and the Copenhagen Consensus finds particularly high benefits for developing countries when revenues are recycled; lifting development-bank bans could connect about 60 million more people per $10bn invested (Moss & Leo 2014).
policies.summary: This policy ends subsidies for every energy source, from fossil fuels to renewables and nuclear, speeds nuclear licensing, opens oil, gas and coal permitting, leasing and LNG export approval, and lets development banks finance gas and coal plants in poor countries. Ending fossil-fuel subsidies removes large deadweight losses and cuts emissions slightly, ending renewable subsidies saves money but adds emissions, and more drilling and gas exports add output. Counting the subsidies removed as transfers, each $1 returns $0.78 to $2.16; below 1 when renewable subsidies are treated as cheap abatement and the GDP loss from ending them is counted.
policies.selected_by: Fraser Economic Freedom of the World, Areas 1 and 5
policies.evidence: The parts of this package pull in opposite directions. Ending fossil-fuel subsidies removes real waste. Davis (2014) finds that road-fuel subsidies totalled $110 billion in 2012, and that "the total annual deadweight loss worldwide is $44 billion." That is 40 cents of pure loss for every subsidy dollar.
policies.ratio: All figures are annual global flows in billions of dollars. Subsidies removed are transfers, counted at $1 on both sides: taxpayers gain each dollar recipients lose. The ratio is (subsidies + efficiency gains + other gains − damages) ÷ (subsidies + other costs).
policies.counter: A higher value of carbon cuts both ways. Rennert et al. (2022) put the social cost of carbon at $185 a tonne at a 2% discount rate, against the $66 used here.

policies.name: Medicare Drug Price Negotiation
policies.why: Medicare is a buyer, and haggling over price is what buyers do; enrollees save about $2.2 billion a year out of pocket on the first 25 drugs. Patients who pay less for medicines take more of them, which on these savings means about 3,583 deaths averted a year. The cost is a small loss of new drugs, about 13 of 1,300 over 30 years, so each dollar returns between 54 cents and $2.79 once the cost of raising the taxes for running the programme is counted.
policies.grade_reason: The high end rests on official CBO and CMS estimates, converted with peer-reviewed estimates (Dubois et al. 2015, RAND Journal, for the value of a lost drug; Chandra, Flack & Obermeyer 2024, QJE, for health gains, applied by extrapolation). The low end rests on think-tank modelling (Hoover), so the best sources are official estimates, which makes it B-.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: it needed ordinary federal legislation (the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022) and is now run by CMS.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Savings are spread across Medicare enrollees and taxpayers.
policies.summary: Medicare negotiates prices for some high-spend drugs, and about 85% of Americans support it (KFF 2024; CES 2022 85.9%). Lower prices move money from drug makers to Medicare and its enrollees, and enrollees save about $2.2bn a year out of pocket on the first 25 drugs (CMS). A Quarterly Journal of Economics study finds Medicare patients who face higher drug costs take fewer medicines and die sooner; applied to these savings, that is about 3,583 deaths averted a year.
policies.evidence: Lower negotiated prices mainly move money from drug makers to Medicare and its enrollees. That transfer is not a gain to society on its own. The real gains and losses lie elsewhere.
policies.ratio: Benefit: savings to taxpayers and enrollees, plus health gains from lower out-of-pocket costs, minus lost innovation. Cost: manufacturers' revenue loss plus administration. Formula: BCR = (savings + health gains - lost innovation) ÷ (manufacturer revenue loss + administration).
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is lost innovation. Philipson and Durie (2021) find that the drug-pricing provisions of an earlier bill (H.R. 5376) would mean 135 fewer new drugs and 331.5 million US life-years lost through 2039.

policies.name: Ocean Protection
policies.why: Marine protected areas look good on paper, with the most complete global model finding $1.40 to $2.70 back per dollar, or up to $2.61 once the cost of raising the taxes for managing the areas is counted. That model assumes they work, and a Nature study of 87 of them found only 9 had the features that make protection effective. Counting benefits only where protection works gives about 10 to 12 cents per dollar, and fishers carry most of the cost through lost access.
policies.grade_reason: The range rests on one global bio-economic model (Brander et al. 2020, peer-reviewed), whose benefit inputs are disputed in Nature (Ovando et al. 2023; Hilborn & Kaiser 2022; Hiddink et al. 2023), and on field evidence that most MPAs do not deliver (Edgar et al. 2014; Gill et al. 2017). No randomized or ex-post global BCA exists.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each country can designate and enforce MPAs in its own waters under ordinary law (many have, e.g. the US Papahanaumokuakea monument); the global 30x30 target is agreed under the 2022 Kunming-Montreal framework, but high-seas protection needs the multilateral BBNJ treaty, and enforcement against fishing is costly.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Benefits (coastal protection, tourism, fish spill-over, biodiversity, carbon) are widely shared, and Balmford et al. estimate a global network would support about one million jobs; but the main cost, lost fishing access, falls on fishing communities, some of them poor, so distribution is mixed.
policies.summary: Marine protected areas close parts of the ocean to fishing and other uses to protect reefs, mangroves and fish stocks. The most complete global cost-benefit model finds $1.40-2.70 of benefit per $1, but it assumes the protected areas work as designed: a Nature study of 87 of them found only 9 had the features that make them effective, and most were ecologically indistinguishable from unprotected waters. Counting benefits only where protection works gives about 12 cents per $1.
policies.selected_by: Peoples' Climate Vote 45%
policies.evidence: Protecting parts of the ocean can pay through fish spilling over into open waters, tourism, coastal protection, biodiversity and stored carbon. The most complete global cost-benefit model finds benefits exceed costs by a factor of 1.4 to 2.7 (Brander et al. 2020). That model assumes protected areas work as designed.
policies.ratio: Benefits counted are fish spill-over, tourism and recreation, coastal protection, biodiversity and carbon storage in reefs, mangroves and coastal wetlands. Costs are setting up and managing the areas, plus the fishing income given up, which is about 90% of the total. High end: 2.7.
policies.counter: The strongest case for ocean protection is that well-chosen areas pay many times over. Brander's Copenhagen Consensus assessment for Africa gives 9.2 for protecting 10% of coastal waters, and an earlier global model found 3.2 to 19.8 (Brander et al. 2015).

policies.name: Global Carbon Tax
policies.why: A $135-per-tonne global tax is about twice the price the leading climate-economy model calls optimal, and published studies put its cost at 5.6% of world output, roughly $5.9 trillion a year. Its climate benefits come to 2.2 to 3.1% of world output, so each dollar returns about 16 to 55 cents. A world economy 5 to 11% smaller also means an estimated 152,000 to 505,000 more infant deaths a year in poor countries.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed benefit-cost results for Paris/1.5 C-strength carbon pricing (Tol 2023, Climate Change Economics; Nordhaus DICE, AER 2019 and PNAS 2024) with the cost side taken from the high end of peer-reviewed and IPCC-assessed GDP-loss estimates, plus a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental mortality adjustment (Chirakijja et al. 2024). Not A: no controlled or quasi-experimental study of a global tax at this level, none scores $135/t exactly, and DICE-2023 reports that a 2 C path passes a cost-benefit test.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: needs a binding agreement among many countries.
policies.who_benefits_reason: IMF (2019): a $75/t tax alone raises electricity prices ~45% and gasoline ~15% over a decade, hitting poorer households and fossil-dependent developing countries hardest; higher heating costs raise winter deaths (Chirakijja et al. 2024).
policies.summary: A $135-per-tonne global carbon tax by 2030 is a 1.5 C-strength price, about twice the social cost of carbon on the cost-benefit optimal path in the latest Nordhaus model and above the $115 optimal price that model reaches only by 2050, which also finds the 1.5 C path infeasible. Published cost-benefit studies put its cost at 5.6% of world output, roughly $5.9 trillion a year, and its author says uneven national implementation 'would readily double' that, against climate benefits of 2.2-3.1% of world output. Higher energy prices add winter deaths, and a world economy 5-11% smaller means an estimated 152,000-505,000 more infant deaths a year in poor countries.
policies.selected_by: Paris-aligned carbon price; IMF international carbon price floor
policies.evidence: The most direct test is Tol (2023), which sets the full cost of the Paris targets against their climate benefits. The 1.5°C target costs just above 5.5% of world output. Its benefits are about 3.1% of output against a high-emissions baseline and 2.2% against a middle one.
policies.ratio: World output is taken as about $105 trillion (Visual Capitalist 2023). Figures are dollars a year. High end: $0.55 per $1.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is a higher value of carbon. Rennert et al. (2022) put the social cost of carbon at $185 a tonne (5–95% range: $44 to $413) at a 2% discount rate, and on that number a $135 tax passes.

policies.name: Conserve Forests
policies.why: Paying people to keep tropical forests standing sounds cheap, and a randomized trial in Uganda did find $2.40 of climate benefit per dollar while the payments lasted. Most of the money ends up buying carbon credits, though, and only about 6% of those reflected real reductions, while 42 to 95% of protection in one place is offset by clearing somewhere else. That leaves about 9 cents back per dollar on a bill of roughly $33 billion a year, and once the cost of raising the taxes that fund it is counted, each dollar returns between 3 cents and $1.79.
policies.grade_reason: A randomized controlled trial published in Science reports a benefit-cost ratio (2.4, range 0.7-12.3), backed by a peer-reviewed quasi-experimental study of Brazilian enforcement (AEJ: Applied 2023) and a peer-reviewed global cost curve (PNAS 2008). The low end is built from a peer-reviewed synthetic-control evaluation of REDD+ credits (West et al. 2023, Science).
policies.difficulty_reason: A sustained funding scale-up with working precedents: Norway's results-based payments, the Amazon Fund, and Brazil's DETER enforcement system, which cut deforestation sharply after 2004-2008 (Assuncao et al. 2023).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Payments flow to rural forest-owning households in low-income tropical countries (Uganda trial); climate benefits are global.
policies.summary: Paying landowners or governments in tropical countries to keep forests standing is often presented as one of the cheapest ways to cut CO2. The best evidence, a randomized trial in Uganda, found $2.40 of climate benefit per $1 while payments lasted, and the authors call longer-lasting gains very tentative. Where the money buys carbon credits like those in voluntary REDD+ projects, only about 6% reflected real reductions, and 42-95% of protection in one place is offset by more clearing elsewhere, leaving about 9 cents per $1.
policies.selected_by: Peoples' Climate Vote 2021 (#1 of 18, 54%); Dechezleprêtre et al. 2025
policies.evidence: Paying people to keep forests standing is often presented as one of the cheapest ways to cut carbon dioxide (CO2). The best evidence is a randomized trial in Uganda. Forest owners in 60 of 121 villages were paid not to clear their land for two years.
policies.ratio: High end: 2.4. This is the Uganda trial's published central ratio (Jayachandran et al. 2017). The working paper puts total programme cost at scale, payments plus administration, at about $0.57 per tonne of CO2 delayed (Jayachandran et al. 2016).
policies.counter: The strongest case for the policy is that the high end understates it. The Copenhagen Consensus Post-2015 assessment rated halving forest loss at about 10, and Markandya's own assessment ran from $30 to more than $100 per $1 (Markandya 2015).

policies.name: Rent Control
policies.why: Over 85% of voters in one large survey support capping rents, while 80 to 89% of the economists on a leading expert panel say caps don't help. In San Francisco and Saint Paul, covered tenants gained but landlords pulled 15% of units off the rental market, which raised rents for everyone else. Add rent boards, apartments held by the wrong households and faster decay, and each dollar moved returns only 4 to 62 cents.

No published benefit-cost study exists, so A-level grades do not apply.

policies.summary: Rent control caps how fast rents can rise on covered apartments. It is very popular: over 85% of about 5,000 voters supported capping rents in Elmendorf, Nall & Oklobdzija's 2024 survey experiment (and 73.9% of US GSS/ISSP respondents say government should 'keep prices under control'). Economists disagree: 89% of the Clark Center panel in 2012 and 80% in 2024 rejected the claim that rent caps help.
policies.selected_by: ~85% support (survey experiment n≈5,000); ISSP price-control items
policies.evidence: Rent control works for the tenants it covers. After San Francisco expanded rent control in 1994, covered tenants gained $7.621 billion over 1995-2012, about $423 million a year, and roughly a third of that came as buyout payments from landlords (Diamond, McQuade, and Qian 2018a). The same study finds that treated landlords cut their supply of rental housing by 15%, by converting to condominiums, selling to owner-occupiers or redeveloping.
policies.ratio: No study publishes a benefit-cost ratio for rent control, so the ratio is built from natural experiments. It measures the value that reaches protected tenants, net of the harm to everyone else, administration and misallocation, per $1 taken from property owners and other renters. The transfer counts $1 for $1, with no extra weight for tenants.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is a calibrated model of New York. Favilukis, Mabille and Van Nieuwerburgh (2023) find that affordability policies, rent control included, carry substantial insurance value, and that targeting the neediest can yield substantial net welfare gains despite supply and misallocation costs.

policies.name: Renewable Energy Subsidies
policies.why: Wind and solar subsidies do cut emissions, but at wildly different prices, up to about $2,100 per tonne of CO2 for solar in Germany and Spain. Counting the federal credits and the higher power bills from state mandates, the cost is around $238 billion a year, and once the cost of raising the taxes behind the credits is counted, each dollar returns only about 1 to 58 cents. Where wind and solar are already cheapest they need no help, and where they aren't, the subsidy buys very expensive tonnes.
policies.grade_reason: The end points come from a peer-reviewed natural experiment (Abrell et al. 2019, weather variation) and a model-based estimate published in Brookings Papers (Bistline et al. 2023), with a quasi-experimental working paper (Greenstone & Nath, revised 2026) in between, converted to BCRs with published SCC values. Results differ in sign by technology and SCC, so not A-range.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate: needs ordinary budget or tax legislation (or state RPS statutes), with abundant precedent (IRA 2022, EU and German feed-in laws, 29 US state RPS laws).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Borenstein & Davis (2016, Tax Policy and the Economy) find the top income quintile received ~60% of US clean-energy tax credits and the bottom three quintiles ~10%; mandates raise retail electricity prices 11-17% (Greenstone & Nath), a cost that weighs more on low-income households.
policies.summary: Subsidies, tax credits and mandates for wind and solar cut emissions, but at very different costs per tonne of CO2. Solar subsidies in Germany and Spain cost up to about $2,100 per tonne, returning about 2 cents per dollar at the former US government carbon value, while US state mandates cost $86-211 per tonne and model estimates of the Inflation Reduction Act's power-sector credits about $88 per tonne on a consistent basis. Overall range: about 2 to 75 cents per dollar.
policies.selected_by: Peoples' Climate Vote 53%; Dechezleprêtre et al. 69.5%
policies.evidence: Subsidies and mandates for wind and solar do cut emissions. The question is the cost per tonne, and that varies widely. The most expensive case is solar subsidies in Germany and Spain.
policies.ratio: The ratio is the social value of a tonne of CO2 avoided, divided by the social resource cost of abating it. The abatement costs used are resource costs: generation, backup, transmission and fuel, or observed changes in retail prices. They already contain the costs borne by firms and ratepayers.
policies.counter: The strongest case for renewable subsidies comes from Wiser et al. (2017) at two Department of Energy (DOE) national laboratories. They find existing state mandates cost up to $31 billion over 2015 to 2050, against $97 billion in health benefits and $161 billion in climate benefits under central assumptions.

policies.name: Combustion Car Ban
policies.why: On coal-heavy grids like most of Asia's, an electric car can do more pollution damage than the gasoline car it replaces, and an analysis of the UK's 2030 ban puts costs at five times the benefits. Battery trucks cost more than twice as much as diesel and carry about 13,800 lb less, and batteries, grid upgrades and chargers for cars run about $535 to $985 billion a year. If electric vehicles are better, people will buy them without being ordered to.
policies.grade_reason: The low end rests on peer-reviewed environmental-damage models (Holland et al. 2016 AER, with the 2020 AEJ: Policy update; Ji et al. 2012 EST) and the main cross-check on a peer-reviewed CGE model of an actual mandate (McKitrick 2024 CJE); the high end is a government self-appraisal (B- alone), and the cost inputs are industry and think-tank figures (Brattle, Mills). No ex-post or quasi-experimental BCR of an ICE sales ban exists.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each market can ban sales of new combustion-engine vehicles through ordinary legislation or regulation, with no treaty required, and the EU has adopted a 2035 rule.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Up-front premiums fall on car buyers, and lower-income and rural households face the largest relative burden and the least access to home charging; Borenstein & Davis (2016) find ~90% of US EV tax credits went to the top income quintile.
policies.summary: Requiring every new car and truck sold to be zero-emission (cars by 2030 worldwide; trucks on California's and the EU's schedules) would cut oil use, but on coal-heavy grids, like most of Asia's, an electric car can do more pollution damage than the gasoline car it replaces (about minus 7 cents per dollar), and an analysis of the UK's 2030 car ban puts costs at five times benefits (19 cents per dollar). Battery trucks cost more than twice as much as diesel, carry about 13,800 lb less, and electrifying US trucking alone needs nearly $1 trillion of chargers and grid; a general-equilibrium model of Canada's mandate finds GDP up to 7% lower by 2035. Battery premiums, grid upgrades and chargers for cars cost about $535-985bn a year, plus about $58bn a year for US truck charging and grid.
policies.selected_by: Only policy asked in all three surveys (PCV, Dechezleprêtre, EIB)
policies.evidence: A ban would cut oil use, but what it does for the climate and for health depends on the power grid. On the 2010 to 2012 US grid, Holland et al. (2016) find that the average electric car did $1,095 more environmental damage over its life than the gasoline car it replaced. The US grid has since become cleaner, and by 2017 electric cars were cleaner than gasoline cars on average (Holland et al. 2020).
policies.ratio: No study evaluates this ban directly, so the ends come from the closest priced analyses. No published ratio covers trucks on the pessimistic side, so the range is anchored on the evidence for cars. Low end: −0.07. 1.
policies.counter: Regulators' own appraisals make the strongest case for a ban. The UK Department for Transport (2023) rates its mandate of 80% zero-emission cars and 70% vans by 2030 at 1.31.

policies.name: Global Plastic Ban
policies.why: Canada's single-use plastics ban returns about 31 cents per dollar and England's straw ban as little as 3 cents. The paper, glass, metal and cotton substitutes usually weigh more and emit more greenhouse gas, adding an estimated $394 billion a year in environmental damage. Add a GDP cost of about $870 billion a year and a global ban returns somewhere between minus 42 and plus 30 cents per dollar.
policies.grade_reason: Built from regulators' own impact analyses (Canada RIAS, UK Defra IA) adjusted with a peer-reviewed life-cycle study (Meng et al. 2024) and peer-reviewed substitution evidence (Taylor 2019); the low end uses an industry-commissioned natural-capital valuation (Trucost 2016), which on its own would rate C+. No study monetises a global ban.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: needs a binding international agreement among many countries.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Bag bans and fees weigh most on low-income shoppers (Reason, Morris & Seasholes 2014), Defra expects 60% of the higher substitute costs to pass through to consumers, and the OECD (2022) finds costs of ambitious action concentrated in non-OECD countries.
policies.summary: Governments that have banned single-use plastics measured costs well above the benefits they could put a number on: Canada's ban returns about 31 cents per dollar and England's straw ban as little as 3 cents. Life-cycle studies find that the substitutes (paper, glass, metal, cotton) usually weigh more and emit more greenhouse gas, so a general ban can add environmental damage; one valuation puts the extra damage at about $394bn a year. Counting compliance and a GDP cost of about 0.8% of world output (~$870bn a year), the return ranges from about minus 42 cents to plus 30 cents per dollar.
policies.selected_by: UN plastics treaty negotiations (UNEA resolution 5/14)
policies.evidence: Governments that have banned single-use plastics have measured the result, and the numbers are poor. Canada's ban returns about 31 cents of monetised benefit per dollar of cost (Environment and Climate Change Canada 2022). England's straw ban returns as little as 3 cents (Defra 2020).
policies.ratio: The cost base is $869 billion a year (see Full cost). The ratio is the regulator's own benefit per dollar of cost, less the extra environmental damage from heavier substitutes per dollar of cost. High end: $0.30 per $1. - Canada's impact statement: benefits C$616 million against costs C$1,990 million = 0.31.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is that waste policy can save money. Lau et al. (2020) find that a scenario of reuse, redesign and recycling could cut plastic flows into the ocean by more than 80% by 2040 with existing technology.

policies.name: Billionaire Wealth Tax
policies.why: A 2% yearly minimum tax on the world's roughly 2,800 billionaires would raise $242 billion a year if perfectly enforced, and that money is a transfer, not a gain. Raising it costs from 34 cents to nearly $2 per dollar, as wealth is hidden, moved or valued down and less capital is built, and valuation and collection add $28.5 billion a year. Counting the cost of raising other taxes to run it, each dollar collected yields between a $1.20 loss and a 59-cent net gain, and once lost-income deaths are counted the middle result is a loss.
policies.grade_reason: The two ends rest on peer-reviewed estimates of the cost of raising tax revenue (Ballard, Shoven and Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999), the same as the other transfer entries, applied to the proposal's own revenue estimate. The wealth-tax responses behind the sensitivity come from peer-reviewed natural experiments in Switzerland, Denmark and Sweden and a peer-reviewed review that reconciles them (Brülhart et al. 2022; Jakobsen et al. 2020; Advani and Tarrant 2021); administration and compliance costs come from a UK commission's costing.
policies.difficulty_reason: It needs a binding agreement among many countries, and the 2024 G20 declaration commits only to 'engage cooperatively ... with full respect to tax sovereignty'.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The tax is paid by about 2,800 billionaires, whose effective tax rate would rise from about 22% to 39% of pre-tax income (Zucman 2024).
policies.summary: A coordinated 2% minimum tax on the wealth of the world's roughly 3,000 billionaires, as proposed to the G20 in 2024, would raise $242bn a year if perfectly enforced. The revenue is a transfer; the costs are the extra burden of raising it, the costs of valuing and collecting the tax, and the output lost as less capital is built. Scored like the other transfer policies, each $1 collected delivers between a net loss of $1.20 and a net 59 cents of value; lost-income mortality lowers both ends.
policies.selected_by: Ipsos 2024 G20 survey (Earth4All): 68%
policies.evidence: About 2,800 billionaires owned $14.2 trillion in 2024. Their current tax is equivalent to 0.3% of their wealth, so a 2% minimum adds 1.7% of wealth: $242 billion a year if perfectly enforced, or $193 billion if a fifth is lost to avoidance and evasion (Zucman 2024). That money is a transfer.
policies.ratio: The revenue is a transfer, so the ratio takes the net-damage form used for the other transfer policies: ratio = (transfer - excess burden - administration - private compliance) ÷ transfer, all per $1 of wealth tax collected. Step 1: the tax base. Billionaires owned $14.2 trillion in 2024 and already pay tax equal to 0.3% of it.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-evidence is Guvenen et al. (2023). When returns differ across investors, a wealth tax falls on idle fortunes and spares productive ones.

policies.name: Block Social Security and Medicare Changes
policies.why: Shielding Social Security and Medicare from any change polls at net +72, but the Trustees put the gap at about $535 billion a year on average over 75 years. Blocking higher retirement ages means that gap gets filled with taxes or borrowing, and it forgoes the extra work and tax revenue of longer careers. Each dollar returns between minus $1.27 and plus 66 cents, and younger workers get the bill.
policies.grade_reason: Combines a peer-reviewed natural experiment on retirement behaviour (Mastrobuoni 2009, JPubE), CBO macro estimates and the Trustees' official fiscal gap, with peer-reviewed excess-burden estimates (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Feldstein 1999). No published benefit-cost ratio exists for keeping current-law benefits, and the labour-supply feedback is from CBO's model rather than a measured welfare change, so the grade is below B+.
policies.difficulty_reason: Keeping current benefit rules needs no change, but paying full scheduled benefits after 2034 (OASDI) and 2033 (HI) needs ordinary legislation to raise payroll taxes or transfer general revenue; Congress has done this before (1977 and 1983 amendments).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Benefits go to nearly all retirees and disabled workers; Engelhardt & Gruber find a roughly unitary elasticity of elderly poverty with respect to benefits, so cuts would raise poverty, which favours the poor.
policies.summary: This policy blocks any rise in the Social Security or Medicare eligibility ages and any cut in scheduled benefits, so the trust-fund shortfalls must be filled with new taxes or borrowing. It is among the most popular ideas tested: 87.5% of US GSS/ISSP respondents say government should provide a decent living for the old, and protecting both programmes from cuts or age increases had net support of +72 in a 2024 YouGov poll of 4,038 voters. The 2026 Trustees put the gap at about $535bn a year on average over 75 years; at the high end, the taxes to fill it and the work forgone could cost the economy more than twice that again.
policies.selected_by: ISSP 88-99%; YouGov net +72
policies.evidence: The gap is large. The 2026 Trustees put the 75-year deficit at 4.42% of taxable payroll for Social Security and 0.56% for Medicare HI, together about 1.67% of GDP, or roughly $535 billion a year (Social Security and Medicare Boards of Trustees 2026). Social Security alone costs 5.3% of GDP in 2026, and its annual deficit rises from 0.8% of GDP in 2026 to 2.4% in 2085.
policies.ratio: Benefits are scored like other transfers on this list: ratio = (1 - excess burden × net fiscal cost) ÷ net fiscal cost. Net fiscal cost includes administration and the fiscal externality of lower work. Step 1: the work effect of blocking an age rise. - Raising the full retirement age to 70 cuts Social Security spending about 13%.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is that benefits keep older people out of poverty. Engelhardt and Gruber (2006) find that cutting benefits would significantly raise elderly poverty, with poverty moving roughly one for one with benefits.

key_studies.title: AIDOLDGOVTS: government responsibility to provide a decent standard of living for the old

policies.name: Student Loan Forgiveness
policies.why: The 2022 forgiveness plan would have cost about $400 billion, roughly $40 billion a year over a decade, and the benefits tilt toward higher earners. Expected future forgiveness encourages more borrowing, which one model says adds 39 to 63% to the cost, and much of the extra student lending ends up as higher tuition. Each dollar is worth a dollar to borrowers but costs taxpayers more, so the return runs from about minus $1.39 to plus 67 cents.
policies.grade_reason: Built from peer-reviewed estimates of the excess burden of taxation (Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985 AER; Feldstein 1999 REStat) applied to official cost estimates (CBO 2022; PWBM 2022), with peer-reviewed distributional evidence (Catherine & Yannelis 2023 JFE). There is no direct benefit-cost study or experiment on broad forgiveness, so B+ or above does not apply.
policies.difficulty_reason: Biden v.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Catherine & Yannelis (2023, JFE), measuring debt in present value, find full or partial forgiveness is regressive: the top income decile gains as much as the bottom three deciles combined.
policies.summary: Broad student-loan forgiveness cancels federal student debt for most borrowers, as in the 2022 plan of up to $10,000-20,000 each. It has majority support: 55.1% backed forgiving up to $20,000 per person in the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (weighted, researcher-computed). CBO put the 2022 plan at about $400bn, roughly $40bn a year over a decade; running it costs very little extra, but the taxes needed to fund it could cost the economy up to about $80bn a year more.
policies.evidence: Forgiveness is a transfer. Each $1 of present-value debt cancelled is worth $1 to the borrower, and CBO's present-value scoring already allows for loans that would never have been repaid (CBO 2022). The Penn Wharton Budget Model put the cancellation at $469-519 billion over ten years (Smetters and Chen 2022).
policies.ratio: Forgiveness is scored like other transfers on this list: ratio = (value to borrowers - excess burden × net fiscal cost) ÷ net fiscal cost. Value to borrowers is $1 per $1 of present-value debt cancelled. Step 1: administration.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is that relief changes lives. Di Maggio, Kalda and Yao (2020) find that borrowers whose private loans were voided by a legal accident cut their debt by 11%, had 24% fewer delinquent accounts, moved and changed jobs more, and earned about $3,000 more over three years.

key_studies.authors: Catherine, S.; Yannelis, C.
key_studies.title: The Distributional Effects of Student Loan Forgiveness
key_studies.finding: Full or partial forgiveness is regressive in present value: the top decile benefits as much as the bottom three deciles combined; enrolling eligible households in income-driven repayment is cheapest and most progressive.

key_studies.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
key_studies.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
key_studies.finding: Marginal excess burden centres around 33 cents per $1 of revenue, range 17-56 cents (per Fullerton & Henderson 1987, NBER w2353).

key_studies.authors: Feldstein, M.
key_studies.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
key_studies.finding: Deadweight loss of nearly $2 per extra $1 of revenue from a proportional rise in all personal income tax rates.

key_studies.authors: Catherine, S.; Perez Clanton, M.; Yannelis, C.
key_studies.title: The Distributional Effects of Student Loan Forgiveness: An Update on SAVE and the COVID-19 Moratorium
key_studies.finding: Income-driven repayment expansions are more progressive than universal forgiveness but may raise moral hazard at the school level.

key_studies.authors: Lucca, D. O.; Nadauld, T.; Shen, K.
key_studies.title: Credit Supply and the Rise in College Tuition: Evidence from the Expansion in Federal Student Aid Programs
key_studies.venue: Review of Financial Studies 32(2): 423-466 (FRBNY Staff Report 733)
key_studies.finding: About 60 cents of each $1 increase in subsidised loan maximums passes through to tuition; used to describe where induced borrowing goes, not added separately.

key_studies.title: Cooperative Election Study 2024 Common Content

policies.name: Digital ID Mandate
policies.why: Only 42% of Britons back the UK plan, and the best evidence comes from two randomized trials in India. When biometric checks became compulsory for food rations, corruption did not fall, costs rose about 8% and hundreds of thousands of legitimate recipients lost benefits, about minus $1 per dollar, or minus $1.94 once the cost of raising the taxes for the new card readers is counted. A carefully managed biometric payment system in Andhra Pradesh roughly paid for itself at about $1.05 per dollar, or 78 cents after the cost of raising taxes, and that is before counting privacy and surveillance risks.
policies.grade_reason: Both ends are converted directly from peer-reviewed randomized evaluations (RESTAT 2025; AER 2016) that report costs and benefits. Applying evidence from Indian welfare delivery to a worldwide mandate is by analogy, and the two trials point in opposite directions, so the grade is B+ rather than A.
policies.difficulty_reason: Each country can mandate a digital ID through ordinary legislation, and India's Aadhaar shows enrolment of more than a billion people is possible.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Exclusion risk falls on the poor.
policies.summary: A digital ID mandate would require everyone to hold and use a government digital identity. Public support is lukewarm: a September 2025 YouGov poll found 42% of Britons for and 45% against the UK plan. The best evidence comes from two randomized trials in India.
policies.selected_by: YouGov 2025: 42% support (UK); Ipsos UK 2025: 57% support a national ID card
policies.evidence: The best evidence comes from two randomized trials in India, both by Muralidharan, Niehaus and Sukhtankar. In Jharkhand, biometric checks were made compulsory for food rations. Corruption did not fall: leakage rose by an insignificant Rs 14 per ration card a month.
policies.ratio: Both ends come straight from the two randomized evaluations. Low end (Jharkhand, compulsory authentication for food rations): - Benefit: the change in leakage, a rise of Rs 14 per ration card a month. - Cost: extra transaction costs of Rs 13.6 per card a month. - Ratio: -14 ÷ 13.6 = -1.03, about -1.0. High end (Andhra Pradesh biometric smartcards): - Benefit: recipients' time savings, $4.3 million. - Cost: the government's cost of running the programme, $4.1 million. - Ratio: 4.3 ÷ 4.1 = 1.05.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is the size of the prize. McKinsey projects that consent-based, privacy-protecting "good" digital ID could unlock value equal to 3% to 13% of GDP by 2030 (White et al. 2019).

key_studies.authors: Muralidharan, K.; Niehaus, P.; Sukhtankar, S.
key_studies.title: Identity Verification Standards in Welfare Programs: Experimental Evidence from India
key_studies.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 107(2): 372-392 (NBER Working Paper 26744, 2020)
key_studies.finding: Randomized rollout of mandatory Aadhaar-based biometric authentication (ABBA) in Jharkhand's food-ration program: 'leakage increased insignificantly by Rs. 14 per ration card x month'; ABBA 'did not decrease (and if anything slightly increased) government spending'; 'overall transaction costs across the government, dealers, and beneficiaries increased by Rs. 13.6 per ration card per month ... a non-trivial 7.8% increase'; beneficiaries' own costs +Rs 7 (17% of control mean); unseeded households lost Rs 49/month (12.6%); nearly 300,000 people lost access to benefits. Biometric (Aadhaar) verification reforms in India's PDS reduced corruption but 1.5-2 million beneficiaries lost access at some point; adverse effects driven mainly by how the transition was managed.

key_studies.authors: Muralidharan, K.; Niehaus, P.; Sukhtankar, S.
key_studies.title: Building State Capacity: Evidence from Biometric Smartcards in India
key_studies.finding: RCT across 157 subdistricts (19m people): 'the investment was cost-effective, as time savings to NREGS beneficiaries alone were equal to the cost of the intervention'; NREGS beneficiary time savings $4.3m vs government cost of implementation and operation $4.1m; NREGS leakage reduction $32.8m a year (eight times cost); SSP leakage reduction $3.3m a year vs $2.3m cost.

key_studies.authors: Gelb, A.; Clark, J.
key_studies.title: Identification for Development: The Biometrics Revolution (Working Paper 315)
key_studies.venue: Center for Global Development Working Paper 315
key_studies.finding: p.17: unit cost of national ID schemes in poor countries 'typically around US$5 per head'; fn 31: unit cost estimates for the UK's abortive ID card US$150-600 per head (BBC 2009).

key_studies.authors: World Bank ID4D
key_studies.title: Identification for Development (ID4D) overview brochure
key_studies.finding: ~40% of adults 15+ in surveyed low-income countries lack ID; 45% of poorest quintile vs 28% richest; 45% of women vs 30% of men; robust ID systems 'have the potential to produce substantial savings in the public sector' (no dollar figure)

key_studies.authors: United Nations DESA
key_studies.title: World population to reach 8 billion on 15 November 2022
key_studies.finding: World population reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022.

key_studies.authors: World Bank (Koshy, T.; Jayaram, P.; Menon, R.; Jain, N.; Prajapat, U. [Ernst & Young]; Chandra, K.)
key_studies.title: Understanding Cost Drivers of Identification Systems
key_studies.finding: Citing Gelb & Diofasi Metz (2018): building a foundational ID likely costs a low-income country ~0.6% of GDP; enrolment and credential issuance ~$4-11 per registrant; recurrent costs ~0.06-0.1% of GDP in a few countries; staff often >80% of annual costs; Aadhaar iris capture added ~Rs 4.40 ($0.06) per enrolment.

policies.name: Medicare for All
policies.why: Medicare for All has 66% support and would add $1.5 to $3.0 trillion a year in federal spending. Taxes on that scale could shrink GDP by as much as 9%, and Canadian-length waits of 30 weeks would cost patients about $67 billion a year in lost time. Even counting lives saved, each dollar destroys 57 to 77 cents of value.
policies.grade_reason: The range rests on official CBO estimates and think-tank models (Urban Institute, Mercatus), plus one peer-reviewed modelling study (Galvani et al., Lancet) whose savings CBO and Urban do not replicate. Health effects of coverage are backed by quasi-experimental and randomized evidence (Miller et al. 2021 QJE; Oregon experiment), but no peer-reviewed BCA of single payer exists.
policies.difficulty_reason: Moderate by the rubric: ordinary federal legislation, with modern precedents abroad (e.g., Canada, Taiwan's 1995 single payer).
policies.who_benefits_reason: Gains go mostly to the uninsured and underinsured, who are disproportionately low-income: covering low-income adults through Medicaid cut their mortality (Miller, Johnson & Wherry 2021) and cut their medical debt (Oregon experiment).
policies.summary: Medicare for All would replace private insurance with one government plan covering everyone. It is popular, with 66% support in the CES 2022. Official and think-tank estimates agree it would add $1.5-3.0 trillion a year in federal spending, but they disagree about whether total national health spending would rise or fall, and one government estimate says the taxes to pay for it could shrink GDP by 9%.
policies.evidence: No published benefit-cost study of single payer exists, so the ratio is built from official and academic estimates. They agree on one thing: federal spending would rise by $1.5 trillion to $3.0 trillion a year by 2030 (Congressional Budget Office 2020). They disagree on whether total national health spending would rise or fall.
policies.ratio: The new federal spending counts as $1 to households per $1, in both benefit and cost. The excess burden of tax financing and the waiting cost are subtracted from benefits. Any rise in national health spending is added to the cost base.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is that single payer saves both money and lives. Galvani et al. (2020) estimate it cuts national health spending by about 13%, more than $450 billion a year, and prevents more than 68,000 deaths a year.

key_studies.authors: Galvani, A.P.; Parpia, A.S.; Foster, E.M.; Singer, B.H.; Fitzpatrick, M.C.
key_studies.title: Improving the prognosis of health care in the USA
key_studies.finding: Single payer (S. 1804) saves about 13% of national health expenditure, more than $450bn a year (2017 USD), and prevents more than 68,000 deaths and 1.73 million life-years lost a year.

key_studies.authors: Miller, S.; Johnson, N.; Wherry, L.R.
key_studies.title: Medicaid and Mortality: New Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data
key_studies.finding: ACA Medicaid expansions cut annual mortality among affected near-elderly adults by 0.132 percentage points (9.4%); CBPP summary: at least 19,200 deaths averted among 55-64-year-olds in expansion states 2014-17.

key_studies.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
key_studies.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
key_studies.finding: Marginal welfare loss from raising an additional $1 of revenue is 34-48 cents; 34 cents used here.

key_studies.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
key_studies.finding: 'The relative deadweight loss caused by increasing existing tax rates is substantially greater and may exceed $2 per $1 of revenue.'

key_studies.authors: Browning, E.K.
key_studies.title: On the Marginal Welfare Cost of Taxation
key_studies.finding: 'MWC can vary from under 10 percent to more than 300 percent of marginal tax revenue.'

key_studies.authors: Broughel, J.; Viscusi, W.K.
key_studies.title: Death by Regulation: How Regulations Can Increase Mortality Risk (research summary)
key_studies.venue: Mercatus Center at George Mason University
key_studies.finding: Regulations costing more than $99.3 million per life saved can be expected to increase mortality risk (range $75.4m-$123.2m): about one statistical death per $99.3m of cost imposed, through lower income and private health spending.

policies.name: Price Controls
policies.why: Price caps poll well, with 65% of likely voters backing a crackdown on grocery price gouging, but 88% of surveyed economists agree widespread controls create substantial distortions. High prices in an emergency are the signal that pulls supplies toward the people who need them most. Under the 1970s gasoline controls, queues alone burned about 116% of the money moved from sellers to buyers, and each dollar shifted destroys 44 cents to $1.29 of value.
policies.grade_reason: Peer-reviewed historical natural experiments measure the losses (Frech & Lee 1987 QJE; Deacon & Sonstelie 1985 JPE; Davis & Kilian 2011 JPE; Blinder & Newton 1981 JME; Cavallo et al. 2014 RIW), and a 2026 working paper (Albrecht, Tabarrok & Whitmeyer) supplies the bounds used in the arithmetic. No published benefit-cost ratio exists.
policies.difficulty_reason: Ordinary legislation.
policies.who_benefits_reason: The transfer goes to whoever obtains the price-capped good, not specifically to the poor.
policies.summary: Price Controls & Price Gouging caps prices, either during emergencies (anti-price-gouging laws) or generally (economy-wide or grocery price controls). It polls well: 65% of likely voters backed cracking down on grocery price gouging (Data for Progress, April 2026), and 73.9% of US GSS/ISSP respondents say government should keep prices under control. Economists are close to unanimous against it: 88% of the Clark Center panel in 2024 agreed that widespread price controls create substantial distortions, and most opposed Connecticut's 2012 anti-gouging bill.
policies.selected_by: Data for Progress 2026: 65%
policies.evidence: A price cap moves money from sellers to the buyers who still get the good. It also destroys value three ways: trades that no longer happen, goods that go to people and places that value them less, and time burned in queues. The best evidence comes from the US gasoline controls of the 1970s.
policies.ratio: The ratio measures the net value to buyers per $1 taken from sellers: (transfer - queuing - lost trades - misallocation - administration and compliance) ÷ transfer. All terms are in points of normal spending on the controlled good, calibrated to the 1973-74 gasoline controls. Step 1: the transfer.
policies.counter: The best counter-evidence comes from Argentina's targeted supermarket controls of 2007-15. Controlled goods stayed available, with no sign of shortages (Aparicio and Cavallo 2021).

key_studies.authors: Frech, H. E. III; Lee, W. C.
key_studies.title: The Welfare Cost of Rationing-By-Queuing Across Markets: Theory and Estimates from the U.S. Gasoline Crises
key_studies.finding: Estimates the welfare cost of improper allocation across markets in the 1973-74 and 1979 gasoline crises (queuing costs could exceed the transfer, per Albrecht et al.).

key_studies.authors: Davis, L. W.; Kilian, L.
key_studies.title: The Allocative Cost of Price Ceilings in the U.S. Residential Market for Natural Gas
key_studies.finding: Allocative cost of natural-gas price ceilings averaged $4.6bn a year 1950-2000 (peak $6.4bn in 1980), roughly tripling earlier net welfare loss estimates; MacAvoy's DWL $10.5bn/yr 1968-77.

key_studies.authors: Blinder, A. S.; Newton, W. J.
key_studies.title: The 1971-1974 Controls Program and the Price Level: An Econometric Post-Mortem
key_studies.finding: Nixon controls cut the non-food, non-energy price level 3-4% by Feb 1974, but catch-up after April 1974 left it only 0-2% below the no-controls path; decontrol explains most of 1974's double-digit core inflation.

key_studies.authors: Cavallo, A.; Cavallo, E.; Rigobon, R.
key_studies.title: Prices and Supply Disruptions during Natural Disasters
key_studies.venue: Review of Income and Wealth 60: S449-S471
key_studies.finding: After the 2010 Chile and 2011 Japan earthquakes, goods available fell 32% and 17% while prices stayed stable for months (sellers fearing 'customer anger').

key_studies.authors: Deacon, R. T.; Sonstelie, J.
key_studies.title: The Welfare Costs of Rationing by Waiting
key_studies.finding: Under gasoline price controls with rationing by waiting, the value of time in queues plus the waste from buying more per purchase may exceed the rent transferred from suppliers to consumers; 'Rent seeking exhausts an estimated 116 percent of the rent transferred.'

key_studies.authors: Tarr, D. G.
key_studies.title: The Welfare Costs of Price Controls for Cars and Color Televisions in Poland: Contrasting Estimates of Rent-Seeking from Recent Experience
key_studies.finding: Colour televisions with rent dissipation: welfare cost 0.46% of GDP, 112% of Polish producers' sales, about ten times the Harberger triangle (rent rectangle 116bn zlotys, triangle 14bn). Cars without dissipation: 0.29% of GDP, 36% of producers' sales.

quotes.text: Rent seeking exhausts an estimated 116 percent of the rent transferred.

policies.name: Global Universal Basic Income
policies.why: A randomized US trial found every dollar paid out cut household earnings by 28 to 37 cents, with partners cutting work as much as recipients. A global version would cost roughly a third of world GDP, far more than taxes can raise without heavy losses, and one model finds it would shrink GDP by about 13%. Each dollar returns between minus $1.26 and minus $1.09, while donor-funded cash in poor Kenyan villages shows the same idea working well as charity.
policies.grade_reason: Built from a modern RCT (Vivalt et al. 2024), a peer-reviewed MVPF for the randomized NIT experiments (Hendren & Sprung-Keyser 2020, QJE) and peer-reviewed excess-burden and dynamic GE estimates (Feldstein 1999; Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985; Daruich & Fernández 2024); no study scores a global UBI directly.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: a global scheme needs binding commitments across many countries, and the ILO puts a poverty-line UBI at 32.7-39.4% of GDP on average and 62-79% of GDP in low-income countries.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Payments go to everyone rather than being targeted, so most spending reaches the non-poor, and financing creates high implicit marginal tax rates on middle earners (Henderson 2019).
policies.summary: A universal basic income pays every adult a regular, unconditional cash amount. It splits opinion: 45% of Americans favoured a $1,000-a-month UBI in Pew's 2020 survey, while 68% of EU respondents said they would vote for one in Dalia's 2017 poll. A randomized US trial (OpenResearch) found every $1 paid out cut recipients' household earnings by 28-37 cents, with partners cutting work as much as recipients, and delivering the money costs about 4-25 cents per $1 on top.
policies.selected_by: Pew 2020: 45% US support for $1,000/month UBI; Dalia 2017: 68% EU
policies.evidence: The best evidence on how people respond comes from a randomized US trial. OpenResearch paid 1,000 people $1,000 a month for three years, against 2,000 controls on $50 a month (Vivalt et al. 2024). The authors report: "For every dollar received, total household income excluding the transfers fell by about 28 cents, and total individual income fell by around 16 cents." Partners cut their hours about as much as recipients did.
policies.ratio: The ratio is built per $1 paid out. A transfer is worth its face value to the person who receives it, so the benefit is $1. The cost to the public purse is larger than $1, because recipients earn less and pay less tax, and because delivery costs money.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case comes from cash trials in poor countries. In Kenya's GiveDirectly trial across 295 villages, "Labor supply did not change overall, but shifted out of wage employment and towards self-employment" (Banerjee et al. 2023).

key_studies.authors: Hendren, N.; Sprung-Keyser, B.
key_studies.title: A Unified Welfare Analysis of Government Policies
key_studies.finding: MVPFs for 133 US policies: Negative Income Tax experiment MVPF = -0.01 (partly due to reduced earnings of children in adulthood, per Price & Song 2018); tax credits and cash welfare to low-income households range from negative values to 1.20 (EITC 1.12-1.20); unemployment insurance 0.43-1.03; housing vouchers 0.65-0.91.

key_studies.authors: Feldstein, M.
key_studies.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
key_studies.finding: Deadweight loss could be as much as 30% of revenue; 'A marginal increase in tax revenue achieved by a proportional rise in all personal income tax rates involves a deadweight loss of nearly two dollars per incremental dollar of revenue.' Used as the high excess-burden case for financing a UBI.

key_studies.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
key_studies.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
key_studies.finding: CGE model of the US tax system: 'The marginal welfare loss to consumers from raising an additional dollar of revenue is in the range of 34 cents to 48 cents' (working-paper abstract). Used as the low (mainstream) excess-burden case.

key_studies.authors: Caldes, N.; Coady, D.; Maluccio, J. A.
key_studies.title: The Cost of Poverty Alleviation Transfer Programs: A Comparative Analysis of Three Programs in Latin America (FCND Discussion Paper 174; published in World Development 34(5), 2006)
key_studies.venue: IFPRI FCND Discussion Paper / World Development
key_studies.finding: Steady-state cost-transfer ratios (non-transfer cost per unit transferred): PROGRESA 0.041, PRAF 0.068, RPS 0.212; programme-life averages including set-up: PROGRESA 0.106, PRAF 0.499, RPS 0.629.

key_studies.authors: Browning, E.K.
key_studies.title: On the Marginal Welfare Cost of Taxation
key_studies.finding: 'MWC can vary from under 10 percent to more than 300 percent of marginal tax revenue.'

key_studies.authors: Jones, D.; Marinescu, I.
key_studies.title: The Labor Market Impacts of Universal and Permanent Cash Transfers: Evidence from the Alaska Permanent Fund
key_studies.finding: Abstract (p.315): 'the dividend had no effect on employment and increased part-time work by 1.8 percentage points (17 percent)'; 'a universal and permanent cash transfer does not significantly decrease aggregate employment'; cites an income effect of about -0.1 from the NIT experiments and lottery studies.

policies.name: Green New Deal
policies.why: Here every Western nation adopts the Green New Deal, and its outlays alone come to about a third of Western GDP, more than four times the most extra revenue US taxes could ever raise. Because only the West cuts, 12% to 130% of the reduction leaks abroad, and at the top of that range world emissions actually rise. Each dollar destroys about $1.19 to $1.38 of value, and the slower growth costs an estimated 42,000 to 164,000 infant lives a year in poor countries.
policies.grade_reason: The parameters that drive the ratio are peer-reviewed (SCC: Nordhaus 2019, Barrage & Nordhaus 2024; mortality elasticity: Chirakijja et al. 2024; marginal deadweight of taxation: Ballard, Shoven & Whalley 1985, Feldstein 1999), combined in a published-model framework (Tol 2023). The cost quantities themselves (AAF, Heritage, CEI) are think-tank estimates (C+ level), and no study computes a BCR for the GND, so B is the ceiling.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: no precedent anywhere; it would replace the US fossil-fuel energy system and add federal outlays of $5-9 trillion a year (AAF), and the resolution failed 0-57 in the Senate on 26 March 2019 (NBC News).
policies.who_benefits_reason: The energy core raises household electricity spending ~30% (Heritage 2019) and costs a typical household >$70,000 in year one in most states studied (CEI 2019); cheaper heating measurably saves lives among the poor and elderly (Chirakijja et al. 2024), so higher energy prices fall hardest on them.
policies.summary: The Green New Deal bundles a crash net-zero energy programme with a job guarantee, universal health care, worker-transition support and clean-energy money for poor countries; here every Western nation adopts it. Its outlays alone come to about a third of Western GDP, more than four times the most extra tax revenue the US could raise at the peak of its Laffer curve, so it cannot be financed without very large losses from taxation. Because only Western nations cut, part or all of the reduction leaks abroad: published estimates run from 12% to 130%, the last meaning world emissions rise.
policies.selected_by: H.Res.109, US Congress 2019
policies.evidence: The package is enormous. The American Action Forum puts its United States cost at $51 trillion to $93 trillion over 2020-2029, most of it health care and the job guarantee (Holtz-Eakin et al. 2019). The Heritage Foundation finds an output loss of over $15 trillion through 2040 and household electricity bills about 30% higher (Dayaratna and Loris 2019).
policies.ratio: Figures are billions of dollars a year for all Western nations. United States estimates are scaled by 1.99. Health-care outlays are transfers, worth $1 to recipients per $1.
policies.counter: The counter-case comes from three directions. Hänsel et al. (2020) update the Nordhaus model and find limiting warming below 2°C economically optimal, with carbon prices above $100 a tonne.

key_studies.authors: Tol, R.S.J.
key_studies.title: Costs and Benefits of the Paris Climate Targets
key_studies.venue: Climate Change Economics 14(4) (Special issue on reaching net zero by 2050)
key_studies.finding: Costs 3.8-5.6% of GDP in 2100 (optimal implementation) vs benefits 2.8-3.2% of GDP; Paris targets fail the cost-benefit test unless risk aversion high and discount rate low (implied BCR ~0.5-0.85).

key_studies.authors: Chirakijja, J.; Jayachandran, S.; Ong, P.
key_studies.title: Inexpensive Heating Reduces Winter Mortality
key_studies.finding: Quasi-experimental (gas vs electric heating areas x price shocks): the 42% fall in natural-gas prices relative to electricity in 2005-2010 averted about 11,000 US winter deaths per year; elasticity of all-cause mortality with respect to heating price ~0.03 (0.057 for winter deaths from relevant causes). Authors: policymakers should consider these effects when evaluating policies that affect home energy costs.

key_studies.authors: Nordhaus, W.D.
key_studies.title: Climate Change: The Ultimate Challenge for Economics (Nobel Prize Lecture)
key_studies.finding: DICE-2016R3 cost-benefit optimal SCC ~$36/tCO2 (2020). Used as low-end benefit per tonne.

key_studies.authors: Ballard, C. L.; Shoven, J. B.; Whalley, J.
key_studies.title: General Equilibrium Computations of the Marginal Welfare Costs of Taxes in the United States
key_studies.finding: Marginal welfare loss from raising an additional dollar of revenue is 34-48 cents (working-paper abstract); average 13-22 cents. The 0.48 figure is used for the deadweight component of the cost total.

key_studies.authors: Feldstein, M.
key_studies.title: Tax Avoidance and the Deadweight Loss of the Income Tax
key_studies.finding: A proportional rise in all personal income tax rates involves a deadweight loss of nearly two dollars per incremental dollar of revenue. Used for the deadweight of financing at both ends of the range.

key_studies.authors: Baird, S.; Friedman, J.; Schady, N.
key_studies.title: Aggregate Income Shocks and Infant Mortality in the Developing World
key_studies.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics 93(3):847-856 (near-final version: GWU IIEP WP 2010-7)
key_studies.finding: 1.7 million births in 59 developing countries: a one percent decrease in per capita GDP is associated with an increase in mortality of between 0.24 and 0.40 infants per 1,000 children born (abstract; Table 2).

quotes.text: GHG control policies in the industrialized countries actually lead to higher global emissions

policies.name: 15-Minute Cities
policies.why: Daily needs within a short walk is a fine planning idea, but this version turns C40's 'ambitious' consumption targets into mandates: no meat or dairy, three new clothing items a year, no private cars and one short-haul return flight every three years. The cost runs from about $1.9 to $8.0 trillion a year, including up to $1.9 trillion of lost productivity as 24-minute car commutes become 48 minutes by transit, against $0.3 to $0.8 trillion of benefits. Every dollar spent destroys between 92 cents and $12 of value, which makes this the worst policy on the list.
policies.grade_reason: No study prices this bundle and per-person caps on meat, dairy, clothing, flights and car ownership have never been applied at scale outside wartime rationing, so the ratio is built by scaling component estimates to the C40 network. The dominant cost terms come from peer-reviewed work but are extrapolations: Lusk & Norwood (2009) describe their 100% meat-removal figure as far outside the data, and Moody et al. (2021) is a stated-preference survey in four US metros.
policies.difficulty_reason: Hard: low-emission zones and building renovation rules have precedents (German LEZs, EU building directives), but binding personal caps on meat and dairy (0 kg), clothing (3 items a year), flights (one short-haul return trip every 3 years) and private car ownership (zero) have no modern peacetime precedent and would need a ration-tracking system; Defra's 2008 pre-feasibility study put even a simpler personal carbon allowance at GBP 1-2bn a year to run for the UK alone, and the scheme was not pursued.
policies.who_benefits_reason: Abbiasov et al. (2024) find that higher local-trip usage goes with higher experienced segregation for low-income residents; travel confined to the neighbourhood cuts access to city-wide job markets (Prud'homme & Lee 1999); LEZs and car bans force owners of older vehicles to replace them first (Wolff 2014).
policies.summary: The 15-minute city is a planning idea (daily needs within a short walk); this version adds the C40 'ambitious' consumption targets as mandates (no meat or dairy, 3 new clothing items a year, no private cars, one short-haul return flight every three years) plus low-emission zones and mandatory retrofits, targets C40 itself does not advocate. Priced at C40-city scale, the full cost runs from about $1.9 trillion to $8.0 trillion a year: lost consumer value from removing meat (Lusk & Norwood 2009) and private cars (Moody et al. 2021), retrofit spending, output lost from smaller aviation, tourism and trade, and up to $1.9 trillion of lost productivity as commutes that took 24 minutes by car take 48 by transit. Benefits from avoided emissions, cleaner and safer streets and fewer energy-wasting buildings come to about $0.3 trillion to $0.8 trillion a year.
policies.selected_by: C40 Cities 'Future of Urban Consumption' (city governments)
policies.evidence: No study prices this bundle, so the ratio is built from its parts. The largest costs are what people lose. Giving up meat at home would take compensation of about 13.0% of output (Lusk and Norwood 2009).
policies.ratio: The caps are rationing, so they are scored like price controls. Lost consumer value, lost output and induced deaths are subtracted from benefits. The cost base is the money spent to carry the rules out: administration plus mandatory retrofits.
policies.counter: The strongest counter-case is that the planning side of the 15-minute city pays. Outer London's "mini-Holland" programme "generates over £1bn health economic benefits for a programme cost of £100 m" (Aldred et al. 2024).

key_studies.authors: Abbiasov, T.; Heine, C.; Sabouri, S.; Salazar-Miranda, A.; Santi, P.; Glaeser, E.; Ratti, C.
key_studies.title: The 15-minute city quantified using human mobility data
key_studies.finding: GPS data from 40m US devices: median resident makes only 14% of consumption trips locally; higher local usage correlates with higher experienced segregation for low-income residents.

key_studies.authors: Lusk, J.L.; Norwood, F.B.
key_studies.title: Some Economic Benefits and Costs of Vegetarianism
key_studies.finding: Demand-system estimate (Raper et al. 2002 parameters): a 1% cut in at-home meat requires compensation of ~$0.16 per household per week; eliminating at-home meat requires ~$200.48 per household per week (~$10,500/yr, 1993 $), ~$1.3T a year for US households (~$1.8T in 2006 $). Authors call the 100% figure an extrapolation 'far outside the range of data'; excludes dairy and meals away from home.

key_studies.authors: Moody, J.; Farr, E.; Papagelis, M.; Keith, D.R.
key_studies.title: The value of car ownership and use in the United States
key_studies.finding: Discrete-choice experiments in Chicago, Dallas, Seattle and Washington DC: respondents need on average ~$11,197 to give up access to their own vehicle for one year, at least as much as the ~$9,000 average total private cost of ownership; more than half the value is non-use (flexibility, status).

key_studies.authors: Parry, I.W.H.; Walls, M.; Harrington, W.
key_studies.title: Automobile Externalities and Policies
key_studies.finding: Table 2 central marginal external costs (2005 $): local pollution 2.0, congestion 5.0, accidents 3.0 cents/mile (mileage-related sum 10.0); greenhouse 0.3, oil dependency 0.6 cents/mile; assumes 21 mpg.

key_studies.authors: Prud'homme, R.; Lee, C.-W.
key_studies.title: Size, Sprawl, Speed and the Efficiency of Cities
key_studies.finding: City productivity rises with the effective size of the labour market (jobs reachable within a given travel time); a 10% rise in average commuting speed raises labour productivity by ~2.9% (as quoted in Strong Towns 2017 from a report citing the paper); a 10% rise in job-home distance cuts effective labour-market size ~11.5%. 23 French cities. Used for the slower-travel component.

key_studies.authors: Wolff, H.
key_studies.title: Keep Your Clunker in the Suburb: Low-Emission Zones and Adoption of Green Vehicles
key_studies.finding: German LEZs reduced PM10 and sped up green-vehicle adoption; back-of-envelope 'health benefits of roughly 2 billion dollars have come at a cost of 1 billion dollars' for upgrading the vehicle fleet (BCR ~2).

quotes.text: need to be paid $11,197 to give up access to their privately owned vehicle for one year
the upfront investment costs are about twice the actual energy savings
generates over £1bn health economic benefits for a programme cost of £100 m
does not advocate for the wholesale adoption of these more ambitious targets
